And so everyone knew that they were at the furthest extreme of obduracy and of hostility to God and His Messenger, knowing all the while. **[Maʿārif]** explains why such an unusual test was needed: the normal way to settle a dispute is discussion, with each side presenting its arguments — and the Jews, knowing they could not win, shied away from that. So the Qurʾān proposed a method that calls for no learning and no reasoning, only a little effort of the tongue; and it predicted in advance that they would never dare. In their hearts they knew the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims stood for the truth and that they themselves were clinging to an abrogated law — so they feared that the moment they wished for death it would come for them, and they would be sent to the Fire. Their recalcitrance is itself an argument for Islam. **[Maʿārif]** adds a necessary qualification: the challenge was directed to the Jews who were the Prophet's ﷺ contemporaries, who denied him out of envy despite recognizing him — not to the Jews of every age.

**The prohibition of wishing for death.** **[Study Quran]** faces the apparent conflict with the ḥadīth, "Let none of you long for death because of an evil that befalls you; if he must say something, let him say: O God, give me life so long as life is good for me, and make me pass away if passing away is good for me." The reconciliation lies in the logic of the challenge itself: death is the only door to the felicity the Jews claim is theirs alone, so a person certain of that claim should rush to the door. The Prophet's ﷺ conditional supplication, by contrast, expresses the uncertainty of one's standing before God that Islam keeps alive — in the manner of 75:14-15, "no, man is a witness against himself," and of the knowledge of one's own sins. Like the claim to a numbered stay in the Fire (2:80; 3:24), the claim to a guaranteed and exclusive entry to Paradise betrays an excess of confidence; and the same challenge stands in 62:6, addressed to those who claim to be God's friends apart from other people. Some exegetes, it notes, read the passage as a species of *mubāhalah*, in which death is invoked upon whichever side, Muslim or Jew, is lying.

**Reflection.** The verse is a masterstroke of argument because it converts a boast into a request. Anyone can say the Garden belongs to him; only a man who believes it will ask to be let in. The refusal recorded in the next verse is the answer to every claim of privilege the Sūrah has been dismantling: a community that will not risk a single sentence in defence of its certainty has already been answered by its own silence. And the Prophet's ﷺ reported word — that had they wished for death they would have died and seen their seats in the Fire — makes the matter sharper still: the test was real, the danger was real, and knowing that, they still chose the world.


## 2:95

*"But they will never long for it, ever — because of what their hands have sent ahead; and God knows the wrongdoers."*

**Meaning.** The prediction attached to the challenge is itself the proof [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn]. **[Ṭabarī]** reads it as God's report of their hatred of death and their refusal to answer the call: they fear that if they were to wish it, the threat would fall on them and death would be upon them at once — and this because they know Muḥammad ﷺ is a messenger sent to them, and that he never told them anything that did not come true. They are on their guard against wishing for death precisely for fear that God's punishment should alight on them for the sins their hands have earned. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report from Ibn Isḥāq, had already given the challenge its plain sense — invoke death upon whichever of the two parties is more lying — and adds: they refused; and God says they will never wish it, *because of what their hands have sent ahead*: that is, because of the knowledge in their possession concerning him, and their disbelief in that knowledge. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk's report is blunter: they know that they are lying; had they been truthful they would have wished it, eager to hasten to God's honour. And Ibn Jurayj: the Jews were the swiftest of people in fleeing death, and would never wish for it.

**Language.** "What their hands have sent ahead" is a metaphor of the Arabs' speech: a man taken for a crime he committed is told, "this has come to you for what your hands have earned" — even if the offence was committed with his tongue or another limb; because most offences are committed by the hands, the whole class of them came to be attributed to the hands [Ṭabarī]. So here, what their hands sent ahead is their disbelief in God by defying His command to follow Muḥammad ﷺ, which they found written in the Torah and knew to be a prophet sent — and God attributes to their hands what their hearts harboured and their tongues uttered of envy toward Muḥammad ﷺ, aggression against him, denial of him and rejection of his mission, because the language of the Qurʾān is the language of the Arabs and knows no difficulty with it [Ṭabarī]. Ibn Jurayj's gloss gives the charge its simplest form: they knew that Muḥammad ﷺ was a prophet, and they concealed it. And "God knows the wrongdoers" is not a general conclusion but a specific one: God knows the wrong of the children of Ādam — Jew and Christian, and people of every other confession — and the wrong of the Jews in particular was their disbelief and their rejection of the messenger they had themselves been invoking for victory before he came [Ṭabarī].

**Context — the parallel.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** sets the challenge beside its Christian counterpart: the Messenger of God ﷺ summoned the delegation of Najrān to mutual invocation of curse after refuting them in a debate they fought with stubbornness, saying, "Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, and ourselves and yourselves, then let us pray and invoke the curse of God upon the liars" (3:61) — and when the Christians heard it, some said to one another, "By God, if you do that with this prophet, none of you will have an eye that blinks." They settled for peace and paid the *jizyah* in submission. He explains why such an invocation counts as a "wish": every just person wishes that God should destroy the unjust opponent who disputes with him, especially when he holds a clear proof for what he calls to; and the *mubāhalah* amounts to invoking death on the unjust party, because to disbelievers life is the greatest prize — the less so when they know the destination awaiting them. **[Study Quran]** makes the same point from the psychology of the verse: those who truly expected no destination but Paradise should long for death, and their awareness of their own sins — "no, man is a witness against himself" (75:14-15) — however deep or undetected, stops them.

**Reflection.** The verse treats silence as testimony. A test that requires nothing but a wish was refused, and the refusal is the verdict — **[Maʿārif]**'s added observation is decisive: if they had wished it in their hearts, they would have declared it with their tongues, since their victory lay precisely in such a declaration and it was the easiest way to refute the Prophet ﷺ; and the fact that no such declaration has come down to us, among a people whose opponents always outnumbered their adherents and would have trumpeted it, settles the matter. The Qurʾān's own word for their motive — what their hands sent ahead — is exact: they feared their own record, and the claim of exclusive Paradise came with an examination they knew they would fail.


## 2:96

*"And you will find them the greediest of people for life — and of those who associate others with God: one of them wishes he could be given a thousand years; and it will not remove him from the punishment that he should live long. And God sees what they do."*

**Meaning.** The verse turns from what they refuse to say to what they cannot hide [Ṭabarī] [Maʿārif]. **[Ṭabarī]** reads it as God's oath-sworn report to His Prophet ﷺ: you will find them — the Jews — the most intense of people in greed for the life of this world and the most averse to death, *more so than the polytheists*, as one says "he is the bravest of people, and than ʿAntarah." The reasoning is exact: they know what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter for their disbelief, so they hate death more than those who do not believe in the raising at all. Ibn ʿAbbās, in Ibn Isḥāq's report: the polytheist has no hope of a resurrection after death, so he loves long life; but the Jew has known what awaits him of shame in the Hereafter for what he has squandered of the knowledge he had. **[Qurṭubī]** records both readings of the sentence — either the comparison is with the polytheists (and the pronoun in "one of them" returns to the Jews), or the sentence closes at "for life" and a separate report begins about the Magians, whose blessing to one who sneezes means "may you live a thousand years," which is why **[Study Quran]** notes the Persian phrase commentators quote; while al-Ḥasan held the idolaters are the Arab polytheists, who crave long life because they do not believe in the raising. **[Study Quran]** also reports al-Rāzī's preference: "a thousand" is an idiom for "many," and he dismisses the identification with the Zoroastrians as too specific.

**Language.** *Zahzaha* is removal and displacement: to push a thing away so that it moves off [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] — as in the poet's petition, "O you who seize the soul from a body when death comes, and forgive the sin: keep me away from the Fire," and the lover's complaint that the darkness "does not shift." On *wa-mā huwa bi-muzahzihihi min al-ʿadhābi an yuʿammar*, **[Ṭabarī]** weighs the analyses and prefers one: *huwa* is a separating pronoun (*ʿimād*), and the sense is "what is he — any one of them — a remover of him from punishment by being given long life," the pronoun standing like the *huwa* in "what is he, standing, ʿAmr." Others took it as the pronoun of "long life": what is that living-on but a thing that will not remove him — and the infinitive "that he should be given life" stands in apposition to it. **[Qurṭubī]** reports the same options and registers a doubt about the *ʿimād*: its proper place is between two mutually dependent things, as in "if this is the truth" and "but they were the wrongdoers" — and he gives the alternative readings: *huwa* as the pronoun of "the one" (no one of them is removed from punishment by being given life), or as the pronoun of the matter and the affair, which Ibn ʿAṭiyyah also judges remote since the preserved usage is to explain it by a clause free of a preposition. He adds the word's finer edge: the thousand is specified because it is the limit of the reckoning's decade. And on "God sees what they do" — *baṣīr* in the Arabs' language is not merely one who sees but one who knows a thing thoroughly, as one says a man is *baṣīr* in medicine, or in law, or in the ways of men.

**āthār.** **[Qurṭubī]** brings a report from al-Nasāʾī on the opposite of this verse's verdict: from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ — "Whoever fasts a day in the way of God, God will keep his face seventy autumns away from the Fire." Against the long life that removes no one from punishment, the Qurʾān sets a short act that does. **[Study Quran]** adds al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's observation that a hypocrite is more covetous of the world than an idolater — perhaps because of a gnawing awareness of the consequences of his own actions; hypocrisy's certainty of salvation is a delusion whose underlying truth, that its owner's deeds preclude such certainty, is not quite hidden from him. **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes the maxim that this world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever, and draws the conclusion that the People of the Book wish to delay the Hereafter as long as possible — though they will surely meet what they flee.

**Reflection.** The verse is a test by appetite. A man's claim about the next world is measured by how tightly he holds this one; and the striking thing here is that those who believed least in the Hereafter clung to life less than those who insisted the Hereafter was theirs by right. **[Maʿārif]** puts the point exactly: the polytheists' love of life is no surprise, since for them physical life was the whole of the matter; but a people who acknowledge the next world, and imagine that its joys are reserved for them, and still wish above all others to remain where they are — their desire publishes what their doctrine denies; they knew, whatever they said aloud, what sort of account awaited them. And the closing clause leaves nothing outside the ledger: God sees what they do, and the thousand years for which they hoped could not have shifted them a hand's breadth from it.


## 2:97

*"Say: 'Whoever is an enemy to Jibrīl — he it is who brought it down upon your heart by God's leave, confirming what was before it, a guidance and glad tidings for the believers.'"*

**Meaning.** The verse answers a complaint about the postman [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** notes the commentators' consensus that it came down in reply to the Jews who claimed Jibrīl was their enemy and Mīkāʾīl their friend. Their reasoning, in the report **[Qurṭubī]** takes from al-Tirmidhī: no prophet ever came but an angel brought him the message from his Lord — so who is your companion? "Jibrīl," he said. "That is the one who descends with war and killing; he is our enemy. Had you said Mīkāʾīl, who descends with rain and mercy, we would have followed you." **[Jalālayn]** condenses the reply to a single dismissive clause — whoever is an enemy to Jibrīl, let him die of his rage — and then states what Jibrīl did: he brought the Qurʾān down upon your heart by God's leave, confirming what came before it of scriptures, a guidance out of error and glad tidings of Paradise for the believers. **[Saʿdī]** lays bare the self-contradiction: Jibrīl is purely a messenger; the One who commanded and sent him is God; the Book he brought agrees with the earlier Books and contradicts none of them; it carries complete guidance out of every kind of error and good tidings for whoever believes. So enmity to such a Jibrīl is disbelief in God and His signs and enmity toward God, His messengers and His angels — and their enmity is not to Jibrīl himself but to the truth he brings down from God to God's messengers. It therefore contains unbelief toward the Sender, the one sent, what was sent, and the one sent to.

**The occasion in full.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the exchange in the report of Ibn ʿAbbās (a chain the editor grades sound, also in Aḥmad): a group of Jews came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said, "Abū al-Qāsim, tell us of certain matters no one knows but a prophet," taking from him an oath that if he told them something they recognized, they would follow him. They asked four things: which food Isrāʾīl forbade himself before the Torah was sent down (camel flesh and its milk, from a vow in sickness); how the fluid of the man and the fluid of the woman determine male or female (whichever overcomes the other); that this ummī prophet's eyes sleep while his heart does not; and — "who is your guardian among the angels? On that we will follow you or part from you." He said: "My guardian is Jibrīl, and God never sent a prophet but he was his guardian." They said: "Then we part from you. Had your guardian been another of the angels, we would have followed you." He asked what prevented them from believing him; they said, "He is our enemy" — and God sent down: *whoever is an enemy to Jibrīl...* **[Ibn Kathīr]** adds the parallel from al-Bukhārī: when ʿAbd Allāh b. Salām heard the Prophet ﷺ had arrived in Madīnah, he came and asked three things no one knows but a prophet — the first portent of the Hour, the first meal of the people of Paradise, and why a child resembles its father or its maternal uncle. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Jibrīl has just told me the answers," and ʿAbd Allāh said, "He, among all the angels, is the enemy of the Jews" — after which the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse, gave the answers (a fire driving the people from east to west; the caudate lobe of the fish's liver; whichever discharge precedes), and ʿAbd Allāh bore witness. He then asked that the Jews be asked about him before he announced his Islam — and when they were asked, they called him the best of them and their master, and when he came out and professed, they called him the worst, exactly as he had feared. **[Study Quran]** gives the second account: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb visiting the Jews while they studied the Torah — he enjoyed the mutual confirmation of Torah and Qurʾān — and their telling him that they believed Muḥammad was a prophet but were "at peace" with some angels and not others; ʿUmar was astonished that one angel could be a friend and another a foe when both stood on either side of God, and when he returned to the Prophet ﷺ he was told the verse had already come down.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** notes that the pronoun in *fa-innahu* carries two senses: either "God sent Jibrīl down upon your heart," or "Jibrīl brought it down upon your heart." The heart is named specifically because it is the seat of reason and knowledge and the place where understanding is received — which is why the verse, he observes, indicates Jibrīl's rank and the blame due to his enemy. *Bi-idhni Allāh* is by His will and His knowledge. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reports the etymology from al-Bukhārī: ʿIkrimah said *Jibr*, *Mīk* and *Isrāf* all mean "worshipper," while *īl* means "God" — the pattern of the theophoric names, in which one element stays constant and the divine name varies, as in ʿAbd Allāh, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, ʿAbd al-Malik.

**Rulings & āthār — the Book on the heart.** **[Maʿārif]** warns against a serious misreading of "upon your heart," refuting the notion that only the meanings of the Qurʾān were revealed while its wording was supplied by the Prophet ﷺ: many verses of the Qurʾān itself name the Arabic language as the vehicle of revelation, and the heart perceives words as much as meanings — indeed the heart is the perceiving agent, while the ears and other organs are its instruments. In the state of revelation the outward senses are suspended and the heart receives the very words without the mediation of the ear; the analogy, imperfect as it is, is that in sleep one hears words and remembers them afterwards though the sense of hearing is dormant. It is, he says, intellectual dishonesty to build a doctrine on conjecture against what the Book says of itself. **[Study Quran]** adds al-Rāzī's reading of the motive beneath the excuse: at least part of the Jews' hostility to Jibrīl came from the fact that Muḥammad was not of Israel, so that invoking Gabriel's severity was a pretext masking displeasure that an Arab had been chosen; and to fault the angel is to fault the One who sent him. It notes the Jewish background in which Michael is Israel's prince and advocate (Daniel 10), the angel of snow and mercy, while Gabriel is the angel of fire and severity, the destroyer of Sodom — the soil, it suggests, in which a tradition of Gabriel as the Jews' enemy could grow, though in Jewish literature as a whole Gabriel is seen positively. And it points to the Qurʾān's own parallel statements that the revelation came down upon the Prophet's heart (26:194; 53:10-11), since the heart in the Qurʾānic anthropology is the seat of knowledge and understanding, not merely of sentiment.

**Reflection.** The passage is a small anatomy of how a pretext works. The objection is not to the message — the Book confirms what they have and guides and gives glad tidings — but to the messenger who carried it, and behind that to the choice of the One who sent him. **Saʿdī**'s chain of consequence is the verse's argument: to hate the angel is to hate the revelation he brings, and therefore the God who sent it, the Prophet who received it, and the truth itself. **[Study Quran]**'s citation of al-Rāzī completes the picture: the quarrel with an angel is often a quarrel, in disguise, with the human being God chose — and it is worth noticing that the man who asked his questions honestly, ʿAbd Allāh b. Salām, heard the same name and believed.


## 2:98

*"Whoever is an enemy to God, His angels, His messengers, and Jibrīl and Mīkāʾīl — then God is an enemy to the disbelievers."*

**Meaning.** The verse generalizes the preceding one and seals the matter [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** sets out the logic: those named here are God's friends and the people of His obedience; whoever takes a friend of God as an enemy has taken God as an enemy and crossed into open war with Him — and whoever is at war with God is at war with everyone who serves and is loyal to Him. So He says to the Jews who claimed that Jibrīl was their enemy and Mīkāʾīl their friend: whoever is an enemy to God and His angels and His messengers, and Jibrīl and Mīkāʾīl — the enemy of Jibrīl is an enemy of Mīkāʾīl and of every friend of God. **[Qurṭubī]** spells out what the two opposing enmities consist in: the servant's enmity to God is his disobedience and his avoidance of obedience and his hostility to God's friends; God's enmity to the servant is his punishment and the bringing upon him of the marks of that enmity.

**Language — why the two angels named.** **[Qurṭubī]** answers the obvious question: God had already mentioned His angels, so why single out Jibrīl and Mīkāʾīl by name? Two reasons — first, to honour them, as in "therein are fruits, and palms and pomegranates" (55:68), where the particular is named after the general; second, and more to the point here, because the Jews had named them, and the verse came down on their account: naming them was required so that they could not say, "We did not become enemies of God and all His angels," and the explicit mention refutes their attempt to make the hostility specific. **[Study Quran]** makes the same grammatical point about the structure of the verse: naming Jibrīl and Mīkāʾīl after "His angels" does not imply that the two are not angels, any more than 55:68 implies that dates and pomegranates are not fruit; and angels are themselves called messengers in the Qurʾān (10:21; 11:77). **[Qurṭubī]** also records the lexicographers' variations for the two names — for Jibrīl, ten dialectal forms, the Ḥijāzī *Jibrīl* the one Ḥassān b. Thābit uses, *Jabrīl* with a vowelled *jīm* the reading of al-Ḥasan and Ibn Kathīr, and forms with *ʾīl* appended; and he preserves the report that Ibn Kathīr said, "I saw the Prophet ﷺ in a dream reciting *Jabrīl* and *Mīkāʾīl*, so I shall never read them otherwise."

**āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** reports that the Prophet ﷺ asked the Jews: "I ask you by your Book which you recite — do you find that ʿĪsā son of Maryam gave glad tidings of me, that a messenger named Aḥmad would come to you?" They answered, "By God, we have found you in our book, but we hated you, because you make lawful our property and shed blood" — and then God sent down, "Whoever is an enemy to God and His angels and His messengers..." (the chain is graded weak by the editor, who notes the report's provenance). He also gives the report from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī Laylā: a Jew met ʿUmar and said, "The Jibrīl your companion mentions is our enemy," and ʿUmar recited this very verse at him — and the report adds that it came down on ʿUmar's tongue (its chain is broken; ʿUmar lived after it could have been revealed). **[Ibn Kathīr]** brings the ḥadīth from al-Bukhārī, from Abū Hurayrah: God, exalted, said, "Whoever takes a friend of Mine as an enemy has declared war on Me" — and draws the consequence: whoever takes one messenger as an enemy has taken all the messengers as enemies, for one who believes in one messenger is required to believe in them all, and one who rejects one has rejected them all, as in 4:150, where those who believe in some and reject others are declared disbelievers outright. His explanation of the angels' position is precise: Jibrīl did not choose his missions on his own; he descends only by the command of his Lord, as in 19:64, and the Qurʾān describes the trustworthy spirit bringing it down upon the Prophet's heart (26:192-194) — so the hostility is to the command, not to the servant who carries it. **[Study Quran]** adds the ḥadīth's other form, "Whoever is an enemy of God's friend, God makes war on him," as the verse's practical complement.

**Belief.** **[Saʿdī]** draws out why the passage is about *kufr* rather than mere dislike: enmity to Jibrīl, in the light of what Jibrīl does, is unbelief in God and His signs and enmity to God, His messengers and His angels. Their quarrel was never with the angel's person but with the truth he brings down from God to God's messengers — and so the enmity gathers in the One who sent, the one sent, the message sent, and the one it was sent to; which is why the verse closes not with "God is their enemy" but with "God is an enemy to the disbelievers," naming their condition rather than their persons, as **[Jalālayn]** observes: the substitution of "the disbelievers" for "them" is there to declare their standing.

**Reflection.** This verse turns a grudge into a doctrine and then shows the doctrine for what it is. The Jews of Madīnah had drawn a line through the angelic host and chosen whose messenger they would accept — and the Qurʾān answers that revelation is not a market in which one picks the courier one prefers. **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s rule is the hinge: to take one messenger as an enemy is to take them all, since the message is one and its source is one. And the verse's closing word is chosen with care: God is the enemy not of the men but of the disbelief that has made them so.


## 2:99

*"And We have sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieve in them except the iniquitous."*

**Meaning.** The charge that no evidence has come is answered with the evidence itself [Ṭabarī] [Maʿārif] [Study Quran]. **[Ṭabarī]** identifies the *āyāt bayyināt* concretely: the marks, clear and indicative of Muḥammad's ﷺ prophethood, contained in the Book God sent down to him — the hidden sciences of the Jews, the buried secrets of their reports and of their earliest forebears among the Children of Israel, and the news of what their own Books contained, which none knew but their rabbis and scholars, together with the rulings of their Torah that their ancestors and later generations had altered and substituted. God brought all of it out into the Book He revealed to His Prophet ﷺ; and in that there were clear signs for the one who dealt justly with himself and was not driven to destroy himself by envy and aggression. For it is in the nature of every sound disposition to affirm the truthfulness of one who brings what Muḥammad ﷺ brought — signs of that kind — without having learned them from any human being or taken any part of them from a man. Ibn ʿAbbās, in al-Ḍaḥḥāk's report: you recite it to them and inform them of it morning and evening, while you are in their eyes an unlettered man who has never read a book, and you tell them what is in their hands exactly as it stands — in that is a lesson and a clarification for them, and a proof against them, if they would only know.

**Occasion.** Ibn Ṣūriyā al-Fiṭyūnī said to the Messenger of God ﷺ, "Muḥammad, you have not brought us anything we recognize, and God has not sent down upon you any clear sign that we should follow you by it" — and God sent down this verse [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. **[Qurṭubī]** notes simply that it is the answer to that man's words, and **[Jalālayn]** records the same occasion in brief and adds the sting of the ending: these men have indeed disbelieved in them — the verse is not merely a general statement but a verdict on the speakers.

**Belief & reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** frames the verse by its two effects: guidance for whoever seeks guidance, and the establishment of proof against whoever is obstinate — signs that have reached such a pitch of clarity and indication of the truth that no one refuses them but one who has left God's command behind, departed from His obedience, and grown arrogant with the furthest arrogance. **[Maʿārif]** makes the same point from the other direction: the objection that no recognizable sign had come is false on its face, since God had sent down clear signs of the prophethood which the Jews themselves understood perfectly well; therefore their denial was not a matter of insufficient recognition but of habitual disobedience — and it is a general rule that no one denies such evidence except those who are willful and stubborn in their disobedience. **[Study Quran]** pictures the signs in a broader way: the marks of Muḥammad's prophethood in his person, his qualities and the knowledge he possessed, which, the commentators say, ought to have been apparent to any believing Jew. The verse is thus not an argument but an exposure: the verdict is already given in what they are looking at, and the only thing left to explain is the eye that will not see it — which the word *fāsiqūn* supplies: not those who lack evidence, but those who have broken out of the command of their Lord.


## 2:100

*"Is it not so that whenever they make a covenant, a party of them cast it aside? No — most of them do not believe."*

**Meaning.** The inquiry is a rebuke, and its form is the point [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Jalālayn]. **[Ṭabarī]** reads it as: is it their custom that every time they give their Lord a covenant — binding themselves again and again to work by what is in the Torah — a party of them throws it away and breaks it? He reproaches them for that, and through them reproaches their descendants, who walked their road in some of what had been taken from them of covenant and pledge concerning belief in Muḥammad ﷺ: they disbelieved and denied what the Torah contained of his description and attributes. **[Saʿdī]** puts the surprise in the foreground: the verse conveys astonishment at how many pledges they made and how little patience they had in keeping them — *kullamā* carries repetition, so that the very existence of a covenant was the occasion of its breach. Why? The answer is in the verse's own last words: because most of them do not believe; their lack of faith was what obliged them to break their pledges; had their faith been true they would have been like those of whom God says, "among the believers are men who were true to what they pledged to God" (33:23).

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** reports the grammarians' dispute over *a-wa-kullamā*: Sibawayh held the *wāw* is a conjunction with the interrogative *alif* placed before it — as the *alif* enters upon *fa* in "is it the judgement of the age of ignorance they seek?" (5:50) and upon *thumma* elsewhere; al-Akhfash said the *wāw* is superfluous; al-Kisāʾī held the word is *aw*, its *wāw* given a vowel for ease; and some read *aw* with a quiescent *wāw*, giving the sense of *bal* — as when a man threatens "I will strike you," and the other replies, "or God will suffice." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah called all this forced and endorsed Sibawayh; and **[Ṭabarī]** agrees, adding a principle he had already established: it is not permissible for a letter in God's Book to carry no meaning — which disposes of the view that the *wāw* or *fāʾ* of *a-wa-kullamā* and *a-fa-kullamā* are meaningless additions. *Kullamā* is an adverb of time here, and *nabadha* is, in the Arabs' tongue, to throw away — whence the foundling is called *al-manbūdh* [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī].

**Occasion.** **[Ṭabarī]** and **[Qurṭubī]** both give the report of Ibn ʿAbbās: when the Messenger of God ﷺ was sent, Mālik b. al-Ṣayf — also called Ibn al-Ḍayf — said, in the face of what had been taken from them of covenant and what God had charged them with concerning him: "By God, He made no covenant with us about Muḥammad ﷺ, and took no pledge from us for him!" And God sent down: *is it not so that whenever they make a covenant, a party of them cast it aside? No — most of them do not believe.* **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Study Quran]** give the other construction of the occasion: that the Jews had pledged that if Muḥammad came out they would believe in him and stand with him against the polytheists of the Arabs — and when he was sent, they disbelieved; and **[Study Quran]** adds that for others it refers to their betraying the Prophet ﷺ by breaking their alliance with him and siding with Quraysh, while quoting al-Rāzī's judgement that the meaning is not restricted to any particular incident.

**Belief.** **[Maʿārif]** distinguishes two offences in the passage and keeps them distinct: to go against a pledge is a sin and a transgression, but to have no faith at all in the pledge one gives to God is outright unbelief — and it is that second thing the verse's closing clause names. He also notes the precision of "a party of them": the Qurʾān does not say all the Jews broke the pledge, for some fulfilled it, so much so that many eventually accepted Muḥammad ﷺ as a true prophet and joined the Muslims. The door left open is part of the verse's meaning, not an accident of its wording.

**Reflection.** The verse is about a pattern rather than an incident, and the interrogative form exposes it: not "they broke a covenant" but "is this what they do *every time*?" A community whose word dissolves on contact with its interests has diagnosed itself, and **[Saʿdī]**'s reading is the one the verse invites: the cause is not weakness of memory but absence of faith — for the man who truly believes in the One to whom he has given his word does not weigh the pledge against his advantage. The line from 2:93, "we hear and we disobey," runs straight through this verse; and the remnant named at the end of the covenant passage — "all but a few of you" — is named again here, in the party that did not cast it aside.


## 2:101

*"And when there came to them a messenger from God, confirming what was with them, a party of those who were given the Book cast the Book of God behind their backs, as though they did not know."*

**Meaning.** The habit of 2:100 is now given its latest and most damning instance [Ṭabarī] [Maʿārif]. **[Ṭabarī]** identifies the actors as the rabbis and scholars of the Jews, and the messenger as Muḥammad ﷺ, who confirms the Torah and is confirmed by it. What they cast behind their backs is *the Book of God* — the Torah — after having acknowledged it, and they did so out of envy and aggression. The phrase is a proverb of the Arabs for a man who turns away from a matter that had been on his mind: "he has put this affair behind his back," meaning he turned aside and went away. Al-Suddī gives the scene concretely: when Muḥammad ﷺ came, they confronted him with the Torah and disputed with him by it — and the Torah and the Qurʾān agreed, so they threw the Torah away and took up the book of Āṣif and the magic of Hārūt and Mārūt, which did not agree with the Qurʾān. **[Qurṭubī]** records the same report and the range of the phrase's reference: the Torah is meant, because their disbelief in the Prophet ﷺ and their denial of him is itself a casting away of it; others allowed that the Book of God here might mean the Qurʾān; and al-Shaʿbī said the Book was before them and they read it, but they cast away acting upon it. Sufyān b. ʿUyaynah described the casting in an image that has stayed: they bound it in silk and brocade and adorned it with gold and silver, and did not make lawful its lawful or forbid its forbidden — that is the casting away.

**"As though they did not know."** The clause is the verse's verdict, and every commentator reads it as the opposite of ignorance in fact [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. **[Ṭabarī]** explains it as God's report that they denied the truth in full knowledge of it and opposed His command knowing that it was binding on them; Qatāda put it as: the people knew, but they corrupted their knowledge, denied it, disbelieved and concealed. **[Qurṭubī]** adds the grammatical point that the phrase likens them to those who do not know because they did the deed of the ignorant — so that the wording itself establishes that they disbelieved knowingly. And **[Maʿārif]** draws the consequence for their own law: the Torah had already given glad tidings of the coming of the Prophet ﷺ, and when he came with all the signs it had indicated and confirming their Book, they refused him; in doing so they were denying the Torah itself and behaving as though they knew nothing of the prophecy or of the Torah being a Book of God — guilty of unbelief even by the Torah's measure. **[Study Quran]** notes the same logic of the phrase: the party might be the learned Jews specifically, or all who take the Torah as their book and disregard what it says; and while "the Book of God" could in principle be the Qurʾān, the mention of "those who were given the Book" indicates the Torah is meant — and specifically its confirmation of the Prophet's mission, for which, as 2:99 said, the signs were clear.

**The law beneath the verse.** **[Saʿdī]** reads the passage as a demonstration of a general rule of God's dealing with people — one that sets up the long excursus on magic that follows: whoever abandons what would benefit him, when he is able to benefit by it, is tried with occupation in what harms him. Whoever abandons the worship of the Merciful is tried with the worship of idols; whoever abandons love of God, fear of Him and hope in Him is tried with love, fear and hope directed at other than Him; whoever does not spend his wealth in obedience to God spends it in the obedience of Satan; whoever abandons humility before his Lord is tried with humility before slaves; and whoever abandons the truth is tried with falsehood. These Jews, having cast away the Book of God, followed what the devils recited — and the verses that follow describe what they took up in its place.

**Reflection.** The verse is about a book made into an object. **[Qurṭubī]**'s Sufyān gives the definitive picture: a Torah wrapped in silk, ornamented with gold, recited and displayed, with neither its permissions permitted nor its prohibitions prohibited — ornament without authority, reverence without obedience. And the last clause strips away the last defence: no one can plead that it was never explained to him. The Qurʾān will say of them elsewhere that they recognize the Prophet as they recognize their own sons (2:146); here it says that they put the evidence behind their backs and pretended not to know. The pretence is the crime, and the verse names it in the language of knowledge, because the alternative — that they really did not know — would be an excuse.


## 2:102

*"And they followed what the satans recited against the kingdom of Solomon. Solomon did not disbelieve, but the satans disbelieved, teaching people sorcery — and what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Hārūt and Mārūt. Yet these two taught no one until they had said, 'We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.' And from them people learned that by which they separate a man from his wife — though they harm no one by it except by God's leave. And they learned what harms them and does not benefit them, and they knew that whoever buys it has no share in the Hereafter. Evil is that for which they sold their souls, had they but known."*

**Meaning.** The next clause after "they cast the Book of God behind their backs" is what they picked up instead [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** names the followers as those rabbis of the Jews, and what they followed as the sorcery the satans used to recite "against the kingdom of Solomon" — that is, in Solomon's time. They rejected the Book they knew to be from God, broke the covenant they had given to work by it, and preferred the magic of the devils: which is the manifest loss and error. **[Saʿdī]** sets the passage in the framework he had just laid down: having cast away the Book, they were tried with what harms them. And he draws the theology the verse teaches about magic's power: it has a real effect, harming only by God's leave — and *idhn* has two kinds, the cosmic decree that attaches to God's will, as here, and the legislative permission, as in the previous verse's "he brought it down upon your heart by God's leave." From this, he says, it follows that causes, however strong, remain subject to God's decree and are not independent — a point of consensus among the community except the Qadariyyah in the matter of God's servants' acts. Then, going on through the verse: magic is pure harm, with no benefit to religion or to worldly life, unlike wine and gambling, of which God said that they contain great sin and some benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit; the forbidden things are either pure harm or their evil outweighs their good, just as the commanded things are either pure benefit or their good outweighs their harm. And "they knew" — the Jews knew that whoever buys sorcery has no share in the Hereafter: their deed was not ignorance but the choice of this world over the next; evil is what they sold their souls for, *had they but known*.

**The two angels, and Solomon's exoneration.** **[Jalālayn]** gives the story as the commentators told it: the devils buried their books of sorcery beneath Solomon's throne when his kingdom was taken from him; or they used to eavesdrop and add fabrications to what they heard and pass them to the priests, who compiled them, until people began to say the jinn know the unseen. Solomon collected the books and buried them; when he died the devils showed people where they were, and they dug them out and said, "Your kingdom was only thanks to what is here" — taking to the learning of them and abandoning the scriptures of their prophets. Therefore, when the Jews said, "Look at this Muḥammad: he counts Solomon among the prophets when he was only a sorcerer," God cleared him: "Solomon did not disbelieve" — he did not practise magic, for magic is unbelief — "but the satans disbelieved, teaching people sorcery." **[Ṭabarī]** gives al-Suddī's version of the same narrative at length: the satans ascending to the eavesdropping stations, adding seventy lies to every true word, the soothsayers and the books written from them, Solomon's ban and his confinement of the books in a chest buried under his throne, the devil disguised as a man leading a group to the "treasure" after his death, the cry that Solomon ruled humans, jinn and birds only by this magic, and the spread of the charge until the Children of Israel took up the books and used them to dispute with the Prophet ﷺ.

**Were Hārūt and Mārūt angels?** **[Ibn Kathīr]** raises the question directly. Al-Ṭabarī, he reports, held that the two angels referred to in the verse are Jibrīl and Mīkāʾīl, that God was denying the sorcerers' claim that magic was sent down by them, and that Hārūt and Mārūt were two ordinary men who taught magic to the people of Babylon — "and this explanation is not plausible," Ibn Kathīr adds. Many of the Salaf held instead that Hārūt and Mārūt were angels who came down from heaven to earth and did what the verse says; al-Qurṭubī transmitted that from ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, al-Suddī and al-Kalbī. Against the objection that angels are immune from sin, Ibn Kathīr answers from God's eternal knowledge of what they would do, as with Iblīs — and notes that what they did was less than what Iblīs did. **[Qurṭubī]** notes the alternative reading *al-malikayn*, "the two kings," which is how those who take them to be men read the word — but the reading *malakayn*, angels, is the one the reports about Hārūt and Mārūt fit. **[Study Quran]** steps back from the details: on no other verse, it says, do commentaries contain material so startlingly incongruous with the Qurʾānic whole — including the legend of the two angels sent down and tempted by a woman, Venus, made drunk and led into sin; most or all of these legends are rejected by major classical commentators such as Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī. It proposes that the verse is well interpreted without them: Solomon, given power over wind and jinn (21:81-82), never denied the true source of his power and never used it for evil such as separating a man from his wife; and the two angels taught people how to read and manipulate the hidden dimensions of the cosmos for wisdom, healing and goodness — knowledge that is a double-edged sword, hence their warning against striking a bargain for such powers. The one who strikes that bargain, it notes, would become famous in the West as Faust: the man who sells his soul for unworthy worldly gain, which is precisely the verse's last image. Spiritually, the passage has been read as turning from the heart and spirit toward the lower ego — from the "Solomon of the spirit" to the satans of the soul — and in some currents of Islamic esoteric tradition the sorcery mentioned here is astrology, born in Babylon, resting on correspondences between heaven and earth.

**The trial.** **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Ibn Kathīr]** preserve the reports of how the two warned: they taught no one until they said, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve." Ibn ʿAbbās, in one report, describes the outcome: the man who insisted would be sent to a place where Satan met him and taught him, and when he learned, the light of faith left him and he saw it shining in the sky, and he cried out in grief at what he had done. **[Maʿārif]** explains the design of the whole episode, following Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī: ignorant people had confused the astonishing effects of magic with the miracles of prophets, taking magicians for holy men; to root out that misguidance God sent down two angels to Babylon to explain magic's true nature and forms, so that people would distinguish it from prophetic miracles and avoid both the magicians and the practice. The task was not given to prophets for two reasons: the need of the hour was to establish the distinction between prophets and magicians, and the prophets were a party to the dispute, so a third party had to arbitrate; and the distinction could not be drawn without citing the very formulas used, and while merely reporting heretical speech is not heresy, God did not wish His prophets to be even the indirect occasion of the practice. So the angels taught, with a pledge and a warning — like a teacher of philosophy who trains a student to answer the philosophers' doubts, having taken his pledge not to misuse what he learns; if the student breaks faith, the teacher is not to blame. **[Qurṭubī]** adds the juristic frame: the craft's effects are God's creation at the occurrence of the sorcerer's act, as satiety is created with eating and thirst is quenched with drinking — the sorcerer is not an independent agent; the Muslims are unanimous that magic can never produce the great signs of the messengers, such as splitting the sea, reviving the dead or making the dumb beast speak, and Abū Bakr b. al-Ṭayyib said that only consensus prohibits this, otherwise they would have allowed it; and the difference between magic and miracle is that magic can issue from many people and be repeated and learned, while the miracle cannot be opposed or imitated, and is tied to a claim of prophethood and a challenge.

**Reflection.** This is the Sūrah's answer to a community that had the Book in its hands and traded it for formulas. The verse is careful in what it concedes: sorcery is real, it can separate a husband from his wife, and it harms by God's leave — it is not waved away as illusion, and it is not inflated into an independent power. Then it delivers its verdict with one contrast: Solomon, to whom the jinn and the wind were subjected, is cleared of the charge, while those who accused him are the ones teaching people to sell their souls for a thing that cannot profit them. And the two angels' warning — *we are only a trial; do not disbelieve* — is the strangest sort of pedagogy in the Qurʾān: knowledge handed over with the instruction not to use it as it is designed to be used, so that the very shapes of the danger are known, and the blame for what follows lies wholly with the one who took the bargain.


## 2:103

*"And had they believed and been reverent, a reward from God would have been better — if they but knew."*

**Meaning.** The verdict on the bargain is stated once more, from the other side [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn]. **[Ṭabarī]** supplies the subject the verse leaves implicit: had those who learned from the two angels that by which they separate a man from his wife believed — affirming God, His Messenger and what he brought from their Lord — and been reverent, fearing their Lord's punishment and so obeying Him by performing His obligations and avoiding His prohibitions, then God's recompense to them for that faith and reverence would have been better for them than the magic and what they gained by it. The clause "if they but knew" removes from them the knowledge of what God's reward actually amounts to; that is, they do not know the measure of His recompense for obedience. **[Qurṭubī]** reads *wa-ittaqaw* with reference to the immediate subject: if they had feared *magic* — stayed clear of it — and **[Saʿdī]** adds the test of what the phrase means: they would not have done what they did had their knowledge been of the kind that bears fruit in action.

**Language.** *Al-mathūbah* is the reward, and its root is return: a thing *thāba* to you when it comes back; to reward a man is to return to him a substitute for his gift or his deed — so God's recompense is what comes back to a person for what he has done [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. The grammatical point behind the verse's shape is whether *law* has an answer: some Baṣrans held the answer is omitted, being understood from the sense — *la-uthībū*, "they would have been rewarded" — the mention of the recompense making the verb unnecessary; others held that *lamathūbatun* is itself the answer, and that *law* is answered with the recompense though it is reported in the past-tense form, since *law* and *la-in* are near neighbours: both are conditions, and both have as their answer faith, so each was given the other's answer [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** reports al-Akhfash's view of the same, and adds al-Mubarrad's principle: *law* cannot take a jussive answer, because the function of conditional particles is to turn the past into the future sense, and *law* does not do this. **[Jalālayn]** notes that the *lām* of *la-mathūbatun* is the *lām* of an oath, and that the subject of the sentence is *mathūbah*, its predicate "from God... better."

**Belief.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gathers the legal consequence that the whole passage was made to carry. Ibn Jurayj said: no one dares practise magic except a disbeliever — for the *fitnah* the angels spoke of is trial and free choice. The scholars who hold that learning magic is unbelief took this verse as their proof, together with the ḥadīth Abū Bakr al-Bazzār recorded from ʿAbdullāh, on a sound chain: "Whoever comes to a soothsayer or a sorcerer and believes him in what he says has disbelieved in what was revealed to Muḥammad ﷺ." And he adds a ḥadīth from Muslim, from Jābir, on the sort of harm magic does to the nearest bonds: "Satan sets his throne upon the water and sends out his raiders among people; the closest to him in rank is the one who causes the greatest trial. One of them comes and says, 'I did not leave so-and-so until he said such and such' — and Iblīs says, 'No, by God, you have done nothing.' Another comes and says, 'I did not leave him until I separated him from his wife' — and he draws him near, embraces him, and says, 'Excellent are you.'" **[Study Quran]** puts the verse in one line: God's recompense is better than what they purchased with their souls.

**Reflection.** The verse is the Sūrah's recurring comparison rendered in arithmetic: what God gives for faith and restraint against what magic sells and what it costs. It is characteristic of the Qurʾān that the alternative to the forbidden thing is never nothing; the passage does not merely say "do not buy sorcery" — it says that the same effort, spent on faith and reverence, purchases something better. And the closing "if they but knew" is not a taunt but a diagnosis: they possessed the information and not the knowledge that moves a man, which is why the very next thing the Sūrah does is turn to those who have no room for such bargaining at all.


## 2:104

*"O you who believe, do not say 'Rāʿinā,' but say 'Unẓurnā,' and listen; and for the disbelievers there is a painful punishment."*

**Meaning.** The verse teaches the believers a change of vocabulary, and the reason for it lies in what the Jews had made of the word [Jalālayn] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the sense of *rāʿinā* first: in the language it is *irʿanā wa-l-narʿak* — watch over us and we shall watch over you, look after us and we shall look after you — from *murāʿāt*, mutual care; or it may come from *arʿinā samʿak*, "lend us your ear, give us your hearing." And he gives Ibn ʿAbbās's report of how the address was used: the Muslims used to say it to the Prophet ﷺ in the sense of request and desire — "turn to us" — but in the Jews' tongue it was a curse, meaning "hear, may you never hear." They seized the opportunity: "We used to curse him secretly; now we shall curse him openly." They would address him with it and laugh among themselves — until Saʿd b. Muʿādh, who knew their language, heard it and said, "God's curse be upon you! If I hear any one of you say that to the Prophet ﷺ, I will strike off his neck." They answered, "Do you not say it yourselves?" — and then the verse came down and the believers were forbidden it, so that the Jews would not use it as a screen for the meaning they intended. **[Ibn Kathīr]** sets the same incident beside 4:46, where their speech is described as twisting words from their places and saying *rāʿinā* "with a twist of their tongues and a slander against the religion," and notes the parallel with the greeting the Jews used — *al-sāmu ʿalaykum*, "death be upon you" — which is why the Muslims were taught to reply only, "and upon you." God, he says, forbade the believers to imitate the disbelievers in speech or in deed.

**Language — what Rāʿinā was.** **[Ṭabarī]** collects the reports and then gives his own ruling. Some held it was a word the Arabs themselves found ugly, derived from *al-ruʿūnah*, foolishness and slackness; some that it was a Jāhiliyyah word of the Anṣār which God forbade them to keep using to His Prophet ﷺ; Abū al-ʿĀliyyah said the polytheists of the Arabs used to say to one another, "arʿinī samʿak!"; Ibn Jurayj called it the word of the mocker — and the believers, he said, were forbidden to mock what Muḥammad ﷺ said. Al-Suddī gives the incident with a name: a Jewish man of Banū Qaynuqāʿ named Rufāʿah b. Zayd b. al-Tābūt used to come to the Prophet ﷺ and say, "arʿinī samʿak — and hear without hearing," and some Muslims, taking it that prophets were honoured in this fashion, began to say it, along with "hear, without humiliation" — and 4:46 was sent down about it. **[Ṭabarī]** strongly prefers a different account of the prohibition: God disliked it as an address for His Prophet, exactly as the Prophet ﷺ told people not to say "the noble vine" (*al-karm*) but "the stock" (*al-ḥabalah*). He insists, as **[Study Quran]** reports, that it was not a Hebrew curse that led to the ban, since it was the believers who were commanded to drop it and they would not have taken up a phrase they did not understand; what the verse forbade is the word they were using, and the command to say *unẓurnā* supplies a word with the same purpose and no such liability. **[Qurṭubī]** notes the same refinement in the choice: from a vocabulary full of options, the believers were told to choose the best word and the gentlest meaning — *unẓurnā*, look at us. **[Study Quran]** adds that *unẓurnā* can elsewhere mean "wait for us" (57:13), but here it means only seeking the Prophet's attention respectfully, and that the command to "listen" carries the sense of obey; it also connects the verse with 24:63, where the Prophet's call among the believers is not to be treated like their calling to one another — an admonition against undue familiarity.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** derives two standing principles from the verse. First, the avoidance of ambiguous expressions that carry an innuendo of diminishment or insult — and out of this he brings the question of slander by innuendo (*qadhf bi-l-taʿrīḍ*), which in his school incurs the fixed penalty, against Abū Ḥanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī and their companions, who held that innuendo is open to more than one meaning and the penalty falls away with doubt. Second, the blocking of means (*sadd al-dharāʾiʿ*): the lawful is forbidden when it becomes a path to the unlawful — precisely what happened here, since the believers' word was innocent in itself but gave the Jews cover for their curse. **[Saʿdī]** states the same rule from the verse's shape: God forbade something permissible because it had become a means to the forbidden, and the passage is a lesson in manners — the use of words that admit nothing but good, the avoidance of obscenity and of phrases that carry a possibility of the improper; and *unẓurnā* is precisely such a word, sufficient for the purpose with no risk attached. **[Maʿārif]** draws the point to its edge: the verse labels the insolent Jews *kāfirūn*, which means that intentional disrespect toward a prophet — even indirectly, even through a word that looks harmless — is unbelief. And **[Jalālayn]** notes the last clause as it stands: the painful chastisement is for the disbelievers — that is, the Fire — the men whose mockery this verse has just exposed.

**Reflection.** This is a verse about the ethics of language, and about the responsibility of the innocent for what their words can be made to mean. The believers had done nothing wrong; they had simply kept a word their neighbours had poisoned. God's answer is not to defend them but to move them: give the word up, say the other one, and listen. **[Qurṭubī]**'s legal reading — that a permitted thing may be forbidden because of what it opens onto — is the verse's most durable legacy, and its practical test is uncomfortable: it asks what use an enemy can make of my speech, not merely what I intended by it.

## 2:105

*"Neither those who disbelieve among the People of the Book nor the idolaters wish that any good should be sent down to you from your Lord; and God singles out for His mercy whom He wills — and God is of tremendous bounty."*

**Meaning.** The verse uncovers what lies under the professions of goodwill that the previous passage had already exposed [Ṭabarī] [Maʿārif]. **[Ṭabarī]** unpacks the wish: *mā yawaddu* is *mā yuḥibbu* — they do not love, do not wish, that there should come down upon you any of the good that was with God and that He sent down to you; the idolaters and the disbelievers of the People of the Book wished that God had not sent down the Furqān and the rulings and signs He revealed to Muḥammad ﷺ at all — and this only out of envy and aggression toward the believers. From this, he says, the verse carries a clear indication: God is warning the believers against leaning on their enemies among the People of the Book and the idolaters, or listening to their talk, or accepting anything they bring in the guise of advice — since God has now shown them the resentment and envy that these people conceal, whatever they profess with their tongues.

**God singles out whom He wills.** **[Qurṭubī]** records ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib's gloss: "singles out for His mercy" means by His prophethood, and He singled out Muḥammad ﷺ with it; others said the mercy is the Qurʾān, and others that it is general, covering every kind of mercy God has granted His servants in earlier and later times — for *raḥmah* in God's dealings with His servants is His favouring them and His pardoning them. **[Ṭabarī]** reads it as the choosing of a messenger: God singles out whom He wills with prophethood and mission, sending him to whom He wills of His creatures and granting faith to whom He loves — the choosing being the setting apart of some from others; and He made His message and His guidance mercy to their recipients, so that He might bring them to His pleasure and love, and to success in the Garden. Then the verse's last words: everything of good that servants attain in religion or worldly life comes from God in the first instance, by His favour and without their deserving it — and in that, **[Ṭabarī]** says, there is a pointed address to the People of the Book: the guidance given to Muḥammad ﷺ and the believers is a favour from God, and His blessings are not reached by wishing — they are gifts He gives to whom He wills of His creatures.

**Context.** **[Maʿārif]** supplies the social setting: some Jews used to assure the Muslims of their sincerity and pretend they would have welcomed the Muslims' receiving from God doctrines and commandments better than their own, so that they too could accept them — but unfortunately, they hinted, Islam did not appear to be better. The Qurʾān refutes the claim to be well-wishers, and declares that the disbelievers, Jews and associators alike, are so jealous of the Muslims that they cannot wish them any blessing whatever. And the jealousy can do the Muslims no harm, because God is bountiful and all-powerful, sending His special blessing on whom He chooses. He also notes the two claims that lay behind the posture — that Judaism was better, and that they were well-wishers — and observes that neither could be established: the first was an empty assertion, and in any case the difference between Islam and earlier religions is not a matter of comparison but of abrogation, since God sent Islam to supersede the earlier laws. **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse as one more disclosure of the motive that has driven the whole passage: they resent that God should single you out with His grace — and that is envy, not argument. **[Jalālayn]** keeps the reference precise: the disbelievers of the People of the Book and the Arab idolaters do not wish that any good — any inspiration — be revealed to you from your Lord; but God singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and God is of abounding bounty. **[Study Quran]** identifies that mercy as the revelation and its wisdom, bestowed through the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ, so that the singling out refers to the gift of prophethood to him rather than to someone more agreeable to the idolaters or the People of the Book — with 3:179 and 40:15 in the background.

**Reflection.** The verse closes a long passage of argument with a statement about motive, and it does something important with the doctrine of grace: it takes a fact the enemies resent — that God chooses — and makes it the ground of the believers' confidence rather than an occasion for dispute. The envious cannot in any case prevent the descent of the blessing they resent [Saʿdī]; and the bounty, being a gift and not a wage, cannot be acquired by wishing or by descent, which is precisely what the long passage about covenant, book and lineage has been saying in a hundred ways. The verse also carries its practical warning, and **[Ṭabarī]** draws it plainly: a people whose private wish is that you had never received guidance should not be your advisers in religion, however courteous their words.


## 2:106

*"Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or its like. Do you not know that God is powerful over all things?"*

**Meaning.** The verse answers a taunt, and in answering it lays down one of the great principles of the Sharīʿah [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif] [Saʿdī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the occasion: when the Jews envied the Muslims their turning toward the Kaʿbah and used it to attack Islam, saying, "Muḥammad commands his companions one thing and then forbids it to them; this Qurʾān can only be from himself — which is why some of it contradicts some of it," God sent down "and when We replace a sign with another sign" (16:101) and this verse. **[Maʿārif]** reconstructs the argument they were making, because the verse's reply is unintelligible without it: if everything God reveals is good, why should one ruling be replaced by another? One of the two must be good and the other evil, and no revelation can be evil — therefore the Qurʾān cannot be revealed. The reply is that abrogation is not the replacement of good with evil: everything God reveals to His prophets is good, and what is abrogated is as good as what abrogates it. **[Saʿdī]** states the principle in the briefest form: *naskh* is transfer — the moving of those under obligation from one legislated ruling to another, or to its being lifted altogether; the Jews denied that it could occur though it is written in their own Torah, so their denial was unbelief and pure caprice. And the verse's ending is the answer to that denial: to find fault with abrogation is to find fault with God's dominion and power — "do you not know that God is powerful over all things?"

**The word and the readings.** In the Arabs' speech *naskh* has two senses [Qurṭubī]: transferring, as when a book is copied from another — and on that sense the whole Qurʾān is "copied" from the Preserved Tablet and brought down to the lowest heaven, though that is not what the verse intends; and abolishing, removing, which is intended here, and which divides into the annulment of a thing without replacement and its annulment with something put in its place. **[Study Quran]** adds that the root *n-s-kh* appears only four times in the Qurʾān: here; at 7:154, of the inscription of Mūsā's tablets; at 22:52, where God effaces what Satan casts; and at 45:29, of the recording of people's deeds; and it notes the imagery the lexicographers give — the erasure the sun performs on a shadow, the wind on dust, old age on youth. **[Ṭabarī]** collects what the early authorities said of *mā nansakh*: Ibn ʿAbbās — "whatever verse We replace"; the companions of Ibn Masʿūd and Mujāhid — "We keep its writing and change its ruling"; and others — "We remove it." On the second verb the readings themselves carry the meaning: *nunsihā*, "We cause it to be forgotten," with a reading from ʿAbd Allāh b. Masʿūd's codex *mā nunsika aw nansakhā* — "whatever We cause you to forget or abrogate, We bring the like of it"; the alternative *nansaʾhā*, "We defer it," which would mean leaving it in place. Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ read *aw tansāhā*, addressing the Prophet ﷺ directly: or you forget it. Qatāda said God used to abrogate a verse with the verse after it, and the Prophet ﷺ would recite a verse or more and then it would be forgotten and raised; al-Ḥasan said plainly that the Prophet ﷺ was made to recite Qurʾān and then forgot it. **[Study Quran]** notes that "cause to be forgotten" can also carry the sense of "abandoning," as in 9:67 — "they forgot God, so He forgot them" — where the meaning is to forsake, since God cannot fail to remember; and it mentions the ḥadīth in which two men who had memorized a sūrah found themselves unable to recite a single letter, and the Prophet ﷺ told them, "It is one of those that has been abrogated and forgotten, so leave it."

**The doctrine of abrogation.** **[Study Quran]** sets out the technical concept as the jurists and commentators developed it. *Naskh* in its mainstream sense is the replacement of one legal ruling by another instituted later in time: the original text remains in the Qurʾān but is no longer binding in law or practice. It can occur only in commands and prohibitions — matters of legal status — and never in descriptive passages concerning God, metaphysics, ethics, history or the Hereafter; hence nothing abrogates "God is powerful over all things," or the promise of 2:62 to whoever believes in God and the Last Day and works righteousness, or the accounts of the earlier prophets. Nor does it touch commandments universal enough to be irrevocable, such as the prohibitions of murder, theft and adultery, or the command to be kind to one's parents. Other kinds were posited as well: the abrogation of text and ruling together, as in ʿĀʾishah's report of commands about suckling that are neither acted upon nor part of the Qurʾān now; and the abrogation of the text while the ruling continues, the example most often cited being the stoning of the adulterer — a verse ʿUmar reported was once part of the Qurʾān and is not, while the penalty remains in force, according to most jurists. It records further that while one Qurʾānic ruling may abrogate another, there is wide disagreement over whether the Sunnah may abrogate the Qurʾān or the reverse, and whether consensus may abrogate a Qurʾānic ruling; that the number of abrogated verses is itself disputed, Shāh Walī Allāh of Delhi counting five, Ibn al-Jawzī two hundred and forty-seven, and al-Suyūṭī twenty-one; and that a minority, such as Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī, denied that abrogation exists in the mainstream sense at all, reconciling the apparently conflicting rulings instead — or taking *āyah* in this verse as "miracle," and the abrogation as occurring between religions, one Sharīʿah replacing another. Even among those who uphold naskh, it must be distinguished from specification (a verse restricting the general scope of another rather than contradicting it), from the simple accumulation of law, and from the disappearance of the circumstances or effective cause behind a ruling. **[Ibn Kathīr]**, reporting al-Ṭabarī's summary, states the boundary sharply: naskh occurs with commands, prohibitions, permissions and the like; as for narratives, they do not undergo naskh — and whether it involves the wording, the ruling or both, it is still called naskh. **[Qurṭubī]** then reports ʿAlī's rebuke, which shows how seriously the science was taken: entering the mosque and finding a man frightening people with his preaching, he asked whether he knew the abrogating from the abrogated; when the man said no, he told him, "Then get out of our mosque and do not preach in it" — in another version, "You have perished and made others perish."

**Why abrogation is wisdom, not inconsistency.** **[Maʿārif]** makes the comparison that has carried the discussion for centuries. Human legislation is changed either because the lawmaker did not understand the situation, or because unforeseen circumstances altered it — both impossible for God. There is a third kind: the lawgiver enacts a rule knowing exactly how circumstances will change and what will replace it, as a physician prescribes a medicine for a patient's present condition knowing that in two days the condition will alter and another medicine will be needed — and instead of handing over the whole course of treatment at once, which would burden the sick man and risk confusion, he gives each prescription in its time. This is the only kind of change possible in divine law, and it is the kind the verse describes; the ḥadīth in Muslim states, "There has never been a prophethood without abrogation." **[Ibn Kathīr]** supports the same conclusion from their own history: God permitted Ādam's children to marry as they then did and later forbade it; allowed Nūḥ's people every kind of animal and later restricted foods; permitted a man to marry two sisters among the Children of Israel and forbade it in the Torah; commanded Ibrāhīm to sacrifice his son and then repealed the command before it was carried out; commanded the worshippers of the calf among the Children of Israel to kill one another and then repealed it so that they were not all destroyed — instances the Jews themselves admit, yet ignore. **[Saʿdī]** draws the conclusion the verse's own words point to: "better than it or its like" shows that what replaces the abrogated ruling is never of less benefit, because God's bounty, especially toward this community whose religion He eased to the utmost, only increases; and whoever finds fault with naskh has found fault with God's dominion and power, which is why the verse follows with "do you not know that God is powerful over all things?" **[Study Quran]** adds the fine point that to make sense of one verse being "better" than another, the commentators read the phrase as referring to the ruling rather than the sign — relief in worldly terms or greater reward in the next; the night prayer lifted was relief, the fast of Ramaḍān imposed was a greater opportunity for reward; and it recalls al-Ṭabarī's comparison with "they were made to drink the calf into their hearts," where the missing "love of" must be understood, since they did not drink the calf itself.

**Reflection.** This verse is the Sūrah's answer to a very modern-sounding objection — that a book which changes its instructions cannot be from God. The answer has two parts: that legislation is not a description of God but a physician's course of treatment for people whose condition changes, and that the alternative to change is not consistency but the absence of a lawgiver who knows the future. **[Saʿdī]**'s observation that the replacement is never worse is the ethical core: what the Jews took as evidence of contradiction, the believers were taught to read as evidence of a mercy that keeps pace with them — and the command "do not know that God is powerful over all things?" is not a rebuke of doubt about doctrine but of a failure to see whose authority is being questioned when a law is revised.


## 2:107

*"Do you not know that to God belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, and that you have, apart from God, neither protector nor helper?"*

**Meaning.** The verse grounds the authority of the previous one [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. **[Qurṭubī]** opens out the terms: the kingdom (*mulk*) is His by bringing into being and originating, and by dominion, power and the carrying-through of command and will; and the clause that follows removes every last rival: you have, apart from God, no *walī* to guard you and no *naṣīr* to drive away His punishment when it comes. **[Jalālayn]** puts the two halves in the same order: to God belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, doing what He pleases; and you have none besides God — neither a protector to safeguard you nor a helper to keep His chastisement from you. **[Saʿdī]** draws the argument the verse is making: if God is the owner, disposing of you as a benevolent owner disposes in His decrees, His commands and His prohibitions, then just as no one may object to the decrees He measures out for His servants, no one may object to the rulings He legislates for them. The servant is managed and subjected under his Lord's commands, both the religious and the cosmic — what business has he with objection? And God is also his protector and his helper: He takes charge of securing his interests and defends him against what would harm him; and part of that protection is precisely that He legislates for him the rulings His wisdom and His mercy toward him require. Whoever reflects on the abrogation that has occurred in the Qurʾān and the Sunnah comes to know God's wisdom and His mercy to His servants, and how He brings them to their interests without their perceiving it.

**The argument in al-Ṭabarī's words.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** reports al-Ṭabarī's paraphrase of the verse: "Do you not know, O Muḥammad, that I alone own the heavens and the earth, and that I decide whatever I will in them? I forbid whatever I will; I change and repeal whatever I will of My previous rulings, whenever I will; and I uphold whatever I will." He then gives the force of the address: although God directed the statement of His greatness toward His Prophet ﷺ, He was also refuting the Jews who denied that the rulings of the Torah could undergo abrogation and who rejected the prophethood of ʿĪsā and Muḥammad ﷺ out of dislike for the changes those messengers brought as God commanded. God therefore proclaimed to them that He owns the heavens and the earth and all authority in them, and that the subjects in His kingdom are His creation, required to hear and obey His commands and prohibitions: He has full authority to command His creation as He wills, forbid what He wills, abrogate what He wills and uphold what He wills.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the grammar and the address: the verb is in the jussive after *lam*, the interrogative particle not changing the operator's effect; *an* is in the accusative place; and the clause "to God belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth" is a nominal sentence whose subject is *mulk* and whose predicate is "to God," the whole serving as the object of "know." The address is to the Prophet ﷺ while the intended audience is his community — since what follows says "and you have, apart from God, neither protector nor helper," which is a plural. He adds the lexical note on *walī*: it is from *waliya amra fulān*, to undertake someone's affair — hence *walī al-ʿahd*, the one charged with the matter of the Muslims — and "apart from God" means other than God, after God, as Umayyah b. Abī al-Ṣalt's line has it: "O soul, you have no guardian apart from God, and nothing against the happenings of time endures." And in the reading of the congregation *naṣīr* is in the genitive, joined to *walī*, though the nominative is also permitted, joined to the place of *walī* in the sentence. **[Study Quran]** notes the shift of addressee: the verse begins by addressing the Prophet and then expands to address human beings generally, as happens elsewhere in the Qurʾān.

**Reflection.** The two verses together answer an objection about legislation by relocating the argument to ownership. The question "why does the law change?" presumes that the law belongs to the people it governs — and the verse says that the heavens and the earth and everything legislated within them belong to their Maker, whose changes are a physician's changes. What remains for the servant is not the right of objection but the need of protection; and the verse's closing clause is its pastoral edge: the same God whose authority permits the change is the only protector and helper available to the one who must live under it.


## 2:108

*"Or do you wish to question your messenger as Mūsā was questioned before? And whoever exchanges belief for disbelief has strayed from the even path."*

**Meaning.** The verse turns from what was asked of God to what was asked of His Messenger [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. *Am* here is the disjunctive, carrying the sense of *bal*: rather, do you wish to question your Messenger as Mūsā was questioned before? And the sense of it is reproach. **[Qurṭubī]** fills in the reference: the questioning of Mūsā was their demand to see God openly — "show us God plainly" (4:153) — while they demanded of Muḥammad ﷺ that he bring God and the angels before them in ranks; and Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid add that they asked him to turn al-Ṣafā into gold. The verse then states the verdict on such demands: whoever exchanges belief for disbelief has strayed from the even path — *sawāʾ* being the middle of a thing, as Abū ʿUbaydah explained, whence "in the midst of the Fire" (37:55); al-Farrāʾ said it means the aim, so that the one who swaps faith for disbelief has missed the road's direction and mark, which is the road of obedience to God.

**Occasions.** **[Ṭabarī]** collects the reports because the occasion determines the sense. Ibn ʿAbbās, in Ibn Isḥāq's chain: Rāfiʿ b. Ḥuraythilah and Wahb b. Zayd said to the Messenger of God ﷺ, "Bring us a book you send down upon us from heaven which we may read, and make rivers flow for us, and we shall follow you and believe you" — and this verse came down about their words. Qatāda and al-Suddī: Mūsā was asked and it was said to him, "show us God plainly," and the Arabs then asked the Messenger of God ﷺ to bring God before them so they might see Him openly.
