Mujāhid: Quraysh asked Muḥammad ﷺ to have God turn al-Ṣafā into gold, and he said, "Yes — but it would be for you as the table was for the Children of Israel if you disbelieve." They refused and turned back. Abū al-ʿĀliyyah's report adds a subtler form of the same error: a man said, "O Messenger of God, if only our expiations were like the expiations of the Children of Israel!" — and the Prophet ﷺ said, "O God, we do not seek that! What God has given you is better than what He gave the Children of Israel: when one of them sinned, he found it written at his door with its expiation, and if he made expiation it was a disgrace for him in this world, and if he did not, a disgrace in the next; whereas God has given you..." — the report continues into the merits granted this community instead. **[Qurṭubī]** records Ibn ʿAbbās's other report of the demand for a heavenly book and flowing rivers, and notes the reading of al-Ḥasan, *kamā sīla*, with the hamzah changed to a *yāʾ*. **[Study Quran]** gathers the demand forms: Quraysh challenging the Prophet to bring a Book with the power to create flowing rivers, or to turn Ṣafā into gold, or to give them a tree on which to hang ritual items — the last comparable to the Israelites' "make for us a god as they have gods" (7:138).

**Rulings — which questions are forbidden.** **[Saʿdī]** states the distinction the passage requires: what is forbidden is the questioning of obstinacy and objection — as 4:153 has it, "they asked Mūsā for something greater than that: they said, 'show us God openly'" — and as 5:101 warns, "O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if they were shown to you, would grieve you." But asking for guidance and learning is praiseworthy and commanded: "ask the people of remembrance if you do not know" (16:43), and the Qurʾān itself answers the Companions' questions about wine, gambling and orphans without rebuke. Since the forbidden kind of questioning is blameworthy and can carry its owner as far as unbelief, the verse follows with the exchange of disbelief for faith and the straying of the path. **[Ibn Kathīr]** documents the same with the ḥadīths: the greatest crime among the Muslims belongs to him who asks about a thing not forbidden, and it becomes forbidden because of his asking; and the Prophet's ﷺ words, "Leave me as long as I leave you; those before you were destroyed only by the abundance of their questions and their disputing with their prophets; so when I command you a matter, do of it what you can, and when I forbid you a thing, avoid it" — which he said after he told them that God had enjoined the ḥajj, and a man asked, "Every year, O Messenger of God?" three times, and he answered, "No — and had I said yes, it would have been made obligatory, and you would not have been able to do it." Al-Mughīrah b. Shuʿbah, in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, reports that the Prophet ﷺ forbade "it was said" and "he said," wasting wealth, and asking many questions. **[Study Quran]** sets the same material beside the praise of the Companions' good questions — many verses came down in response to questions about orphans, charity, women and other matters — so that the prohibition falls on a manner of asking, not on asking as such; and it notes the Prophet's ﷺ words, "Those who came before you were ruined only through the multiplication of their questions and their differences with their prophets." **[Maʿārif]** gives the reason such demands are improper at all: there is a purpose behind everything God does, but divine wisdom alone knows what it is, and the creature has no right to determine the precise mode of his Creator's acts — he should not ask the why and wherefore of a divine action, but accept and submit.

**Reflection.** The verse does not forbid questions; it forbids the kind of question that is really a demand that God perform for our satisfaction. The test is in the motive: a question that seeks guidance opens the road, while a question that sets terms for belief has already left the road and is only looking for a way to be excused. **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s ḥadīth about the man who asked whether ḥajj was due every year shows how costly such questions can be: the answer, when it comes, becomes law — which is why the Prophet ﷺ preferred the community to keep silent about what had not been made obligatory. And the closing clause gives the diagnosis in the Qurʾān's own terms: the one who turns belief into unbelief has not merely failed an examination, he has left the middle of the road — *sawāʾ al-sabīl* — for the ditch on either side.


## 2:109

*"Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after your belief, out of envy from their own selves, even after the truth has become clear to them. So pardon and forbear until God brings His command; surely God is powerful over all things."*

**Meaning.** The verse names the wish and then its source [Jalālayn] [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. **[Qurṭubī]** parses it closely: *wadda* is "wished"; "disbelievers" is the second object of "turn you back"; "from their own selves" attaches either to the wish or to "envy," in which case the pause falls after "disbelievers" — and the phrase means that the envy came from their own prompting, with no ground found in any book and no command given for it; which is why the words "envy from their own selves" are there at all, to fix the blame and confirm it, as in the Qurʾān's other formulations: "they say with their mouths," "they write the book with their own hands," "no bird flies with its two wings." The verse concerns the Jews. **[Jalālayn]** notes the same structure and adds the motive: envy is the object denoting the reason — their own wicked souls prompted the wish, and this after the truth about the Prophet ﷺ had become clear to them from the Torah. **[Maʿārif]** fills in the conduct: some of the Jews, posing as the well-wishers of the Muslims, kept inventing stratagems to turn them from Islam, and though they failed repeatedly they would not desist; the verse warns the Muslims of intentions that spring not from sincerity but from envy, and that not from anything the Muslims have done but spontaneously from within themselves, even after the truth had become clear to them.

**Envy, its kinds and the command of forbearance.** **[Qurṭubī]** distinguishes two kinds of envy. The blameworthy is to wish that God's blessing be removed from your Muslim brother — whether or not you wish it transferred to yourself — and this is the kind God censures, as in "or do they envy the people for what God has given them of His bounty?" (4:54). The other kind, which he calls the praised, is *ghibṭah*: to wish for the like of what another has without wishing its removal — and the ḥadīth permits this, "there is no envy except in two: a man whom God has given wealth and who spends it in God's way, and a man whom God has given knowledge and who acts by it and teaches it." **[Study Quran]** gives the same ḥadīth and observes that this business of envying after the truth has become clear is treated elsewhere as well (3:19; 2:213; 4:54; 42:14), and that envy is commonly understood to be the first sin of Satan, who said of Ādam, "I am better than him" (38:76). **[Ṭabarī]** notes that some of the early authorities identified "many of the People of the Book" here with Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf, the Jewish poet who used to satirize the Prophet ﷺ — a report adduced by al-Zuhrī and Qatāda. **[Study Quran]** records another setting for the verse: formerly Jewish Companions who, after the battle of Uḥud, were taunted by their former coreligionists about their condition and were turned back to Judaism — a scenario that pairs with 3:186, "you shall surely hear much hurt from those who were given the Book before you and from those who are idolaters; but if you are patient and reverent, that is indeed a course worthy of resolve."

**Rulings — the command to pardon, and the question of abrogation.** The command is: pardon and forbear — leave them, take no action against them — until God brings His command [Jalālayn]. **[Study Quran]** sets out the dispute that has grown around the clause. On the view of many — al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr among them, and al-Rāzī in his report — this command to pardon was abrogated by 9:29, "fight those who believe not in God and in the Last Day... among those who were given the Book, until they pay the *jizyah* with a willing hand, being humbled." But, it notes, al-Rāzī argues that if the verse is read as a command to a certain kind of virtuous behaviour, it is not subject to abrogation at all, since it is not a legal ruling; and it points out that the first verse permitting fighting is variously identified — some say 22:39, "permission is granted to those who are fought, because they were wronged," others 9:5 — and that an expansive view of abrogation would nullify dozens of verses of peace and forbearance. In this case, al-Rāzī holds, the question need not arise: commanding forbearance and tolerance does not contradict the just-war commands, since even in fighting the Muslims are commanded to practise such virtues, as 2:190-194 shows. **[Maʿārif]** connects the clause to the situation of the Muslims: they were conscious of their own weakness and the strength of their enemies and could have wondered how they would carry out a new law; so the verse reminds them that God's power extends over everything, small or great, and that the command to forbear was proper to their situation at that time — God later fulfilled the promise of the verse and sent down the injunction of jihād, which was then applied to the Jews and other mischief-makers "to prevent disorder and make peace."

**Reflection.** The verse is a psychological portrait of a poisoned relationship, and its most striking feature is the phrase "after the truth has become clear to them." This is not a dispute about evidence; the evidence has done its work, and what remains beneath the argument is envy — a wish to unmake the Muslims' faith because it exists. Against that, the instruction is not argument but restraint: pardon, forbear, wait for God's command. It is worth noticing what **[Maʿārif]** says about the reason: the creature has no right to dictate the mode of God's action, and a community too weak to enforce a law must be taught first that God's power is not limited by their weakness. The next verse makes the same point positively: while they wait, they should be found in prayer and alms, so that the pause is not an idle one.


## 2:110

*"And establish the prayer and give the alms; and whatever good you send ahead for your own selves, you will find it with God. Surely God sees what you do."*

**Meaning.** The verse returns the believers to their own business after the long exposure of the People of the Book [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** explains why the command comes precisely here: God ordered them to establish prayer, give alms and send good deeds ahead for themselves so that they might purify themselves from the fault that had gone before — the seeking of the Jews' counsel, the leaning of some of them on the Jews, and the rudeness of those who had addressed the Prophet ﷺ with *rāʿinā* — since the establishing of prayers is an expiation for sins, the giving of alms a cleansing of souls and bodies from the stains of offences, and the sending ahead of good deeds the attaining of God's good pleasure. "Whatever good you send ahead for your own selves": whatever righteous work you do in the days of your life and store up as a treasure for your own return, you will find its reward with your Lord on the Day of Resurrection, and He will recompense you for it. The verse says "you will find it" where the sense is "you will find its reward," the omitted word being understood — as the poet says "the city glorified," meaning its people did. **[Saʿdī]** reads the same command as a summons to the present hour: God set them to occupy their time with prayer, alms and every act of nearness, and promised that whatever good they do is not lost with God but found with Him, complete and preserved. **[Study Quran]** notes that here and in the similar passage at 73:20 the good the believers perform and find with God is tied to prayer and charity, and that the fruits of one's actions are reaped on the Day of Judgement — a promise in the form of a description; it also records the practice of one Companion, who said that when he heard the Prophet recite this verse he would afterwards say, "He sees all things," and notes the Prophet's ﷺ habit of pausing in his recitation to glorify, supplicate or prostrate in accord with the verse's content.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** notes a small morphological point: *baṣīr* here is *mubṣir* — the one who sees — shifted to the pattern *faʿīl*, as *mubdiʿ* becomes *badīʿ* and *muʾlim* becomes *alīm*. And the closing sentence, though it comes in the form of a report, carries within it a promise and a threat, a command and a prohibition: God informed them that He sees all their deeds, hidden and open, so that they should labour in His obedience — since it is stored up with Him for reward — and beware of disobeying Him, since He is aware of the one who rides it. **[Jalālayn]** gives the phrase's reach: whatever good you send ahead, of obedience such as maintaining kinship and charity, you will find its reward with God; assuredly God sees what you do and will requite you for it.

**Reflection.** The placement of this verse is the whole of its teaching. Having told the believers to pardon and forbear until God brings His command, the Qurʾān does not leave them waiting in idleness or in resentment: it sets them to prayer and almsgiving, to the two acts that keep the heart connected to God and the hand connected to people. **[Maʿārif]**'s point answers the objection that a community not yet permitted to fight might feel its merit wanting: prayer, fasting and every good deed performed in the interim carry their full reward, and not a particle of them is lost. The verse is thus a lesson in how to hold a grievance — with the palms busy and the record accumulating, rather than with the tongue.


## 2:111

*"And they said, 'None shall enter the Garden unless he is a Jew or a Christian.' Those are their hopes. Say: 'Bring your proof, if you are truthful.'"*

**Meaning.** The claim of exclusive salvation is stated in its two halves and then dismissed [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. The sentence is reported as one, but **[Ṭabarī]** explains what it means: the Jews said, "None shall enter the Garden but one who is a Jew," and the Christians said, "None shall enter the Garden but a Christian" — and because the sense was plain to those addressed, the two parties were joined in a single report. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same reading and adds the grammatical note of al-Akhfash: "whoever" is singular in form but plural in meaning, which is why the word for Jew is given in the plural, and why the following clauses shift between singular and plural pronouns. Then the verdict: *those are their hopes* — wishes with no ground beneath them, as Abū al-ʿĀliyyah, Qatāda and al-Rabīʿ said; and the challenge: *bring your proof, if you are truthful* [Jalālayn] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Qurṭubī]** unpacks *burhān*: it is the evidence that produces certainty, its plural *barāhīn* on the pattern of *qurbān* and *qarābīn*; and he records al-Ṭabarī's observation that the command to produce a proof here establishes the validity of rational inquiry and refutes anyone who would deny it — a point worth pausing over, since the same commentator is often charged with the opposite. **[Study Quran]** notes that the proof (*burhān*) is a demonstration or evidence, used in the same way at 21:24, 23:117, 27:64 and 28:75, and it lists the parallel passages in which each community claims God's favour exclusively: 2:113, where each says the other stands on nothing; 2:135, where guidance means following only their religion; 5:18, where Jews and Christians call themselves the sons and beloved of God; and 62:6, where the Jews claim to be God's friends apart from other people.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives two views of *hūdan*. On one, it is the plural of *hāʾid*, on the pattern of *ʿūṭ* from *ʿāʾiṭ* and *ḥūl* from *ḥāʾil* — the singular meaning one who repents and returns to the truth; on the other, it is a verbal noun applied to the whole group, like "a fasting man and a fasting people." Others held that the word is simply *yahūdan* with the added letter dropped; and in the codex of Ubayy the verse reads, "unless he is a Jew or a Christian" (*yahūdiyyan aw naṣrāniyyan*) [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. **[Jalālayn]** notes the occasion in one clause: this is what the Jews of Madīnah and the Christians of Najrān said, each party claiming Paradise exclusively for its own members — and the Qurʾān calls such sayings their desires, their false passions.

**Rulings — the demand for proof.** **[Saʿdī]** makes the verse the basis of a general principle of argument: anyone who advances a claim must produce the evidence for its soundness; otherwise, if the claim were simply reversed and another asserted the opposite without proof, there would be no difference between the two. The proof is what verifies claims or falsifies them — and since they had no proof in hand, their claim is thereby known to be false. **[Maʿārif]** explains how such a claim could arise among people who read the Book: the Jews and the Christians had forgotten the essence of religion — adherence to true doctrine and the performance of prescribed good deeds — and had identified it with affiliation to a racial or social community. Each party asserted, in its malice, that the other's religion was baseless; and this quarrel gave the idolaters an excuse to say the same of both. The Qurʾān dismisses the pretension as fancy and self-delusion — and the verse that follows supplies the principle that settles it.

**Reflection.** The verse is a one-line demolition of inherited salvation. Its logic is not that the claim is unkind but that it is unproven, and the Qurʾān's test is refreshingly bare: produce the evidence. **[Saʿdī]**'s observation is the sharpest part of it — that a claim which can be reversed with equal justification is worth nothing either way — and it is a test that the passage will apply to the Muslims themselves in the very next verse, as **[Maʿārif]** warns: membership in a community, however true its religion, is not a substitute for submission and good deeds. The claim to Paradise is a legal claim, and the Qurʾān asks every claimant for his deed.

## 2:112

*"Nay — whoever submits his face to God while being a doer of good, his reward is with his Lord; and no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve."*

**Meaning.** *Balā* overturns the claim, and the verse substitutes a criterion [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** explains the phrase: to submit one's face to God is to humble oneself before Him in obedience and to yield to His command; the root of *islām* is *istislām*, submission, and the one who is called a Muslim is so named because his limbs submit to the obedience of his Lord. Al-Rabīʿ read it as sincerity: "he is sincere toward God." And God specified the face rather than the other limbs because the face is the most honoured part of a person — if the face, which has the greatest claim and sanctity, is humbled before something, the rest of the body is all the readier to be humbled; that is why the Arabs say of a man that he has given his *face* when they mean the man himself, as al-Aʿshā says, "I set the judgement upon its face," meaning upon the matter itself. Zayd b. ʿAmr b. Nufayl's line gives the same sense: "I submitted my face to the One to whom the rain-clouds have submitted, carrying sweet, clear water." **[Jalālayn]** adds the second clause: "while being a doer of good" — affirming God's oneness and acting rightly — and gives the promise in its full form: his reward is with his Lord, the reward of his deeds being the Garden; no fear shall befall them, and they shall not grieve, in the Hereafter.

**Belief — the two conditions.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** states the rule that the verse's two clauses embody: the deed must be performed for God alone and must conform to the Sharīʿah — two conditions, sincerity and conformity; a deed that is sincere but does not conform is not accepted, and a deed that conforms but is not sincere is not accepted either. **[Study Quran]** develops the point and the disagreement around it: al-Ṭabarī reads "submits his face" as submitting one's body and actions; Ibn Kathīr adds the condition of conformity to the Sharīʿah, which excludes the hypocrite for want of sincerity and the Christian monk for want of conformity; al-Rāzī excludes, on the same reasoning, the Hindu, who in his view displays repugnant actions whatever his intentions. The Study Quran notes that the condition of physical conformity allows the exclusion of other religions, although the plain sense of this passage and those like it does not of itself necessitate the exclusion that some authorities assert from it. **[Saʿdī]** extracts the corollary the verse implies: whoever is not so described is among the people of the Fire, so that deliverance belongs only to people of sincerity toward the One worshipped and of following to the Messenger; and he explains the closing promise as the meeting of both hopes — they obtained what was desired and escaped what was feared.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** handles the grammar: "his face" is mentioned because the face is the noblest part of a person and the place where honour and abasement appear; the Arabs commonly report the whole by naming the face; and the pronouns move between the singular of "whoever" and the plural of "his reward... upon them... they grieve," the plural returning to the sense. He reports the reading of the clause as "whoever submits his face to God" in the sense of surrender and humility, or of sincerity of action. **[Study Quran]** notes that the same expression appears at 4:125 and 31:22, and that the metaphor is weighty because the face is the noblest part of the body — and because in a sense the most profound action of the prayer is the prostration, in which the face touches the ground. **[Maʿārif]** sets out the two principles the verse makes the essence of religion in every dispensation: obedience to God in belief and in action, and sincerity rather than expediency — *aslama* meaning total submission, *muḥsin* meaning one who performs good deeds according to the Sharīʿah; and it then turns the verse on its Muslim readers with a warning that the passage is meant for them too: no one, not even a member of the Muslim community, may hope for the promised reward while dispensing with obedience and the following of the law.

**Reflection.** The verse dissolves the two claims of privilege that the Sūrah has been dismantling — descent and affiliation — into two acts: turning the face to God and doing well. And it places them where the claimants cannot reach: "his reward is with his Lord" — not in a register of nations but in the keeping of the One who receives the submission. **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s two conditions are the verse's practical translation, and they are severe in exactly the way the passage intends: sincerity without the law produces a monk whose devotion is his own invention, and law without sincerity produces a hypocrite whose deeds are his own service. What the verse asks for is the person who does both — and the promise attached is not the Garden in the first instance, but the disappearance of fear and grief.


## 2:113

*"The Jews say, 'The Christians stand on nothing,' and the Christians say, 'The Jews stand on nothing' — yet they recite the Book. So said those who do not know the like of their words. And God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they differed."*

**Meaning.** The mutual denial of the two communities is reported and then dated [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn] [Qurṭubī]. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the occasion from Ibn ʿAbbās: when the Christian delegation of Najrān came to the Messenger of God ﷺ, the Jewish rabbis came to them and they disputed in his presence — Rāfiʿ b. Ḥuraythilah said to the Christians, "You stand on nothing," denying ʿĪsā b. Maryam and the Gospel, and a man of the Najrān delegation said to the Jews, "You stand on nothing," denying the prophethood of Mūsā and disbelieving the Torah; and God sent down this verse about their two sayings. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same report and the sense of it: each party claimed that its counterpart stood on nothing and that it was more entitled to God's mercy. **[Ibn Kathīr]** adds that the verse explains the dispute, hatred and stubbornness that the People of the Book hold toward one another.

**The argument in the verse.** "Yet they recite the Book" is a circumstantial clause, and **[Ṭabarī]** shows what it does in the sentence: God informs them that each party has squandered the ruling of the Book whose truth it acknowledges as from God, and has denied what God sent down in it — since the Gospel, whose truth the Christians profess, confirms what is in the Torah concerning the prophethood of Mūsā and the obligations God laid on the Children of Israel; and the Torah, whose truth the Jews profess, confirms the prophethood of ʿĪsā and what he brought. **[Jalālayn]** states the same equation: the Jews rejected ʿĪsā and the Christians rejected Mūsā, though both recite the scriptures revealed to them, in which each prophet is confirmed. **[Study Quran]** records the same reading of the clause — that in what they espouse they should affirm rather than deny the truths in the other religion — and notes that some commentators took "stand on nothing" to mean that the Jews and Christians had indeed once followed what was true, then differed and altered their religion; but others, it says, point out that this reading would negate the obvious censure in the verse, which indicates that the two communities are wrong to level the accusation against each other in the first place.

**"Those who do not know."** **[Qurṭubī]** reports the views: for the majority, the ignorant are the idolaters of the Arabs, because they have no book; ʿAṭāʾ said they are nations that came before the Jews and the Christians; al-Rabīʿ b. Anas read the clause as applying to the Jews' own earlier denial of the Christians before them. **[Ibn Kathīr]**, in the same line, understands them as peoples who preceded the Jews and the Christians, while **[Study Quran]** allows either that or the idolaters who opposed Islam, and gives al-Rāzī's view among them. The point in every case is the same: the two communities who possessed revelation had descended, in their quarrel, to the level of those who had none.

**The suspension of judgement, and its meaning.** The verse does not settle the dispute in this world; it defers the verdict — "God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they differed" — and **[Study Quran]** observes that this suspension of a final verdict regarding religious differences is a consistent theme of the Qurʾān, recurring at 3:55, 5:48, 6:164, 10:93, 16:92, 22:69, 32:25 and 39:3, alongside the Qurʾān's statements that mankind was once a single community (10:19) and that even if they were made one again they would not cease to differ (11:118). It reports al-Kāshānī's observation on the two communities: the Christians are veiled from the outward by their attachment to the inward, and the Jews veiled from the inward by their attachment to the outward — and, it adds, similar problems beset certain schools of thought within Islam. **[Saʿdī]** draws the conclusion the passage implies: affairs had reached the point where desire and envy led each party to declare the other astray and unbelieving, just as the unlettered idolaters had done; and God will judge between those who differ with the justice He has told His servants of — for there is no success and no deliverance except for the one who affirms all the prophets and messengers, obeys his Lord's commands and avoids His prohibitions; everyone else is ruined. **[Maʿārif]** notes the same: the disputes of the Jews, the Christians and the associators will be decided by God on the Day of Judgement, and the question has in fact already been settled both by what God revealed in His Books and by rational argument — the final decision on that Day being of the visible kind, the followers of truth sent to Paradise and the followers of falsehood cast into the Fire.

**Reflection.** The verse is a portrait of a quarrel whose parties have more in common than either will admit: each appeals to a revelation that testifies to the other's prophet, and each denies what its own book affirms. The Qurʾān's rebuke is not that they disagree — disagreement is expected — but that they have made the denial of one another into the content of their religion, and have done so while holding the evidence against themselves in their hands. And the deferral of the verdict is a lesson in proportion: the reader is told neither to settle the dispute with a slogan nor to despair of judgement, but to leave the accounting to the One who will make it — and to make sure that his own position is the one the verse describes as deliverance: affirming all the messengers, obeying the Lord, avoiding what He forbade.


## 2:114

*"And who is more unjust than he who bars the mosques of God from having His Name remembered in them, and strives for their ruin? It is not for such to enter them except in fear. For them is disgrace in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment."*

**Meaning.** The verse states the extreme of injustice, and then the sentence that follows from it [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** defines the terms first: injustice is putting a thing out of its place, and the question — who is more unjust than the man who bars God's mosques from having God worshipped in them? — is a question with no answer but one. *Masjid* is the place of prostration, formed like *majlis* and *manzil*; and it is any place where God is worshipped. **[Saʿdī]** reads the crime in its full breadth: no one is more unjust and more criminal than the one who bars God's mosques from His remembrance, from prayer and the rest of the acts of obedience, and exerts himself — bends his energy — to their ruin. And ruin, he says, is of two kinds: the physical ruin of demolition, destruction and defilement; and the moral ruin of keeping out those who would remember God's name in them. The description covers everyone marked by this quality: the People of the Elephant, the Quraysh when they barred the Messenger of God ﷺ from the House in the year of Ḥudaybiyyah, the Christians when they ruined Bayt al-Maqdis, and every other kind of oppressor who strives for the ruin of mosques in enmity to God and in defiance of Him.

**Context — which mosques, which enemies.** **[Ṭabarī]** reports the disagreement and the reports beneath it. Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid: those who barred the mosques were the Christians, and the mosque was Bayt al-Maqdis — Mujāhid's version has them casting filth into it and preventing people from praying there. Others said the verse came down about Bukhtanassar, who destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis. Ibn Zayd's view, reported by **[Ibn Kathīr]**, is that the idolaters of Quraysh are meant, who barred the Prophet ﷺ from entering Makkah at al-Ḥudaybiyyah until he slaughtered his sacrificial animals at Dhū Ṭuwā; and Ibn Kathīr cites the Prophet's ﷺ words to them: "No one before has ever prevented people from entering the House; a man would even see the killer of his father and his brother, and would not prevent him from entering the House of God." They answered that those who killed their fathers at Badr would never enter it while one of them remained alive. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same reports and adds the sharp turn Ibn ʿAbbās makes of it: this came down about the Christians — how can you claim, O Christians, to be the people of Paradise, when you have ruined Bayt al-Maqdis and prevented those who prayed from praying in it? Their motive in ruining it, he says, was enmity to the Jews, which makes the wonder all the greater given their own veneration of the place. **[Ṭabarī]** notes that the verse leaves the general sense available to all who do this, and **[Study Quran]** records the range: for al-Ṭabarī, since the idolaters never attempted to destroy the Kaʿbah, the Temple in Jerusalem is meant; others, such as **[Qurṭubī]**, hold the meaning general and apply it to anyone who prevents people from entering any house of worship; and one reading of *ruin* holds that in filling the Kaʿbah with idols and the practice of idolatry the idolaters were striving to ruin it, since it had ceased to be the mosque of the One God and had become a temple of idols.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the grammar and the lexical detail: *man* is the subject and *aẓlam* its predicate, meaning no one is more unjust; *an* may stand in the accusative as a substitute for "mosques," or with an implied "hatred of," or with an elided preposition; *masjid* is the place of prostration, with a variant *masjad*, and *al-masjad* with the *jīm* vowelled, meaning the forehead of a man where the mark of prostration strikes; and *al-ārāb* — the seven limbs — are called "mosques" because the prostration touches them. Al-Farrāʾ's rule is cited for the vowel: names on this pattern are usually vowelled in the middle with *fatḥah*, but a handful keep the *kasrah* as the mark of the noun — *masjid*, *maṭliʿ*, *maghrib*, *mashriq*, *maskan* and others like them. **[Ṭabarī]** notes also that "striving for its ruin" is joined in the sentence to "barring," so that the two crimes are one description. And on the clause "it is not for such to enter them except in fear," **[Jalālayn]** reads it as a predicate that functions as a command: frighten them with threats, so that none of them enters feeling secure — while others read it as a report of what God decreed for them: they will not enter them save in fear and humiliation.

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]** draws out the practical injunctions the verse carries. All mosques are equally worthy of respect: just as it is a grave sin to desecrate Bayt al-Maqdis, the Sacred Mosque or the Prophet's ﷺ mosque, the same prohibition holds for every other mosque. The three named mosques do enjoy a higher rank: prayer in the Sacred Mosque is rewarded as a hundred thousand prayers elsewhere, and prayer in the Prophet's ﷺ mosque or in Bayt al-Maqdis as fifty thousand; the journey made to pray in one of the three is a meritorious act that carries a special blessing, while the Prophet ﷺ forbade setting out on a journey to pray in any other mosque in the belief that this is meritorious. Second, it is forbidden to prevent people — by any means — from praying or remembering God in a mosque: the obvious form is barring entry; the subtler forms include making noise in the mosque or playing music nearby, disturbing those at prayer or in remembrance; and reciting loudly so as to disturb others is the same offence, though one may recite or make *dhikr* aloud when no one is present. On this principle, he adds, begging or collecting donations even for religious purposes while people are praying or in *dhikr* is forbidden. Third, every form of laying a mosque waste is prohibited — not only demolition, but producing conditions in which the mosque empties or is deserted; for a mosque's flourishing is not in the beauty of its architecture but in its worshippers. **[Saʿdī]** sets the verses in parallel: if no one is more unjust than the one who bars God's mosques and seeks their ruin, then no one has greater faith than the one who works for their flourishing, outwardly and inwardly — "only he who believes in God and the Last Day maintains the mosques of God" (9:18) — and God has commanded that His houses be raised and honoured (24:36). He also notes what the verse establishes by the fate of these people: God barred them from entering the mosques both by law and by decree, save in fear and abasement; as they frightened God's servants, God frightened them. The People of the Elephant were destroyed; the Quraysh who barred the Prophet ﷺ saw Makkah opened to him and were themselves barred from the Sacred Mosque — "the idolaters are but impurity, so let them not approach the Sacred Mosque" (9:28) — and the Christians who ruined Bayt al-Maqdis had the believers given power over them and were driven out. And **[Jalālayn]** gives the worldly disgrace in its historical forms: the killing, the captivity, the *jizyah* — and in the Hereafter, the Fire. **[Study Quran]** notes the same identification of the disgrace with the *jizyah* of 9:29 in some commentaries, while others point out that disgrace is a broad notion; it records that the Prophet ﷺ would often pray that disgrace not be visited upon him and his community in this world, and it preserves the Sufi reading of the verse: the heart is the house of the love and knowledge of God, and one does wrong by destroying it through false desires.

**Reflection.** The verse measures a person by what he does to the places where people meet God, and it treats the ruining of a mosque as a continuum — from demolition to intimidation to noise. Its most uncomfortable implication is the one **[Saʿdī]** draws out in the negative: if the worst of men is the one who empties God's houses, then the best is the one who fills them. And it is worth noticing how the verse ends: the punishment for driving people away from the worship of God is to be driven away from it oneself, to enter only in fear — an echo of a rule the Sūrah has been establishing from its beginning, that a man is repaid in the currency he spends.


## 2:115

*"And to God belong the East and the West; wherever you turn, there is the Face of God. Surely God is All-Encompassing, Knowing."*

**Meaning.** The verse answers an objection with a statement about ownership and presence [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. **[Ṭabarī]** reads the first clause as a claim of dominion: the East and the West belong to God — theirs is His, in ownership and in creation and disposal, as one says "this house belongs to so-and-so." And the reason the East and West are named rather than everything is that the sun rises each day from a place it will not rise from again until the year comes round, and sets likewise; so the sense is that all that lies between the two horizons is His. **[Qurṭubī]** notes that the naming honours them as "the house of God" and "the she-camel of God" honour what is named, and that the occasion of the verse required it — since the dispute was precisely about a direction.

**Context — the change of the qiblah.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives Ibn ʿAbbās's account: the first thing abrogated in the Qurʾān was the qiblah. When the Messenger of God ﷺ migrated to Madīnah, a city whose people were largely Jews, God at first commanded him to face Bayt al-Maqdis, at which the Jews rejoiced; he faced it for some ten months, though he loved the qiblah of Ibrāhīm and used to look up at the sky and supplicate — until "We have seen the turning of your face to the heaven; so We shall turn you to a qiblah that pleases you... wherever you are, turn your faces toward it" (2:144) came down. The Jews were disturbed and said, "What has turned them from the qiblah they used to face?" and God sent down, "Say: to God belong the East and the West" and this verse. **[Maʿārif]** frames the same sequence and draws the theological point: had God been limited to any one direction, a fixed and permanent orientation would have been required; but He is beyond all limitation, the Lord of East and West and of every conceivable direction, encompassing everything — wherever a man turns, he finds God facing him. **[Qurṭubī]** records five occasions given for the clause "wherever you turn": the report of ʿĀmir b. Rabīʿah, who said that on a dark night during a journey with the Prophet ﷺ they could not determine the qiblah, so each man prayed facing his own guess, and when morning came they mentioned it to the Prophet ﷺ and the verse came down; the change of qiblah and the Jews' objection; the permission to pray supererogatory prayers on a mount in whatever direction it faces; the prayer the Prophet ﷺ offered for the Negus, when those present objected that he had not faced the qiblah; and the question "in which direction shall we call upon Him?" concerning 40:60. **[Study Quran]** lists the same occasions — including the dark-night travellers and the Negus, and the addition that some thought this verse permitted praying in any direction until 2:144 abrogated it, while others read it as giving the mounted traveller the direction he faces for non-obligatory prayers — and observes that where several occasions are given, the commentators often take a neutral attitude and let the doctrinal content, which here is profound and universal, govern.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** explains the grammar: "wherever you turn" is a condition, which is why the *nūn* of the verb is dropped; *thamma* — "there" — is an adverb in the accusative, built on the *fatḥah* because it is vague, standing to *hunāka* as "over there" stands to "here." **[Ṭabarī]** weighs what "the Face of God" means in such a sentence and concludes with the plain reading: His countenance, His direction of pleasure — the qiblah with which He is pleased, so that wherever the servant is commanded to turn, there God's Face is. **[Study Quran]** sets out the range of interpretations: for al-Ṭabarī it means simply "there is God," or "there is the qiblah of God"; for al-Rāzī, "there is God's contentment." It gathers the verses that belong to the theme — "all things perish save His Face" (28:88); "all that is upon it passes away, and there remains the Face of your Lord, possessed of majesty and bounty" (55:26-27); "He is with you wherever you are" (57:4; 58:7) — and notes al-Rāzī's observation that the very fact that the verse says "wherever" is the strongest argument against anthropomorphism, since a body can be in one place and not in more than one at the same time. Finally, on *wāsiʿ*, which can mean "unstinting" or "generous" as well as "all-encompassing," it reports al-Rāzī's reading in connection with the ruined mosques of the previous verse: despite the destruction of the mosques, God's remembrance cannot be hindered, since He is wherever one turns. And it records that the verse is taken as an allusion to the omnipresence of the One who is "the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward" (57:3), and is one of the scriptural foundations of the Sufi doctrine of the oneness of being.

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** sets out the cases the verse governs: if your turning is by God's command — after He commanded you to face the Kaʿbah where you had faced Bayt al-Maqdis; or commanded the traveller to pray on his mount, so that his qiblah is wherever he faces; or when the direction is uncertain and a man does his best and then finds he was wrong, or is excused by illness or incapacity — in all these the servant is either following an order or excused, and no direction he faces lies outside his Lord's dominion. And the verse affirms the Face of God in the manner befitting Him, without resemblance: He has a Face that no face resembles; He is vast in bounty and in the greatness of His attributes, and He knows your secrets and your intentions — and it is out of His vastness and His knowledge that He has eased the matter for you and accepted from you what He commanded.

**Reflection.** The passage answers a quarrel about direction by removing the premise on which the quarrel rested: that God is somewhere in particular. The qiblah matters because He commanded it, not because He is lodged in one place — and once that is said, the change of qiblah stops being a scandal and becomes an illustration: the servants turn where they are told, and the Lord is present to every turning. **[Saʿdī]**'s summary is the verse's practical sense: what matters is that the turning be obedience or excused necessity; and the closing pair of names is the comfort: a Lord vast enough to have given the command, and knowing enough to accept the excuse.


## 2:116

*"And they said, 'God has taken a child.' Glory be to Him! Nay, to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him."*

**Meaning.** The verse names a claim and removes its possibility in a single stroke [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Qurṭubī]. **[Qurṭubī]** identifies the speakers: this is a report of the Christians in their saying that the Messiah is the son of God, of the Jews in their saying that ʿUzayr is the son of God, and of the disbelieving Arabs in their saying that the angels are the daughters of God — the like of these reports being given elsewhere of the ignorant disbelievers, in Sūrat Maryam and Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ. **[Study Quran]** makes the same point: the verse is not restricted to Christian theology; it also addresses the pagan Arab belief that the angels were God's daughters, and the disavowals of divine sonship concerning ʿĪsā recur through the Qurʾān (5:17, 72; 9:30; 19:35). *Subḥānahu* — glory be to Him — is exaltation and removal: God is far above what they attribute to Him [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. And then the argument: to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth — all of them His property and His servants, disposed of as an owner disposes of what he owns, all obedient to Him. **[Saʿdī]** presses it: if all creation are His servants, poor before Him, and He is rich beyond them, how could one of them be a child to Him — when a child must be of the kind of its father, being a part of him, while God is the master who subdues and they are the mastered who are subdued, He the rich and they the poor? This is the most futile and the most absurd of claims. He also notes God's forbearance in the face of it: He is patient with them, forbearing, granting them well-being and provision although they diminish Him.

**"All are devoutly obedient to Him."** **[Ṭabarī]** reports the interpretations and then rules on them. Qatāda, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn ʿAbbās: obedient — and Mujāhid adds that the obedience of the disbeliever lies in the prostration of his shadow, which prostrates to God while he dislikes it. ʿIkrimah: all acknowledge His servitude. Al-Rabīʿ: all shall be standing before Him on the Day of Resurrection. *Qunūt* in the Arabs' speech, says **[Ṭabarī]**, carries three senses — obedience, standing, and holding back from speech and keeping silent — and the reading he prefers here is obedience and the acknowledgment of servitude, the bodies themselves testifying by the marks of craftsmanship in them to the oneness of God and to Him as their maker. He then adds a procedural principle of his own: it is not permissible to claim that a verse whose wording is general is in fact particular without evidence that commands assent — and so he rejects the claim that "all are devoutly obedient" applies only to the people of obedience. The verse, he concludes, is God's report that the Messiah whom the Christians call His son bears witness against them, he and the heavens and the earth and all that is in them, either with speech or by indication: for God told of their obedience and their acknowledgment of His servitude immediately after reporting their claim, and the Messiah is one of them. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the several senses of *qunūt*: obedience and submission; silence, as in Zayd b. Arqam's report that they used to speak during prayer until "stand before God, devoutly obedient" (2:238) was revealed, whereupon they were commanded to be silent; and prayer itself. **[Study Quran]** adds that *qānit* includes compliance, humility, standing and silence, and reports the view that since these are qualities the opposite of which mark human beings in this world, the verse may describe the state of all on the Day of Resurrection, when everyone will be forced to obey, stand and be silent before God — while others connect it to 13:15, "and to God prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly." The context, it observes, also supports reading the phrase as including ʿĪsā, ʿUzayr and the angels themselves: far from being implicated in the false belief, they are sincere in God's worship — "the Messiah would never disdain to be a servant of God, nor would the angels brought nigh" (4:172).

**Belief.** **[Qurṭubī]** brings the ḥadīth of al-Bukhārī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet ﷺ: "God, exalted, said: The son of Ādam has denied Me, and it was not for him to do so; and he has reviled Me, and it was not for him to do so. As for his denying Me, it is his claim that I cannot restore him as he was; and as for his reviling Me, it is his saying that I have a child — while glorified be I above taking a consort or a child." He also gives the grammar: *subḥān* is in the accusative as a verbal noun, its sense being exoneration, transcendence and exclusion — the answer to their claim. **[Study Quran]** sets out al-Rāzī's four arguments, representative of mainstream thought: the beings said to be God's offspring are contingent and created, while offspring is begotten; the offspring is either eternal or not — if eternal, there is nothing to make one father and the other son, and if not, the offspring is a created being who is begotten; the offspring is of the same species as the progenitor, similar in some ways and different in others, which would require both to be composed of parts, and that cannot be said of God; and one has offspring out of needs — happiness, care in old age, pride — none of which are attributable to God. And it states the principle from which these arguments flow: the Islamic objection to divine sonship rests on the conception of God's oneness, transcendence, absoluteness and uniqueness — that He is like nothing in creation, beyond need of all things, and never implicated in the limitations that fatherhood entails; Islam denies every relativizing of God through a relationship of that kind. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the summary argument in its plain form: all creatures are God's servants and His property, so how could one of them be His son, when the son of any being is born of two comparable beings, and God has no equal or rival — "how can He have a child when He has no consort? He created all things and knows all things" (6:101).

**Reflection.** The verse takes a doctrine and answers it not with sentiment but with the terms of ownership: everything in the heavens and the earth is His, and everything is in service to Him — which leaves no room in the universe for a second category of being from which a son might come. **[Saʿdī]**'s reductio makes the absurdity vivid: a son must be part of his father and of his kind, whereas a servant is owned and a master owns. And the verse's closing word is its most searching: everything obeys Him — so that the very creation the claimants invoked as evidence against Him testifies, in its prostration and its subjection, to what they denied.


## 2:117

*"Originator of the heavens and the earth; and when He decrees a matter, He but says to it, 'Be' — and it is."*

**Meaning.** The verse continues the refutation by naming God as the one who has no model and needs no instrument [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** explains *badīʿ* as *mubdiʿ* — brought over to the pattern *faʿīl* as *muʾlim* became *alīm* and *musmiʿ* became *samīʿ* — and *al-mubdiʿ* is the one who brings into being and originates what no one preceded him in making. He notes that this is why an inventor in religion is called *mubtadiʿ*: he introduces into it what no one before him introduced. And the connection to the previous verse is the heart of it: how can God have a son when He owns what is in the heavens and the earth, when they all bear witness to His oneness and acknowledge His obedience, and He is their maker — bringing them into being with no origin and no model to copy? The verse then informs His servants that among those who testify to this is the very Messiah whom they attached to God as a son: the One who originated the heavens and the earth without origin and without model is the One who originated the Messiah without a father, by His power. **[Saʿdī]** gives the same reading of *badīʿ*: the Creator of the two, who made them with perfect mastery and beauty without any prior example; "and when He decrees a matter, He but says to it, 'Be' — and it is": nothing resists Him and nothing withholds itself from Him. **[Qurṭubī]** develops the linguistic point: *badīʿ* is *faʿīl* used for emphasis, raised as the predicate of an omitted subject; the active participle is *mubdiʿ*; one says *abdaʿtu al-shayʾa* — I brought the thing into being without a model; and whoever originates what has no precedent is a *mubdiʿ*, whence the people of innovations (*ahl al-bidaʿ*). He then draws a distinction the term requires: an innovation issuing from a creature is either something with a basis in the Sharīʿah — in which case it falls under the general scope of what God encouraged and His Messenger ﷺ specified, and belongs to the praiseworthy — or something without precedent, such as a new kind of generosity and beneficence, which is a praiseworthy action even if no one preceded him in it; and al-Bukhārī's report that ʿUmar said of the night prayer of Ramaḍān, "what a good innovation this is," supports the distinction.

**Belief — the command "Be".** **[Study Quran]** sets out what the phrase does theologically. The creative command appears in 6:73, 16:40, 36:82 and 40:68, and its point in each case is that nothing more than God's word is needed to bring a thing into being; and in relation to the previous verse it recalls 3:59 — "the likeness of ʿĪsā with God is that of Ādam: He created him from dust, then said to him 'Be', and he was" — and 19:35, which is almost this verse's twin. For al-Rāzī, *Be* conveys the ease and power by which God creates, requiring no preparation, practice or effort; and he rejects any sequence of (1) nonexistence, (2) God's saying *Be*, (3) existence, since one cannot address nothing, and if the thing exists it does not need the command in order to exist. Others hold that *Be* neither precedes nor follows the creation of a thing but is coterminous with it, and that the verse confirms God's knowledge of things prior to their creation. **[Study Quran]** then reports that Ibn ʿArabī and many of his school expand this: God says *Be* to the forms — the "immutable essences" — in His knowledge, meaning His knowledge of His own qualities and attributes; He knows what He will create and brings His will and power to bear upon that object of knowledge to create it, so that it is not nothing, yet is not created and possesses no existence — the views converging on the unity of God's knowledge, will and power as His inseparable attributes, and on His complete self-sufficiency in relation to what He creates; and it notes that *kun* corresponds to the Biblical *fiat lux* and stresses that existence comes from God and His will alone, human beings having no power to bring anything out of nothing. **[Maʿārif]** gives the two dialectical-theological approaches to the same problem: the Ashʿarī school reads *Be* as figurative, an illustration of omnipotence indicating that no interval separates God's will from its realization; the Māturīdī school reads it literally, and resolves the difficulty by distinguishing the order of creation (*takwīn*), which gives existence to the nonexistent and needs no existent addressee, from the order of legislation (*tashrīʿ*), which does. **[Ibn Kathīr]** closes the circle with the verses of Sūrat Maryam: "it is not fitting for the Most Merciful to take a son; there is none in the heavens and the earth but comes to the Most Merciful as a servant; He has counted them and numbered them; and every one of them will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection" (19:92-95) — and with Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ, "He begets not, nor is He begotten, and there is none comparable to Him."

**Reflection.** The two verses answer the claim of sonship from both ends: everything that exists is owned and obedient (2:116), and everything that exists was originated without precedent by a word (2:117). Once creation is understood as *Be*, the objection of the previous verse — that a son would require a consort, a kind, a begetting — dissolves into a category error: the One who needs no material and no model, and whose mere decree is the existence of what He decrees, is not a being within the world who propagates. And the argument from ʿĪsā is the sharpest point of the pair: the same power that made the heavens without a template made him without a father, which is precisely why he can be cited as a witness against the claim built upon him.


## 2:118

*"And those who do not know say, 'Why does God not speak to us, or a sign come to us?' So said those before them, the like of their words; their hearts are alike. We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain."*

**Meaning.** The demand of the obdurate is reported, and then it is dated and diagnosed [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** reports the disagreement over who spoke: Mujāhid said it was the Christians — and al-Ṭabarī leant to that view because they are the party mentioned just before — while Ibn ʿAbbās, in Ibn Isḥāq's report, gave it a name and an incident: Rāfiʿ b. Ḥuraylah said to the Messenger of God ﷺ, "If you are a messenger from God as you say, then say to God to speak to us so that we may hear His speech"; and Qatāda, al-Rabīʿ and al-Suddī held it was the idolaters of the Arabs. The question is: why does God not speak to us — telling us himself that you are His messenger — or why does no sign come to us of the kind we have asked for? **[Qurṭubī]** notes the particle: *lawlā* here is *hallā*, the *lawlā* of urging, demanding haste — as in the poet's taunt, "you count the hamstringing of she-camels your finest glory — would that there were a brave man with his helmet on." He distinguishes it from the *lawlā* that denies one thing because of another: the *lawlā* of urging is followed only by a verb, expressed or implied, while the other is followed by a nominal clause with its predicate usually omitted. And the sense of the demand: would God not speak to us of the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ so that we know he is a prophet and believe him; or bring us a sign that is a mark of his prophethood.

**The verdict.** "So said those before them, the like of their words; their hearts are alike" [Jalālayn] [Saʿdī]. **[Jalālayn]** reads the clause as consolation for the Prophet ﷺ: the earlier communities said the like of what these say, in obstinacy and in demanding signs, and their hearts resemble one another in disbelief and stubbornness. **[Saʿdī]** attends to the words "those who do not know": this is the speech of the ignorant, whether of the People of the Book or others, who demanded the kind of signs their own corrupt minds proposed — signs of challenge rather than of guidance — and in doing so grew bold against the Creator and arrogant toward His messengers. He lists the family of such demands from the Qurʾān: "we shall not believe you until we see God openly" (2:55); "the People of the Book ask you to bring down upon them a book from heaven, and they asked Mūsā for something greater than that" (4:153); "what is this messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets? Why has no angel been sent down to him to be a warner with him, or a treasure cast down to him, or a garden for him to eat from?" (25:7-8); and "we shall not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth" (17:90). Their conduct with their messengers is always the same: they demand the signs of *taʿannut* — of wilful testing — and not the signs of guidance, and their goal was never to establish the truth, for the messengers had already come with signs on which human beings would believe. Hence the closing sentence: "We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain" — everyone who has certainty has come to know, from God's dazzling signs and manifest proofs, what gives him certainty and drives off every doubt. **[Study Quran]** notes that "those who do not know" are variously identified — Christians by some, pagan Arabs by others, and "those who came before" as Jews, Christians, Arabs, all three, or anyone matching the description; that some read the demand not as a sincere question but as a taunt; and that a similar stream of requests or taunts appears at 17:90-95, with the wider discussion of incredulous demands at 4:153.

**Reflection.** The verse is a small treatise on why some questions cannot be answered. The demand it reports is not a request for evidence — the evidence had been given, and the Qurʾān says so in its own closing clause — but a request that God appear in the courtroom to satisfy the plaintiff. And the phrase "their hearts are alike" is the diagnosis: the demand is not a product of the age but of a disposition, so that the same speech keeps recurring in every generation that finds the messenger inconvenient. The verse's answer is not a further sign but a people: "clear for a people who are certain" — those who have certainty about God do not need God to negotiate.

## 2:119

*"Indeed We have sent you with the truth, a bearer of glad tidings and a warner; and you shall not be questioned about the companions of the Blaze."*

**Meaning.** The verse is a consolation following a hard passage [Maʿārif] [Jalālayn]. **[Maʿārif]** explains its placement: the previous verse showed that those who persisted in denial did so out of malice and ignorance and could not be expected to reform, and since the Prophet ﷺ was sent as a mercy to the worlds, the thought of their incorrigibility was likely to sadden him — so God consoles him: he has been sent to people bearing the truth and the genuine faith, and his function is twofold, to give glad tidings to those who accept and to warn those who deny; and he will not be held responsible for those who willingly pursue the way to the Fire. All that is required of him is to keep performing his own function, without regard to who accepts and who does not. **[Jalālayn]** renders the last clause the same way: you shall not be questioned about the inhabitants of the Fire — that is, about why the disbelievers did not believe, since your responsibility is only to deliver the message — and it notes the variant reading that turns the verb into a prohibition: *lā tasʾal*, "do not ask." **[Study Quran]** records the same range: "you shall not be questioned about" can carry the sense of "you are not answerable for," and the alternative reading makes the verb an imperative, "and ask not," or a nominative, "and you ask not" — with the first preferred by most, in keeping with the many places where the Prophet ﷺ is absolved of responsibility for the error of others, such as "you are not tasked with their guidance" (2:272), "let not your soul be expended in regrets over them" (35:8), and "you are not a warder over them" (88:22). **[Ibn Kathīr]** sets the same verses side by side and adds 13:40, "your duty is only to convey, and on Us is the reckoning," and 50:45, "We know best what they say; and you are not one to compel them."

**Context and āthār.** **[Qurṭubī]** reports the occasions the exegetes attached to the imperative reading: Muqātil said the Prophet ﷺ remarked, "If God sent down His might upon the Jews, they would believe" — and the verse came down; and Ibn ʿAbbās and Muḥammad b. Kaʿb al-Quraẓī report that the Messenger of God ﷺ said one day, "Would that I knew what became of my parents" — and this verse came down. **[Ṭabarī]** transmits both reports — Muḥammad b. Kaʿb's version has the Prophet ﷺ saying it three times — and notes in his own editorial voice that both are *mursal* and weak in their chains, since Muḥammad b. Kaʿb is a Successor and the *mursal* report cannot establish a proof; and he adds that the Prophet ﷺ never mentioned them again until God took him.

**Belief.** **[Saʿdī]** reads "with the truth" as the comprehensive description of what the Prophet ﷺ brought, and divides the signs that attest him into three: the fact of his sending itself — for anyone who knew the state of the earth before his mission, sunk in the worship of idols, fires and crosses with the remnants of the People of the Book extinguished, would know that God does not leave His creation idle, and that His wisdom and mercy required this great messenger; his life and character, before and after the mission, whose traits could only be those of a complete prophet; and what he brought of the great law and the noble Qurʾān, with its truthful reports, its good commands, its prohibitions of everything base, and its dazzling miracles. All the signs, he says, fall within these three. And the verse's ending is the release from a burden the Prophet ﷺ never carried: "you shall not be questioned" — his charge is the delivery, the reckoning belongs to God.

**Reflection.** The two verses together give the messenger his limits, and the limits are a mercy. He is not required to make hearts certain; he is required to bring the truth, to gladden, and to warn — and the accounting for those who choose the Blaze belongs to no creature. It is worth noticing how often the Qurʾān returns to this absolution, as **[Ibn Kathīr]** and **[Study Quran]** show: the Prophet's grief over his people is honoured and then set down. The lesson has outlived its first audience: the one who carries the message is not the one who answers for its rejection.


## 2:120

*"Never will the Jews be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their creed. Say: 'God's guidance is the guidance.' And if you follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you will have against God neither protector nor helper."*

**Meaning.** The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ plainly what no amount of accommodation can buy [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. **[Qurṭubī]** draws out the logic: their aim in the signs they demanded was never to believe — had he brought them everything they asked, they would still not be pleased with him; what pleases them is that he abandon Islam and follow them. **[Maʿārif]** explains the placement: the Prophet ﷺ took great pains to convince the deniers and was especially gentle with the People of the Book, and this verse informs him that their denial is not due to a lack of arguments but to pride and self-satisfaction — each of the two groups believes its own religion alone to be genuine, so that nothing will please either of them except his acceptance of their religion. It adds a necessary qualification: the religions of the Jews and Christians were once genuine, instituted by God, but each had since distorted its shape; and with Islam as the final Sharīʿah, God had abrogated all earlier ones, so that Islam has become the only Sharīʿah acceptable to God and, in this final age, the only real guidance. It is because of that distortion and abrogation that the verse equates their religions with *ahwāʾ* — desires, individual opinions and baseless conjectures. **[Study Quran]** notes that for some commentators this verse confirms that the question of 2:118 was not sincere but a taunt, and that *millah* can mean a community as well as the law or way that defines it; it also reports the setting some give: when the qiblah was changed from Jerusalem to the Kaʿbah, resentment grew among the Jews and Christians, who wanted to use a truce as a delaying tactic while trying to turn the Prophet away from the new religion.

**Al-Ṭabarī's argument.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the impossibility its sharpest form: they will never be pleased with you, so give up seeking what pleases them and turn to seeking God's pleasure by calling them to what you were sent with — for that message is itself the way by which they may join you in affection and the upright religion. And there is no way to please them by following their creed, because Judaism is the opposite of Christianity and Christianity the opposite of Judaism; the two cannot be combined in one person at one time, and the Jews and Christians cannot both be pleased with you unless you were at once a Jew and a Christian, which is impossible, since you are one person and two contradictory religions cannot gather in you in one moment. Since there is no way for the two to gather in you, there is no way for you to please the two parties — and since that is so, hold to the guidance of God, which is the way to gathering all creation in affection. And "Say: God's guidance is the guidance" is the call to the Book of God and its clarification, in which the truthful among us is distinguished from the false, and it becomes clear who are the people of the Garden and who the people of the Fire.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the grammar and the lexicon: *riḍā* is pleasure, a hollow-*wāw* word with several verbal nouns, and *tattabiʿ* is in the subjunctive after *an* which is not expressed with *ḥattā* — as al-Khalīl explained, since *ḥattā* governs the noun in the genitive and what governs a noun does not govern the verb; al-Naḥḥās held rather that *tattabiʿ* is governed by *ḥattā* itself, *ḥattā* standing in place of *an*. *Al-millah*, he says, is the name for what God legislated for His servants in His Books and on the tongues of His messengers, so that *millah* and *sharīʿah* are the same, while *dīn* is distinguished from them: the *millah* and *sharīʿah* are what God called His servants to do, and the *dīn* is what the servants do in obedience to His command.

**Rulings — is all disbelief one creed?** **[Qurṭubī]** records a legal dispute that turned on this verse's wording: a group of scholars — Abū Ḥanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī, Dāwūd and Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal in one narration — held that all unbelief is a single *millah*, relying on the singular "their creed," on "to you your religion and to me mine" (109:6), and on the Prophet's saying, "the people of two creeds do not inherit from one another" — with the intended contrast being Islam and unbelief, since the Muslim does not inherit from the disbeliever. Mālik, and Aḥmad in the other narration, held that unbelief comprises several creeds, so that a Jew does not inherit from a Christian, nor do the two inherit from a Magian, taking the outward sense of "the people of two creeds do not inherit from one another." To those who object that the verse uses the singular, **[Qurṭubī]** answers that the singular is intended to cover the many, since it is attached to a plural pronoun — as one says, "I took from the scholars of Madīnah, for instance, their knowledge, and heard from them their reports," meaning their knowledges and their reports.

**Belief.** "And if you follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you..." — **[Saʿdī]** notes that although the address is to the Messenger of God ﷺ, his community is included in it, since the lesson lies in the generality of the meaning rather than in the particular addressee, just as the lesson lies in the generality of the wording rather than the particular occasion. And the clause carries the strongest prohibition against following the desires of the Jews and Christians and against imitating them in what is peculiar to their religion. **[Maʿārif]** handles the difficulty in the hypothetical: other verses establish that God is and remains pleased with His Prophet ﷺ, so he can never be the object of divine wrath — and since divine wrath necessarily follows upon accepting baseless fancies, it is logically impossible for him to follow their opinions at all. The warning is thus addressed to the community through its messenger, its force being that no privilege shields the one who follows desire after knowledge; he will find, against God, no protector and no helper [Ṭabarī].

**Reflection.** The verse is a lesson in the futility of courting a disapproval that cannot be cured. **[Ṭabarī]**'s observation is exact and belongs to every age: since the two communities contradict one another, no single man can satisfy both, and the attempt to please those who will accept nothing but your conversion is a road with no end — while **[Saʿdī]**'s reading of the warning is the other half of the lesson, that the danger is not only to the one who seeks their favour but to the one who drifts into their ways. The verse's remedy is a single sentence: *God's guidance is the guidance* — the one criterion that cannot be bargained.


## 2:121

*"Those to whom We have given the Book, who recite it as it should be recited — they are the ones who believe in it. And whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers."*

**Meaning.** After the warning of the previous verse the Sūrah turns to the other side, and describes the People of the Book who got it right [Maʿārif] [Ṭabarī]. **[Maʿārif]** puts the turn in context: 2:120 dealt with the hopeless condition of the opponents among the People of the Book; the present verse speaks of those Jews and Christians who were honest and just and, having recognized the truth, affirmed the Prophet ﷺ and accepted Islam. The verse tells us how such a radical change was possible: God had given a Book to the Christians as well as to the Jews, and these men — unlike most of their co-religionists — were reading it "observing the rights of its recitation": they had distorted neither its words nor its meanings, nor tried to misinterpret or conceal the prophecies about the coming of the Prophet ﷺ; they had used their intellect to understand the meanings and their will to accept and follow the truth. In affirming the Qurʾān they were in fact affirming their own Books, and acting on them, insofar as those Books explicitly foretell the Last Prophet and the last Book of God. As for those who persist in denial, they are bound for the greatest loss, having refused to believe in the last revelation — and having, in fact, shown little belief in their own Books and little following of the guidance those Books provide on this very point. **[Saʿdī]** gives the definition that the phrase requires: *tilāwah* here is following — they follow it as it should be followed; they make lawful what it makes lawful and forbid what it forbids, act on its clear verses and believe in its ambiguous ones; these are the fortunate among the People of the Book, who recognized God's blessing and thanked Him and believed in all the messengers without distinguishing between any of them — truly the believers, not those who said "we believe in what was sent down to us" while disbelieving what came after it. **[Jalālayn]** reports the occasion the exegetes gave: the verse came down concerning a group of Abyssinians who came to the Prophet ﷺ and accepted Islam, and adds the contrast at the end: whoever disbelieves in it — that is, in the revealed Book, by distorting it — those are the losers, destined for the Fire made everlasting for them.

**Language — what "true recitation" means.** **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Ibn Kathīr]** collect the explanations, and they turn entirely on the double sense of *talā*. ʿIkrimah, Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd: to follow it with true following, by obeying its commands and prohibitions, making lawful what it permits and forbidding what it prohibits, acting on what it contains — and ʿIkrimah cites the Qurʾān's own usage, "and the moon when it follows it (*talāhā*)" (91:2), meaning follows after it. Ibn Masʿūd's version in **[Ibn Kathīr]** is fuller: by Him in whose hand is my soul, the right *tilāwah* is to make lawful what it makes lawful, forbid what it forbids, recite it as God revealed it, not change the words from their places and not interpret it with other than its true interpretation. **[Qurṭubī]** records the same sense in a report attributed to the Prophet ﷺ through Ibn ʿUmar — "they follow it as it should be followed" — noting that its chain contains unknown narrators although the meaning is sound. ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb gave a different practical description: they are those who, when they pass a verse of mercy, ask God for it, and when they pass a verse of punishment, seek refuge from it — and this meaning is reported of the Prophet's ﷺ own practice, that when he recited a verse of mercy he asked, and when he recited a verse of punishment he sought refuge. Al-Ḥasan: they act on its clear verses, believe in its ambiguous ones, and refer what is obscure to the One who knows it. **[Qurṭubī]** adds his own judgement on the narrowest reading — that it means merely to pronounce the words correctly — that it is remote, unless the sense be that they recite its words well *and understand its meanings*, for it is by understanding the meanings that following is achieved by whoever is granted success. **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes al-Suddī's report from Ibn ʿAbbās on the same lines — they make lawful what it allows and prohibit what it forbids and do not alter its wording — and gives the sense of the whole: those among the People of the Book who adhered perfectly to the Books revealed to the earlier prophets will believe in what has been sent to Muḥammad ﷺ, as 5:66 has it: "had they established the Torah and the Gospel and what was sent down to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet." **[Maʿārif]** notes the disagreement over the referent — some hold those "given the Book" to be the Prophet's ﷺ Companions and the Book to be the Qurʾān, others that they are the Jews and Christians who accepted Islam, with the Torah meant — and observes that the verse is general enough to include both.

**Reflection.** The verse is the Sūrah's answer to the charge that it has been unfair to the People of the Book: here is the pattern of the ones who were saved, and it is not a pattern of rejecting their own scriptures but of reading them honestly. The test, as **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Ibn Kathīr]** present it, is deliberately unglamorous: recite the words rightly, understand them, and then let them govern what you permit and forbid — and the community that does this will recognize the messenger its own Book announced. The verse thus puts the loss at the end where it belongs: not in ignorance of the Qurʾān, but in disbelieving a Book one claims to have been following all along.


## 2:124

*"And when his Lord tried Ibrāhīm with certain words, and he fulfilled them, He said: 'I am making you a leader of the people.' He said: 'And of my offspring?' He said: 'My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers.'"*

**Meaning.** The Sūrah now turns from the history of Israel to the man both communities claim, and the turn is polemical [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif] [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** explains the placement: when the Kaʿbah and the qiblah were mentioned, that connected to the mention of Ibrāhīm — the one who built the House — and it was the right of the Jews, who are of Ibrāhīm's seed, not to turn away from his religion. **[Maʿārif]** sets out the section's design more fully: the Jews were proud of being the children of Yaʿqūb and Ibrāhīm and believed that, as the chosen people, they had the exclusive privilege of leadership, so that prophethood could not be conferred on anyone outside their race.
