The Sūrah refutes this line of thought by telling the story of Ibrāhīm and his elder son Ismāʿīl: that only the one who is not a transgressor and who has passed God's trial can be a guide to humanity; that the Kaʿbah, which the Muslims face in prayer and which the Jews reject, was built by Ibrāhīm himself; that Islam is the way of Ibrāhīm and the Muslims are his real followers; that it was Ibrāhīm who prayed for the Last Prophet; and that Ibrāhīm had two sons, so that the superiority once enjoyed by the children of Isḥāq has now passed to the children of Ismāʿīl. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the vocabulary: *ibtilāʾ* is testing and trial — as in "test the orphans" (4:6) — and God's testing of Ibrāhīm was by obligations He imposed and commands He gave, and those are the *kalimāt*, the words, which He revealed to him and charged him to perform. The point of the trial is stated in a principle **[Saʿdī]** draws out: it is God's way with His servants, so that the liar who does not stand firm when tested may be distinguished from the truthful one whose rank is raised, whose worth increases, whose deed is purified and whose gold is assayed. Ibrāhīm was among the foremost in that station, and he completed what God tested him with, and God thanked him for it — for God is ever grateful.

**What were the "words"?** **[Ṭabarī]** reports the answers of the early authorities. Ibn ʿAbbās, in ʿIkrimah's report: no one was tried with this religion and stood by it entirely except Ibrāhīm — he was tried with Islam and he completed it, and God wrote for him a declaration of innocence, "and Ibrāhīm, who fulfilled" (53:37). And the trial is, on this account, the thirty shares of Islam, which Ibn ʿAbbās locates in the Qurʾān's own descriptions of the believers: ten in Sūrat al-Tawbah — "the repentant, the worshipping, the praising..." (9:112) — ten in Sūrat al-Aḥzāb, "the Muslim men and Muslim women..." (33:35), and ten in Sūrat al-Muʾminūn and Sūrat Sāʾil, "those who are humble in their prayers..." down to "those who guard their prayers" (23:1-9; 70:22-34). **[Qurṭubī]** adds further views: the rites of the pilgrimage specifically; and al-Ḥasan's six — the star, the moon, the sun, the fire, the emigration and circumcision — with al-Zajjāj's comment that these accounts do not contradict one another, since Ibrāhīm was tested with all of it. **[Study Quran]** records the same range: commands to institute various kinds of bodily cleanliness and ritual purification; the rituals and prayers of the ḥajj, which Muslims consider to have originated with Ibrāhīm, including the circumambulation, the running between Ṣafā and Marwah and the pelting of the pillar; trials of suffering such as his circumcision, the sacrifice of his son (37:102) and the fire into which his people cast him and which God made cool (21:68-69); and the virtuous human qualities catalogued in verses such as 9:112 and 33:35, with the report that some take "Ibrāhīm fulfilled" to mean his selection as *imām*. **[Qurṭubī]** then pursues one of the "words" into the law: the scholars agree that Ibrāhīm was the first to be circumcised, and the reports differ only over his age — one report has him at one hundred and twenty years, living eighty more; the well-known report has him circumcised at eighty, and with an adze. And he records Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib's list: Ibrāhīm was the first to be circumcised, the first to offer hospitality, the first to use the razor, the first to trim the nails, the first to cut the moustache, and the first to turn grey — and when he saw the grey he asked what it was, and was told it was dignity, and he said, "O Lord, increase me in dignity." He also records the report that Ibrāhīm was the first to speak from pulpits, the first to break bread into broth, the first to strike with the sword, the first to clean his teeth, the first to purify himself with water and the first to wear trousers — and Muʿādh b. Jabal's report that the Prophet ﷺ said, "If I take a pulpit, my father Ibrāhīm took one; and if I take a staff, my father Ibrāhīm took one."

**The leader and the covenant.** *Imām*, **[Study Quran]** explains, is most generally a leader — religious or political, or the one who leads the prayer; in Shiism it carries the particular sense of one designated by divine decree in whom the Muhammadan Light is present. **[Saʿdī]** describes what the rank involves and why it was given: God made him one whom people follow in guidance, walking behind him to their eternal felicity, and for whom there is lasting praise, ample reward and the esteem of everyone — and this, he says, is the best rank for which competitors compete, the highest station the strivers aim at, the most complete state attained by the resolute among the messengers and their followers; and when Ibrāhīm rejoiced in the station and grasped it, he asked it for his offspring, out of his love that guides should be many among God's servants. Then came the answer: *my covenant does not reach the wrongdoers.* **[Saʿdī]**'s comment on the word: the imamate in religion cannot be attained by one who wrongs himself and diminishes his own worth, for wrongdoing is incompatible with the station — the station whose equipment is patience and certainty, and whose fruit is a great share of faith, good deeds, noble character, sound traits, complete love, fear and penitence. **[Study Quran]** reports the exegetical options: that a wrongdoer or tyrant would not deserve a covenant with God and could not rightly be an imām; or that such a person might be an imām but would not receive the promise of the Hereafter; or simply that not all of Ibrāhīm's descendants would be virtuous, as in 37:113: "and among their progeny are the virtuous and those who clearly wrong themselves" — and it notes that in Shiism the fifth and sixth Imams cited this verse to show that God does not set up or allow an unjust imām, and it compares 25:74, "make us imāms for the reverent."

**Belief.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** frames the verse as an address to the idolaters and the People of the Book who pretend to follow the religion of Ibrāhīm while not following it, while Muḥammad ﷺ and his followers are its true followers; and the rank of leader was given to Ibrāhīm only after he adhered to God's commands and prohibitions, as 53:37 says, "and Ibrāhīm, who fulfilled." He adduces 16:120-123 — "verily Ibrāhīm was an ummah, obedient to God, ḥanīf, and he was not of the idolaters; thankful for His favours; He chose him and guided him to a straight path; and We gave him good in this world, and in the Hereafter he shall be among the righteous; then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Ibrāhīm, ḥanīf" — and notes that this is the sense in which the Qurʾān uses "ummah": a man who is a whole community in himself by his obedience and his guidance.

**Reflection.** The verse gives the Sūrah's argument its hinge: the leadership of humanity is not an inheritance but a covenant, and the covenant is granted after the trial, not before it — to the man who was tested and fulfilled what he was tested with. That single sentence dismantles the claims the Sūrah has been encountering: descent from Ibrāhīm means nothing to a people who do not walk in his way, while the one who does walk in it has joined his line whatever his tribe. And the closing clause is the permanent criterion: not "my covenant does not reach the children of others," but "my covenant does not reach the wrongdoers" — a principle that every community that imagines itself chosen must reckon with, since it was revealed precisely about the descendants of the friend of God.


## 2:125

*"And when We made the House a place of return for people, and a sanctuary — 'Take the station of Ibrāhīm as a place of prayer.' And We charged Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl: 'Purify My House for those who circumambulate, and those who retire there, and those who bow and prostrate.'"*

**Meaning.** The Sūrah continues Ibrāhīm's story with the House his descendants would dispute about [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif] [Ṭabarī]. **[Maʿārif]** states the argument the verse serves: the Jews denied the Prophet ﷺ on the assumption that prophethood could not go outside their clan, and scoffed at the Muslims for turning toward the Kaʿbah and thought the ḥajj no more than a custom of the ignorant Arabs. The previous verse established that prophethood cannot be given to the unjust and disobedient even of Ibrāhīm's progeny, which destroys the basis of their vanity; the present verse reminds them that the Kaʿbah was built under divine command by Ibrāhīm himself with his son Ismāʿīl, so that both the orientation and the pilgrimage are of divine institution, that the Prophet ﷺ is a direct descendant of Ibrāhīm through Ismāʿīl, and that he is reviving the Abrahamic way which the Jews too must follow. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the sense of the first clause: *mathābah* is a place of return and refuge — people come to it every year and return to it, and never leave it having had their fill. He reports Waraqah b. Nawfal's line in praise of the sanctuary: "a place of return for the branches of all the tribes; the lean she-camels trot toward it." **[Qurṭubī]** adds Mujāhid's observation inscribed in a poet's line: the House was made a place of return "from which they never, all their lives, attain their desire" — they keep coming back because departure only increases the longing. And on the second noun: *amn* is security, and **[Qurṭubī]** records what it meant concretely in the Jāhiliyyah — a man could meet the killer of his father or brother inside the sanctuary and not raise a hand against him.

**The station of Ibrāhīm.** **[Study Quran]** explains that the station is a place in the close vicinity of the Kaʿbah marked by a stone said to have borne Ibrāhīm's footprint; that some commentators take it as the ḥajj rites as a whole, or as another location important to the ḥajj such as ʿArafah, Muzdalīfah or Minā. **[Saʿdī]** prefers the view that *muṣallā* means a place of worship, so that the command is to follow Ibrāhīm in the rites of the pilgrimage — the circumambulation, the running, the standing at ʿArafah and Muzdalīfah, the pelting of the pillars and the sacrifice — since the first reading is included in it and the wording admits it; while the majority hold the station to be the well-known place facing the door of the Kaʿbah, so that the verse recommends the two units of prayer after the circumambulation behind it. **[Study Quran]** reports the ḥadīth that the Prophet ﷺ took ʿUmar by the hand and said, "This is the station of Ibrāhīm," and ʿUmar asked, "Shall we take it as a place of prayer?" and the Prophet said he had not been commanded to — and that some commentators say this verse came down before sunset of that day. **[Jalālayn]** reads the command as addressed to the community: take the station of Ibrāhīm as a place of prayer. **[Study Quran]** further notes that some read the verb in the past tense, "they took," referring to people who had already done so.

**The purification and the worshippers.** "Purify My House" [Jalālayn] [Ibn Kathīr] [Saʿdī]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the meaning: cleanse it of graven images, for the sake of those who go round it, those who cleave to it in ritual residence, and those who bow and prostrate — that is, those who pray. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reports the glosses: al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, that God ordered them to purify it from every kind of filth and impurity, so that none of it should touch the House; ʿAṭāʾ, that the "covenant" is God's command; and Ibn ʿAbbās, "purify it of the idols," with Mujāhid and Saʿīd b. Jubayr adding fornication and the practices of the Jāhiliyyah. **[Saʿdī]** gives the several senses: purify it of polytheism and unbelief, of disobedience, of physical filth and impurity. Then he attends to the order of the classes: the circumambulators are named first because circumambulation is peculiar to the Sacred Mosque; then those in retreat, because the condition of retreat is the mosque generally; then prayer, though it is the most excellent, because of what the context demanded. And he observes why God called it "My House": it obliges Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl to expend their utmost in purifying it, since it bears God's name; it carries honour and veneration, and thus an implicit command to His servants to magnify it; and it is the cause that draws hearts toward it. **[Study Quran]** defines the classes: the circumambulation is walking around the Kaʿbah, one of the major rites of the ḥajj; bowing and prostration are movements of the prayer; and "those who retire" translates *al-ʿākifīn*, from the root meaning to hold to a place — the practice of *iʿtikāf*, secluding oneself in a mosque for prayer and remembrance, based on the Prophet's ﷺ practice in the last ten days of Ramaḍān, and the ultimate basis, it notes, of the Sufi practice of spiritual retreat.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** derives from the security of the House a legal dispute that has lasted: Abū Ḥanīfah and a group of the jurists of the garrison cities argued from this verse, and from "whoever enters it is safe" (3:97), that the fixed penalties should not be carried out within the sanctuary against the adulterer or the thief who has taken refuge there — the verse, on their reading, meaning "grant security to whoever enters the House." The sound position, **[Qurṭubī]** says, is that the penalties *are* established within the sacred precinct, and that the promise of security is among the abrogated texts. He also records the grammatical dispute over *mathābah*: whether the *hāʾ* is added for intensification because of the multitudes who return — like *allāmah* and *nassābah* — or is the *hāʾ* of the verbal noun; al-Aʿmash read *mathābāt* in the plural; and the noun is in any case the second object of "We made," with the sense that no one leaves the House without believing he has not yet attained his desire, so that the whole body of pilgrims is always returning. **[Maʿārif]** cites 22:26-27, where the same commission is given in the pilgrimage sūrah — "and when We prepared for Ibrāhīm the place of the House: that you associate nothing with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate and stand and bow and prostrate" — and gives the same reading of the worship classes as **[Saʿdī]**.

**Reflection.** The verse gives the House two marks — a place men return to, and a place where they are safe — and then asks of those who serve it that they keep it clean for the people who come. The three classes it names are the whole of religion in miniature: the one who travels around the centre, the one who stays beside it, and the one who bows and falls before God. And the argument the verse serves is worth holding in view: the House was not built to make one family privileged; it was made a place of return *for people*, secured for whoever enters, and the purification demanded of its founders was precisely of the things that would turn it into a possession — idols, filth, the quarrels of the Jāhiliyyah.


## 2:126

*"And when Ibrāhīm said, 'My Lord, make this a secure land, and provide its people with fruits — those of them who believe in God and the Last Day.' He said, 'And whoever disbelieves — I shall grant him enjoyment for a while, then I shall compel him to the punishment of the Fire; and what an evil destination!'"*

**Meaning.** The founder of the House prays for the city, and the answer teaches a lesson about provision [Jalālayn] [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif]. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the sense of *āminan*: secure from tyrants and the powerful, and from the punishments of God that fall upon other lands — the swallowing of the earth, its overturning, drowning and the rest of His wrath. **[Qurṭubī]** reports the story attached to the gift of fruits: when Ibrāhīm made this prayer, God commanded Jibrīl, who lifted al-Ṭāʾif from Syria, carried it around the House for a week — whence its name, from *ṭāfa* — and then set it down in Tihāmah; for Makkah at that time was a barren waste with neither water nor vegetation, and God blessed what was around it and brought forth fruits of many kinds, the details of which come in Sūrat Ibrāhīm. **[Maʿārif]** observes the wisdom in the shape of the prayer itself: Ibrāhīm did not ask that the land of Makkah itself be made fertile, but that fruits should come to its people, so that his descendants would not be absorbed in agriculture — his purpose in founding the settlement being, as 14:37 says, that they "should establish the prayer." The word *thamarat*, fruit, recurs in the same context at 28:57, "the fruits of every kind are drawn toward it," and the verb "drawn" shows that the prayer was answered by import rather than by local abundance.

**The sanctity of the land.** **[Ṭabarī]** and **[Ibn Kathīr]** record the Prophet's ﷺ proclamation at the conquest of Makkah, in Abū Shurayḥ al-Khuzāʿī's report: when Makkah was opened, Khuzāʿah killed a man of Hudhayl, and the Messenger of God ﷺ stood and said, "O people, God made Makkah sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth; it is sacred by God's sanctity until the Day of Resurrection; killing was never lawful in it for anyone before me, and will not be lawful for anyone after me." **[Ṭabarī]** reports Qatāda's tradition that the Ḥaram was made sacred to the height of the Throne, and that the House came down with Ādam — God telling him, "I have sent down My House with you, that it be circumambulated as My Throne is circumambulated" — so that Ādam and the believers after him circled it, until at the time of the Flood God raised it and purified it, and it was untouched by the punishment of the earth's people; afterwards Ibrāhīm traced its traces and built upon foundations that had been laid before him. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the ḥadīth of Jābir: "Ibrāhīm made God's House sacred and safe, and I have made Madīnah sacred between its two lava-fields, so that its game is not hunted and its thorn-trees are not cut." And **[Qurṭubī]** notes the visible sign of the sanctity: inside the sacred boundary the dog and the game it chases come together and the dog does not startle the game nor the game flee from it, until they leave the Ḥaram, when the dog attacks and the game takes flight again. **[Maʿārif]** adds that the inhabitants of Makkah were respected throughout Arabia and their caravans to Syria and Yemen passed unmolested, that even birds and animals within the Ḥaram show a sense of security, and that Islam reinforced the sanctity — and where killings did occur inside it, as at the hands of al-Ḥajjāj b. Yūsuf or the Qarāmiṭah, they were the work of men calling themselves Muslims, not of an outside invasion; a man who burns his own house does not disprove its protection from strangers. He also records that, in answer to the prayer, al-Ṭāʾif was made fertile and its fruits brought into Makkah, with the Israelite tradition that it had been lifted from Syria by Jibrīl on God's command.

**The qualification and the answer.** **[Saʿdī]** explains the shift: Ibrāhīm's first prayer had been unrestricted, and the answer had come back qualified — "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers" — so when he prayed for provision he tied it to the believers, out of courtesy toward God. But God's provision in this world encompasses everyone, Muslim and disbeliever, obedient and disobedient: so the answer came, "and whoever disbelieves — I shall grant him enjoyment for a while." And the two fates are stated: the Muslim uses the provision as an aid to worshiping God and then passes from it to the bliss of the Garden; the disbeliever enjoys it briefly, and then God compels him — drives him unwillingly — to the punishment of the Fire. "And what an evil destination." **[Jalālayn]** notes the reading of the verb of enjoyment both ways — *umtiʿuhu* and *umattiʿuhu* — and the sense of *aḍṭarruhu* as God driving him to the chastisement so that no escape is found. **[Ṭabarī]** records the debate over whether the Ḥaram was always secure and Ibrāhīm's prayer only confirmed it, or whether its security came in answer to that prayer; he favours the former, the reports of the Prophet ﷺ on the primordial sanctity being decisive. **[Study Quran]** records the same ḥadīth on the day of the conquest, and notes that the root of *āmin* connects to the *amn* of the previous verse, while Ibrāhīm's prayer for the valley "without cultivation" appears at 14:37, and that the Arabs were said to visit the Kaʿbah for no worldly need — presumably for only spiritual reasons.

**Reflection.** The verses hold together the two things a city can be given and the two things it can do with them. Makkah received security and food; the prayer that asked for them asked for a place where people would be free to worship, and the wisdom in the shape of the request — abundance drawn toward the sanctuary rather than grown in it — is that the settlement exist for the House rather than the House for the settlement. And the qualification that God appended to the answer is the verse's quiet correction of every claim to a monopoly on God's gifts: provision is for all in this world, while the promise is for the believers — a distinction that makes the world's prosperity a poor proof of one's standing, and its absence equally poor.


## 2:127

*"And when Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl were raising the foundations of the House: 'Our Lord, accept it from us; surely You are the Hearing, the Knowing.'"*

**Meaning.** The verse shows the two of them at work and at prayer [Maʿārif] [Saʿdī]. **[Maʿārif]** draws from the scene one of Ibrāhīm's essential qualities: in obedience to God he had left the fertile land of Syria, settled his wife and child in a barren desert, and now took up the labour of building the House of God — a moment when a man who had borne such hardships could be expected to feel satisfied with himself and relax in self-congratulation. But the Friend of God recognized God's majesty and knew that no creature can worship or obey his Creator as is His due, only within his own limited powers; and so, in performing the greatest of tasks, he did not grow proud of his achievement but humbly prayed that God accept the little effort he had been capable of — and that too only by God's own grace. The prayer itself acknowledges why such a prayer can be answered at all: God is the Hearing of words and the Knowing of intentions. **[Saʿdī]** notes the state the two were in even while engaged in so great a work: fear and hope together, so that they asked God to accept the deed and to place benefit in it for others.

**The foundations.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the lexical point: *al-qawāʿid* are the foundations, per Abū ʿUbaydah and al-Farrāʾ; al-Kisāʾī said they are the walls, but the well-known sense is the foundations — the singular being *qāʿidah*, while the *qawāʿid* of women, the elderly, has the singular *qāʿid*, since the word there comes from "sitting back from menstruation" with no masculine counterpart, so the feminine *hāʾ* is dropped, exactly as one says "a woman in purity, a woman menstruating." **[Ṭabarī]** makes the same grammatical observation and then raises the historical question: did the two of them build the foundations from nothing, or were they foundations that already existed before them? **[Qurṭubī]** reports the range of opinion on who first founded the House: the angels — with the report from Jaʿfar b. Muḥammad that when God said "I am placing a vicegerent on the earth" and the angels asked about one who would shed blood while they glorified Him, God was angry with them, and they sought refuge at His Throne and circumambulated it seven circuits until He was pleased, and He told them to build Him a house on earth where those who come after might seek refuge as they had done; and Ādam, who built it by God's command after his descent, from five mountains, with its centre from Ḥirāʾ; and the report of Ibn ʿAbbās that the House was placed upon pillars he saw two thousand years before the world was created, and then the earth was spread out from beneath it. **[Qurṭubī]** also gives the report that when the House was demolished and great stones were brought out of it, Ibn al-Zubayr said, "These are the foundations that Ibrāhīm raised" — and the view that the foundations had been effaced and God showed them to Ibrāhīm. **[Study Quran]** summarizes the traditional lore — Ādam, having ceased to hear the voices of the angels because of his sin, is told that God will send down a House around which people will circumambulate as the angels go round the Throne; the House is raised up, then disappears with the Flood, until Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl bring out the foundations again rather than building from nothing — and notes that al-Ṭabarī recounts these stories while stating they are not reliable as actual history, though many other commentators accept them. **[Jalālayn]** reads the clause straightforwardly: the foundations, or the walls, of the House, "of the House" being connected to the verb "raising," with Ismāʿīl joined to Ibrāhīm as a partner in the work and in the prayer.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** connects the verse to 22:26, where God assigns the place of the House to Ibrāhīm, and to 3:96, "truly the first house established for mankind was that at Bakkah" — Bakkah being an alternate pronunciation of Makkah, also referenced in Psalm 84:6 — and observes that the Qurʾān elsewhere returns to the subject again and again, supplying the details of the ḥajj in separate passages. **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s material on the sanctity of the House, given under the previous verse, stands behind the scene: the Prophet's ﷺ proclamation that God made Makkah sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth, that its game is not chased, its fallen objects not picked up except by one who announces them, its thorny shrubs not uprooted and its trees not cut — with al-ʿAbbās asking for the *idhkhir* grass used by their goldsmiths and for their graves, and the Prophet ﷺ allowing it.

**Reflection.** The scene is the Sūrah's answer to anyone who thinks of the Kaʿbah as an achievement. Two men are laying the first stones of the House that will stand at the centre of the world's worship, and what the Qurʾān records of them at that moment is not triumph but a request that the work be accepted. **[Maʿārif]**'s observation is the verse's practical lesson: it is precisely when the deed is greatest that a man most needs to distrust his own satisfaction with it, since what he offers is little at best and His acceptance is the whole of its worth. The prayer also names the attributes that make acceptance conceivable: a Lord who hears the words said in the desert and knows the intentions behind them.


## 2:128

*"Our Lord, make us both submissive to You, and from our offspring a community submissive to You; and show us our rites; and relent toward us. Surely You are the Relenting, the Merciful."*

**Meaning.** The prayer continues, and its first word is its own argument [Maʿārif] [Jalālayn]. **[Maʿārif]** draws attention to the wonder of it: Ibrāhīm had spent his whole life in exemplary obedience, and here he prays to *be made* obedient — and the reason is that the more a man grows in knowledge of God's majesty, the more he realizes how far short his obedience falls of what is due. The verse's second clause shows something else: the man of God who does not flinch at sacrificing himself and his children in God's way still loves them deeply, but knows what the requirements of parental love truly are. Ordinary people suppose their children's well-being lies in physical health and comfort and spend all their care on providing it; those who have received God's favour are more solicitous for their children's spiritual welfare than their physical, more anxious about what becomes of them in the next world than in this. So the prayer is for a group from his descendants fully obedient to God. **[Jalālayn]** notes the grammar that carries the meaning: "from our offspring" is partitive, and this follows God's earlier answer — "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers" — so that the request is made for a portion, not for all. **[Study Quran]** observes that *muslim* here, the participle of a transitive verb, is tied to the *islām* of 2:132, and that these verses testify to the universal sense of *islām*, which existed before the revelation of the Qurʾān.

**The rites.** "And show us our rites" [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** reports the readings and their sense: the common reading is from the seeing of the eye — show them to our eyes so that we may see them — and the exegetes differ over what the *manāsik* are. Qatāda said God showed them their rites: the circumambulation of the House, the running between Ṣafā and Marwah, the departure from ʿArafāt and from Muzdalifah, and the pelting of the pillars — until God completed the religion. Al-Suddī gives the scene that follows: when Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl finished building the House, God commanded him to call out — "and proclaim the ḥajj among the people" (22:27) — and he called between the two rough mountains of Makkah, "O people, God commands you to make pilgrimage to His House." **[Study Quran]** notes the range of the term: the rites are often taken as the rituals of the ḥajj, or as sacrifice, or as worship in general, with the general sense appearing in 22:34 and 22:67, "for every community We have appointed a rite." **[Saʿdī]** prefers to keep both possibilities open: the context and the occasion point to the rites of the pilgrimage, while the generality of the wording points to the whole religion and all acts of worship, since *nusuk* is worship — and so the prayer's sum is a request for success in beneficial knowledge and righteous action. **[Maʿārif]** notes that the word *mansak* signifies the mode and place of worship, so that the prayer is for instruction in worship that has been seen and demonstrated, which is more emphatic than mere information.

**Relent, and why.** When a servant, whatever his station, is never free of shortcoming and always in need of repentance, the two said: "and relent toward us; surely You are the Relenting, the Merciful" [Saʿdī]. **[Jalālayn]** notes the wonder that they asked Him to turn toward them despite their moral impeccability — out of humility, and to teach their descendants. **[Study Quran]** explains the reciprocity built into the term: *tawbah* is an act in which God "turns" toward human beings in compassion while they "turn" to Him in repentance, so that the prayer for God to relent is the counterpart of the servant's own turning. It also notes the commentators' explanation for praying for their progeny rather than for all beings: that one's kin have the first right to one's kindness and concern, as in 66:6, "shield yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is mankind and stones."

**The answer given.** **[Maʿārif]** observes that God heard this prayer too: among Ibrāhīm's descendants there has always been a group obedient to God and firm on the straight path — and even in the Age of Ignorance, when the world and Arabia in particular were lost in the darkness of idol-worship, there remained men of his line who believed in the One God and the Hereafter and obeyed Him: Zayd b. ʿAmr b. Nufayl, Quss b. Sāʿidah, and, it is reported, ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib b. Hāshim, the Prophet's ﷺ grandfather, who shunned the worship of idols. He adds another advantage the prayer sought: when people of standing and their descendants keep to the right path, they are naturally held in esteem and their conduct moves others to reform.

**Reflection.** The verse is a lesson in how a man who has done everything still asks. Ibrāhīm has left his homeland, survived the fire, settled his family in a desert and built the House — and his prayer is: make us submissive, teach us how to worship, and forgive us. **[Maʿārif]**'s explanation is the one the verse itself intends, that knowledge of God's greatness and satisfaction with one's own service cannot coexist; and the second half of the prayer gives the shape of a prophet's love — not comfort for his children, but a portion of them, a community, submissive to their Lord.


## 2:129

*"Our Lord, raise up among them a messenger from among themselves, who shall recite Your signs to them, and teach them the Book and the Wisdom, and purify them. Surely You are the Mighty, the Wise."*

**Meaning.** The prayer of the two builders ends by asking for the one who would come at the end of the line [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Jalālayn]. **[Ṭabarī]** makes the identification plain: this is Ibrāhīm's and Ismāʿīl's supplication for Muḥammad ﷺ specifically — the supplication of which the Prophet ﷺ used to say, "I am the supplication of my father Ibrāhīm and the good news of ʿĪsā." The report comes through Khālid b. Maʿdān, that a group of the Companions said, "O Messenger of God, tell us about yourself," and he said, "Yes — I am the supplication of my father Ibrāhīm and the good news of ʿĪsā" [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives also the reading in Ubayy's codex: "and raise up in their last ones a messenger from among them," and the lexical note on *rasūl* as *mursal*, the one sent. **[Ibn Kathīr]** uses the verse to settle a question of theology: Ibrāhīm prayed for a messenger God had already decreed would come — as the Prophet ﷺ was written as the final prophet while Ādam was still clay — and God accepted the supplication although He knew beforehand it would occur by His decree; the prayer and the decree are not rivals, since the prayer itself was part of what was decreed.

**What the messenger would do.** Four functions are named, and **[Jalālayn]** gives them briefly: he recites God's signs — the Qurʾān — to them; he teaches them the Book and the Wisdom, the latter being what it contains of judgments; and he purifies them, cleansing them of idolatry [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. **[Maʿārif]** attends to the words. *Tilāwah* lexically signifies following and obeying, but in the usage of the Qurʾān and Ḥadīth it denotes the recitation of a divine Book — for one who reads a divine Book is also obliged to obey it fully; and the word also carries the implication that the Book must be read exactly as God revealed it, with nothing added or subtracted, not even a pronunciation changed, since in Arabic a change of pronunciation often changes the meaning. It cites al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's observation that *tilāwah* in current usage applies only to the reading of God's Word. On *ḥikmah*, it records the range: arriving at truth, justice, exact knowledge; for God, the perfect knowledge of all existents and flawless creation; for others, a proper knowledge of things and good deeds; the Companions' and Successors' interpretations — the commentary and exegesis of the Qurʾān, the understanding of religion, the injunctions of the Sharīʿah, what was received through the Prophet's ﷺ word — and concludes that, despite the variety of expressions, the substance is the same: the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ and the Ḥadīth, which is Qatāda's interpretation as reported by both Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same identification with more of the detail: the Book is the Qurʾān; the Wisdom, says Mālik, is knowledge of religion and understanding of interpretation, and the grasp of things that is a gift and a light from God; Qatāda said it is the Sunnah and the clarification of the laws; others said it is judgment and adjudication — the meanings, he notes, are close to one another. Purification, on Ibn Jurayj's reading, is cleansing from the filth of idolatry. And he arranges the three functions in a hierarchy: the signs are the recitation of the outward words, the Book is the meanings of the words, and the Wisdom is the rulings — God's intention in address, in its absolute and restricted forms, in its explained and its summarized, in its general and its particular.

**Why a prophet from among them.** **[Maʿārif]** answers the question the prayer invites: Ibrāhīm asked that the prophet be raised from among his descendants for two reasons — the appearance of a prophet from a people is itself an honour and blessing to them, and a prophet who is one of them is thoroughly familiar to them, and they familiar with him, his ways and his life before and after the mission, which makes acceptance easier. And it notes the fulfilment: the prayer was answered in the Prophet ﷺ, and the answer is written into the Sūrah itself in 2:151, where the Prophet is described in the identical terms — "as We have sent among you a messenger from among yourselves, reciting to you Our signs, purifying you, and teaching you the Book and the Wisdom." **[Study Quran]** makes the same observation about the response in 2:151, and notes that the Book is most often taken as the Qurʾān and the Wisdom as the Sunnah or, more generally, knowledge and understanding of religion, while observing that the pairing of Book and Wisdom has a wider use in the Qurʾān — connected also with ʿĪsā (3:48; 5:110), the Children of Israel (45:16), and the House of Ibrāhīm (4:54).

**Belief.** The prayer closes with two names, and **[Qurṭubī]** explains why they fit. *Al-ʿAzīz*: the mighty whom none can reach or overcome; the one nothing can frustrate, as 35:44 says; or the one who overcomes, whence the saying "whoever overcomes, despoils"; or the one with no like, even as "there is nothing like Him." There was no obstacle that could prevent this supplication from being granted, nor was there any step in it that wisdom would not have chosen. **[Saʿdī]** draws the practical lesson from all four clauses: the prayer's sum is a request for success in beneficial knowledge and righteous action — signs recited so as to be heard and preserved, a Book taught for its meanings, a Wisdom given, and souls purified — the four together describing what the messenger does for the community he is sent to.

**Reflection.** The verse is the seed of the Sūrah's own fulfilment. Two men, laying the foundations of a house in a barren valley, ask for a messenger who will teach their descendants the Book — and thirteen centuries of history later, the answer to that prayer stands in the middle of the Sūrah, describing the Prophet ﷺ in the same four words. **[Maʿārif]**'s observation about familiarity is worth keeping: part of the mercy of the sending is that the messenger was one of them, so that those who were asked to believe could see, in a neighbour whom they had known all their lives, what a life looks like when God teaches it. And the closing pair of names is the seal of the prayer: what was asked for was great, and the One asked is mighty and wise — able to grant it, and wise in the granting.


## 2:130

*"And who turns away from the creed of Ibrāhīm but one who fools his own soul? And We chose him in this world, and in the Hereafter he is among the righteous."*

**Meaning.** The verse states the consequence of everything the passage has established [Saʿdī] [Jalālayn] [Maʿārif]. **[Saʿdī]** puts the rhetorical question to work: who turns away from the creed of Ibrāhīm after having known its excellence, except the one who has fooled his own soul — that is, who is ignorant of it, holds it cheap, is content with the lowest for it, and sells it in the transaction of the cheated? And just as no one turns away from that creed but a fooled soul, so there is no one better guided or more complete than the one who desires it. Then the verse reports Ibrāhīm's own state in both worlds: "We chose him in this world" — We selected him and enabled him for the deeds by which he became one of the chosen and the excellent — "and in the Hereafter he is among the righteous": those who have the highest ranks. **[Jalālayn]** fills in the sense of "fools his own soul": the one who ignores that his soul was created for God and is obliged to worship Him, or who treats it with frivolity and degrades it; and specifies that God's choosing of Ibrāhīm in this world was for prophethood and for His friendship, while in the Hereafter his place is among the righteous.

**Context.** **[Maʿārif]** sets the verse in the sequence: the previous verses have defined the basic principles of Ibrāhīm's religion, called people to follow it, warned against turning away from it, and refuted the claims of the Jews and Christians to be its followers while indicating Islam as the religion now faithful to the Abrahamic tradition — and the present verses show the prophets' solicitude in giving religious instruction and guidance to their descendants. On this verse he observes that only a man who has no understanding, or has lost it entirely, can turn away from this religion, since it is the religion of "nature" itself, and no one denies it so long as his nature remains intact in its essential and integral sense. The honour God gave Ibrāhīm in this world on account of this very religion is visible to all: how Namrūd with all his might failed to impress him; how he gladly accepted being thrown into the fire rather than give up the worship of the One God; and how the Lord of the worlds turned the fire into a garden for him, so that believers and unbelievers alike came to recognize his uprightness and his unalloyed faith. And the idolaters of Arabia, after all, were his progeny, and despite their idol-worship had always held him in great esteem and claimed to be his followers, with certain remnants of his religion still present among them, though distorted by their ignorance.

**The creed and the ancestors of the faith.** **[Study Quran]** notes that Ibrāhīm's creed is often associated with the notion of *ḥanīf* (2:135), and that "We chose him" means he was given special favour in this world in addition to his rank in the Hereafter — a choosing that the Qurʾān attributes to other figures as well: Maryam (3:42), Mūsā (7:144), Ādam (20:122), the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ (35:32) and other prophets (6:87). On the identity of those who turn away, many commentators understand the Jews and Christians to be meant, since it is their claim to Ibrāhīm's legacy that the passage has been dismantling. And it records two further readings of the verse's bearing: for some commentators it demonstrates the continuity between the law of Ibrāhīm and the law of Muḥammad, the latter in principle retaining the former except where it abrogates it; and this continuity is visible concretely in the connection of the Islamic rites of the ḥajj with Ibrāhīm, and in the opinion that many of the Sunnah practices relating to bodily cleanliness go back to him — the very "words" with which he was tested at 2:124. **[Saʿdī]**, reading the verse together with the verses that follow, draws the contrast the Sūrah is building: the fool is the one who turns away from such a legacy, while Ibrāhīm himself, chosen in this world and righteous in the next, is the model the descendants were commanded to follow.

**Reflection.** The verse offers a criterion rather than an argument: it does not say that turning away from Ibrāhīm's religion is wicked in the first place, but that it is self-inflicted damage — the soul that does it is cheating itself. That is a claim about human nature, and it is the Sūrah's recurring claim: the Abrahamic religion, in its essence, is what a sound disposition already acknowledges, so that departing from it requires a man to ignore what he knows about the purpose of his own existence. And the second half of the verse supplies the measure of what is being refused: the honour God gave the man who held to it, in this world and the next.


## 2:131

*"When his Lord said to him, 'Submit!' he said, 'I submit to the Lord of the worlds.'"*

**Meaning.** The verse gives the moment God's choosing of Ibrāhīm was grounded [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** explains the command: God said to him, make your worship purely Mine and humble yourself before Me in obedience — and Ibrāhīm answered his Lord: I have submitted in obedience and made my worship sincere to the owner of all creation and their disposer, to the exclusion of any other. **[Saʿdī]** gives the response its full texture: *aslamtu* spoken in compliance with his Lord, in sincerity, in affirmation of oneness, in love and in turning back to God — so that tawḥīd was his very description; and then, he says, God made that word pass into Ibrāhīm's offspring and enjoined it upon them, and made it a word remaining in his posterity, so that it was inherited among them until it reached Yaʿqūb, who enjoined it upon his sons. **[Jalālayn]** compresses the same: when his Lord said to him, "Submit" — obey God and devote your religion purely to Him — he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds."

**Language and time.** **[Ṭabarī]** ties the *idh* — "when" — to the previous verse's "We chose him in this world": the choosing took place when God said to him, "Submit," and he said, "I submit to the Lord of the worlds." He also notes the shift from direct speech to report of the absent — God says "his Lord said to him" after the passage had been addressing itself — which is ordinary in the Arabs' tongue, as in Khufāf b. Nudbah's line, "I say to him while the spear bends his back: mark Khufāf well, for I am that one." As for when the command came, **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Ṭabarī]** answer: at the time of the star, the moon and the sun (6:74-79), when Ibrāhīm was searching through the heavenly bodies for his Lord and came to the declaration, "I have turned my face to the One who originated the heavens and the earth, ḥanīf, and I am not of the idolaters" — that is the hour in which his Lord said to him, "Submit." Ibn ʿAbbās gives another setting: it was when he came out of the cave. **[Qurṭubī]** adds the lexical point on which the verse's argument rests: *islām* in the Arabs' speech is submission and surrender to the one to whom one submits, and it is used here in its most complete sense — and he takes care with the relation between the two terms: not every *islām* is *īmān*, but every *īmān* is *islām*, since whoever believes in God has surrendered and submitted to Him, while one may submit outwardly for a motive less than faith. **[Study Quran]** reads the command and the answer as the continuation of the message of submission that runs from 2:128 through this verse to Yaʿqūb and his children: submission to God, which is the proper name of the religion of Muḥammad ﷺ, is generalized in the Qurʾān to mean the primordial religion and true religion as such, and a fundamental orientation of the soul toward God that is universal and part of the bequest prophets make to their progeny.

**Reflection.** The verse records one word of command and one word of answer, and between them lies the whole of religion. God asks for submission; Ibrāhīm does not negotiate, argue, or ask what it will cost — he answers with the title of the Lord he is submitting to, the Lord of the worlds, as if to say that submission to the owner of everything is the only reasonable act. **[Saʿdī]**'s observation that this declaration became the family inheritance is the passage's link to everything that follows: the religion of Ibrāhīm is not a private experience but a bequest, and the verses now trace how it was passed down.

## 2:132

*"And Ibrāhīm enjoined it upon his sons — and Yaʿqūb: 'O my sons, God has chosen for you the religion, so do not die except as submitters.'"*

**Meaning.** The verse follows the bequest of the faith down the line of the prophets [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran]. **[Saʿdī]** reads it as the natural sequel to the answer Ibrāhīm gave: God made that word pass into his offspring, and he enjoined it upon them and upon Yaʿqūb, and it was inherited among them until it reached Yaʿqūb, who enjoined it upon his sons — so that the children of Yaʿqūb stand addressed by their own father's charge and are obliged to complete submission and to follow the seal of the prophets. The content of the charge: "God has chosen for you the religion" — He selected it and preferred it for you, out of mercy and kindness — "so stand by it, take on its laws, be dyed with its character, and persist in it, so that death comes to you only while you are on it; for whoever lives on a thing dies on it, and whoever dies on a thing is raised on it." **[Jalālayn]** gives the same sense: Ibrāhīm bequeathed the creed to his sons and Yaʿqūb to his, saying, "O my sons, God has chosen the religion for you, so do not die except as those who submit." **[Ibn Kathīr]** identifies the submitters and the bequest: Ibrāhīm charged his sons — Ismāʿīl and Isḥāq — and Yaʿqūb charged his twelve sons, the tribes; the charge being the very religion which the passage has been expounding, the monotheism of Ibrāhīm from which only a fool turns away. **[Study Quran]** notes simply that this verse continues the message of submission from 2:128 through to Yaʿqūb and his children, and refers to the wider treatment of submission at 3:19, 3:85 and 5:3, and to the essay on sacred history and other religions.

**Language.** *Wa-waṣṣā bihā* — "and he enjoined it" — the pronoun returning to the creed, or to the word *aslamtu*, or to the religion named in what follows; the bequest is the same act in both prophets, with Yaʿqūb joined to Ibrāhīm in the verb [Jalālayn] [Ṭabarī]. **[Ṭabarī]** notes that the verse may also be read with Yaʿqūb as the subject of a second verb, "and Yaʿqūb enjoined" — so that the chain of testament is explicit at every link. The form of the command — "do not die except as submitters" — is worth pausing over, since one cannot choose the moment of death: the sense is that submission must be the settled condition of a life, so that death can find nothing else in the man; and the classical formula **[Saʿdī]** cites is the rationale — one dies on what one lived on, and is raised on what one died on.

**Reflection.** The verse turns a creed into a family ordinance. Ibrāhīm, who answered "I submit" in a single breath, spends his legacy making sure the answer outlives him; Yaʿqūb, at the end of the chain, does the same; and the form the command takes — *do not die except as submitters* — is the most practical sentence in the passage, because it locates the obligation in the whole of life rather than in its final moment. **[Saʿdī]**'s maxim gives the reason: what a man lives on will be what he dies on, and what he dies on is what he will be raised as. It is the same counsel the Prophet ﷺ would later give the community in a single instruction, and the Sūrah's next verses show the children of Yaʿqūb answering it.


## 2:133

*"Or were you witnesses when death came to Yaʿqūb, when he said to his sons, 'What will you worship after me?' They said, 'We shall worship your God, and the God of your fathers Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl and Isḥāq — one God; and to Him we submit.'"*

**Meaning.** The Sūrah turns the Jews' own claim back on them with a question about presence [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Jalālayn]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the occasion: when the Jews said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Do you not know that on the day of his death Yaʿqūb charged his sons with Judaism?" the verse came down: *Or were you witnesses when death came to Yaʿqūb?* **[Ṭabarī]** spells out the argument: the *am* is the interrogative of denial — *a-kuntum* — and the sense is, you were not present at that death, so do not impute falsehoods to My prophets and do not claim them for Judaism and Christianity; for I sent my friend Ibrāhīm, and his sons Isḥāq and Ismāʿīl and their seed, with the ḥanīf submission, and that is what they charged their sons with and entrusted to their children after them. Had you been present and heard them, you would have known that they were on other than the religions you have fastened on them. **[Qurṭubī]** adds the grammar and the sense: *shuhadāʾ* is the plural of *shāhid*, one present; "when death came to Yaʿqūb" means its preliminaries and causes — for had death itself come, he could not have spoken; the address is reproachful: did you attend upon Yaʿqūb and learn what he charged his sons, so that you claim to speak from knowledge? You did not attend; rather you are inventing. The first *idh* is governed by the sense of witnessing, and the second *idh* stands in apposition to it. And on the deliberate choice of "what will you worship" rather than "whom": he wanted to test them, and "what" serves that purpose — though the reply named the One worshipped.

**The answer.** "We shall worship your God and the God of your fathers — Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl and Isḥāq — one God, and to Him we submit" [Jalālayn] [Saʿdī]. **[Jalālayn]** notes that Ismāʿīl is counted among the fathers, since the uncle holds the rank of a father and he was the ancestor of the Prophet ﷺ; and that "one God" stands as an apposition to "your God," so that the sentence is a declaration of pure tawḥīd. **[Saʿdī]** draws the lesson from the form of their answer: they joined tawḥīd to action, saying "and to Him we submit" — belief not left as a statement about God's oneness but carried into their own submission. And he makes the point the verse is arguing: it is obvious these Jews were not present at Yaʿqūb's death, since they did not yet exist; and since they were not present, God has told us what Yaʿqūb actually charged his sons with — the ḥanīf religion, not Judaism.

**Context — the bequest and its lesson.** **[Maʿārif]** sets out why the prophets were so particular about this counsel. Whether one calls it the religion of Ibrāhīm or Islam, it was meant for the whole world; the special mention of Ibrāhīm's and Yaʿqūb's descendants, and their insistence in charging their sons with it, shows that love for one's progeny and solicitude for their well-being is in no way incompatible with the station of prophethood or even of the Friend of God — for Ibrāhīm, who was once willing and happy to sacrifice his son in obedience, on another occasion prayed for his progeny's well-being in both worlds and wished, as he left this world, to bequeath them what was in his eyes the greatest blessing, namely Islam. The difference between the prophets and ordinary men is only in what they think worth transmitting: ordinary men count the goods of this world and wish to leave as much of them as they can, while in the eyes of the prophets and their true followers the only thing that counts is faith and good deeds — one word, Islam — and that is the eternal wealth they strain to pass on. He also derives from this practice a guidance for parents generally: they should be as solicitous for their children's faith as they are for their worldly comfort. **[Ibn Kathīr]** records the ḥadīth that states the unity behind this family history: "We, the prophets, are brothers of different mothers — our religion is one." **[Study Quran]** frames the verse as part of the general Qurʾānic argument that the patriarchs named here cannot be claimed by the People of the Book exclusively and narrowly; rather they were followers of the pure religion of Ibrāhīm, identified with primordial monotheism and therefore also belonging to Islam. It notes that Yaʿqūb's story with his children is told more fully in Sūrah 12, and that he appears in the lists of prophets elsewhere (2:136; 4:163; 12:38), and observes that the word translated "God" in their answer is *ilāh*, the general noun, with the apposition "one God" supplying the affirmation.

**Reflection.** The verse catches the two communities in the act of speaking for the dead. They claim a dying man's testament; the Qurʾān asks whether they were there — and then reports what was said, and it is not Judaism. And the answer they did not hear is the one the Sūrah keeps holding up: a God, named as the God of a family line, confessed as one, and answered by submission. **[Maʿārif]**'s observation completes the scene: this was not a doctrinal lecture but a father's farewell, a man leaving his children the only inheritance he thought worth the leaving.


## 2:134

*"That is a community that has passed away. Theirs is what they earned, and yours is what you earn; and you will not be asked about what they used to do."*

**Meaning.** The verse closes the argument about ancestors with a principle about accountability [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Ṭabarī]** identifies those meant: Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb and their sons — a *ummah*, a generation and company of people, that has passed on its way. He then gives the lexical root of *khalat*: a thing is said to have passed away because it has emptied itself of the world and become solitary, from the Arabs' saying that a man *khalā* when he comes to a place where he has no companion and is alone among people; and the word was applied to the dead in that sense. And the point of the verse is addressed to the Jews and the Christians: stop describing Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb and the Muslims among their children in terms that do not belong to them, and stop fastening the unbelief of Judaism and Christianity on them; they are a community that has gone. To those you have claimed from among My prophets and messengers belongs what they earned; and to you belongs what you earn, and you will not be asked about what they used to do. Each soul has what it has earned and against it what it has acquired: so give up these claims, for claims will not avail you with God; what will avail you is the good deeds you have sent ahead, if you have done and sent them.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** parses the sentence: *tilka* is the subject and *ummah* its predicate, with "has passed away" as an adjective of *ummah* — or, if one prefers, "has passed away" is the predicate and *ummah* an apposition to *tilka*; "theirs is what they earned" begins a new sentence with *mā* in the nominative. And he draws from the phrase a point of theology: the verse establishes that acts and acquisitions are attributed to the servant — though God gave him the power for them, since if the act be good it is by God's grace, and if evil, by His justice — which is the doctrine of the people of the Sunnah; and he sets it against the two extremes: the Jabriyyah, who deny the servant's acquisition and make him like a plant turned about by the winds, and the Qadariyyah and Muʿtazilah, who say the servant creates his own acts. The servant, in the Sunni account, is an acquirer of his deeds, in the sense that power was created for him conjoined with the act, by which he perceives the difference between a movement of choice and, say, a shiver — and it is that capability which is the ground of obligation. **[Study Quran]** notes the verb: *kasaba* can mean to earn, and also to commit or perpetrate, depending on context; and that "you will not be asked" means the later generations bear no responsibility for the actions of those earlier people. It also notes that the statement is repeated at 2:141, framing the intervening passage.

**āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the verse's application in the Prophet's ﷺ own words: "Whoever was slowed by his deeds will not be sped up by his lineage" — and sets beside it the ḥadīth that the prophets are brothers of different mothers whose religion is one. **[Jalālayn]** states the sense exactly: they will not be asked about what you did, just as you will not be asked about what they did — the second clause affirming the first. **[Qurṭubī]** adds the Qurʾānic parallel: no bearer of a burden bears another's burden (6:164; 17:15; 35:18; 39:7; 53:38).

**Reflection.** This is the Sūrah's most economical dismantling of inherited religion, and it is placed like a reframe at both ends of the passage about Ibrāhīm. Descent from the prophets is not a credit balance; the community that is invoked is dead, and what it earned it has taken with it. What remains for the living is their own ledger — which is why the verse ends not with a threat but with an accounting: claims of lineage avail nothing where deeds are what is asked, and the ancestors, whatever their rank, will not be asked about the descendants either. It is the same principle the Sūrah will state at the gate of the new community, and the same one the Prophet ﷺ repeated for his own family: the line that runs to God runs through deeds.


## 2:135

*"And they say, 'Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided.' Say: 'Rather, the creed of Ibrāhīm, ḥanīf — and he was not of the idolaters.'"*

**Meaning.** Each community offers the Muslims its own religion as the price of guidance, and the verse answers with a third option [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Ṭabarī]** sets out the address: the Jews said to Muḥammad ﷺ and his followers, "Be Jews and you will be guided," and the Christians said to them, "Be Christians and you will be guided" — *guided* meaning that you will hit the road of truth. And he reports Ibn ʿAbbās's account of the words that occasioned the verse: ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣūriyā al-Aʿwar said to the Messenger of God ﷺ, "Guidance is nothing but what we are on; so follow us, Muḥammad, and you will be guided" — and the Christians said the like. **[Qurṭubī]** notes that each party was calling to its own religion, and God refuted them with "rather, the creed of Ibrāhīm," explaining the accusative *millata* as governed by an implied verb — "rather, we follow the creed of Ibrāhīm" — or by the dropping of a preposition: "rather, we are guided *by* the creed of Ibrāhīm," which became accusative when the preposition was removed; and he records the reading of al-Aʿraj and Ibn Abī ʿAblah with *millatu* in the nominative, the sense being "rather, the guidance is the creed of Ibrāhīm," or "rather, our religion is Ibrāhīm's religion." **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the same occasion and renders the answer: we have no need of the Judaism or the Christianity you call us to — rather, we follow the religion of Ibrāhīm, ḥanīf, that is, on the straight path, as Muḥammad b. Kaʿb and ʿĪsā b. Jāriyah said; and Abū Qilābah said, "The ḥanīf is what the messengers, from beginning to end, believed in."

**The word ḥanīf.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the lexical ground: it means inclining — from *ḥanafa*, to lean — and Ibrāhīm is called ḥanīf because he inclined to God's religion, which is Islam; whence a crooked-footed man is *aḥnaf*, whose feet lean one toward the other, and the poet describes the chameleon as *ḥanīfan* in the evening because it faces the qiblah, and "turning Christian" at mid-morning because it faces the east, which is the Christians' direction. Others held *ḥanaf* to mean straightness, so that Ibrāhīm's religion was called ḥanīf for its uprightness — and the man with twisted legs was called *aḥnaf* by way of good omen, as the stung man is called *salīm* (sound) and a deadly desert *mafāzah* (a place of escape). **[Study Quran]** gives the word a fuller treatment: in the Qurʾān *ḥanīf* often describes Ibrāhīm (4:125; 6:161; 16:120, 123), and though not specifically linked with any other prophet, its usage is not restricted to him (22:31; 98:5); it is associated with being virtuous and submissive before God, straight, upright and devoutly obedient, and corresponds to the unspoiled primordial nature (*fiṭrah*) given to human beings by God (30:30). In almost all verses the ḥanīf is one who is not an idolater, an unbeliever, or a follower of Judaism or Christianity — the latter two being seen as particularizations of the universal primordial religion which Islam reestablishes. It notes that *ḥanīf* and its plural *ḥunafāʾ* appear in the Qurʾān only in the indefinite accusative, so that they describe a state rather than a party — one who is, or does something, "in the state of being ḥanīf" — denoting pure *tawḥīd* unencumbered by distortion and idolatry, joined to a life of virtue; and that even among the non-Muslim Arabs of the Prophet's time, some of whom were ḥanīfs, the quality was associated with Ibrāhīm, the renunciation of idolatry and a moral life, and was no label for Jews or Christians nor the name of an organized group. It also reports the etymological debate — the word can mean lame or crooked as well as inclining, and its cognates in other Semitic languages carry senses such as hypocrite or heathen — and suggests that a term for one who "inclined away" from a group could acquire the positive sense of one not bound to that group's limitations and errors, so that *ḥanīf* can carry the sense of refusing to be hidebound, parochial or sectarian at the expense of universal truth. It records the exegetical alternatives: pilgrim, follower of Ibrāhīm's practices such as circumcision, or one devoted entirely to God — and al-Ṭabarī's judgement that the word means the straight following of Ibrāhīm's way, and cannot be confined to pilgrims, which would include pagans, or to the circumcised, which would include the Jews.

**Context.** **[Maʿārif]** frames the exchange: the previous verses established that the present form of Ibrāhīm's religion is Islam, and the Jews and Christians, despite their pretension to follow him, did not in fact follow his religion; each of the two groups, instead of accepting Islam, asked the Muslims to accept its own religion in order to find guidance. Each religion was genuine in its own time, but in its present form each had been distorted and abrogated. So God answers through His Prophet, on his own behalf and his followers', that they hold to the religion of Ibrāhīm, who shunned every kind of association, adored nothing but the One God and obeyed no one but Him, and whose religion therefore carried no trace of distortion. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the argument its final turn: the point of the answer is not mere rivalry but the search for common ground — come, let us follow the creed of Ibrāhīm, which all of us agree to be the religion God chose and commanded, and let us leave aside the other creeds about which we differ, since those we can never agree upon, while Ibrāhīm's creed is one on which we can. And the closing clause removes the last objection: "and he was not of the idolaters" — so that neither the polytheists of Arabia nor anyone else can claim him against this reading.

**Reflection.** The verse refuses the terms of the offer: not "which of us is right about Abraham's legacy?" but "what was that legacy?" And the answer is stated in a single word whose meaning is a posture rather than a party — *ḥanīf*: the one who leans away from everything crooked toward the One. **[Study Quran]**'s observation that the term is not a label for any group is the point the Sūrah is making: what the verse recommends is not a third sect but a direction, and the claim that one must join either the Jews or the Christians in order to be guided is answered by a man who belonged to neither and whom both claimed.


## 2:136

*"Say: 'We believe in God, and in what was sent down to us, and in what was sent down to Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb and the Tribes, and in what Mūsā and ʿĪsā were given, and in what the prophets were given from their Lord. We make no distinction among any of them, and to Him we submit.'"*

**Meaning.** The answer to "be Jews or Christians" is a creed, and the Sūrah has the believers recite it [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Jalālayn]. **[Ṭabarī]** supplies the address: say, O believers, to those Jews and Christians who said to you, "Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided" — we have believed in God; and in the Book He sent down to our Prophet ﷺ, the revelation attributed to us because we are its followers and are commanded and forbidden by it; and in what was sent down to Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb and the Tribes — the prophets of Yaʿqūb's line; and in what Mūsā was given, the Torah, and ʿĪsā, the Gospel, and the Books given to all the prophets — affirming and believing that all of it is truth, guidance and light from God, and that all the prophets God named were on truth and guidance, each confirming the other on one path of calling to God's oneness and working in His obedience. And "we make no distinction among any of them": we do not believe in some prophets and disbelieve in others, disowning some while embracing others, as the Jews disowned ʿĪsā and Muḥammad ﷺ while acknowledging the rest, and as the Christians disowned Muḥammad ﷺ while acknowledging the rest — but we bear witness of all of them that they were God's messengers and prophets, sent with truth and guidance. **[Jalālayn]** gives the list in the same order and adds the detail that "the Tribes" are the sons of Yaʿqūb, and that the scrolls — the ten given to Ibrāhīm — are included among what was sent down to him. **[Study Quran]** notes that the Tribes (*asbāṭ*) are the twelve tribes descended from Yaʿqūb's children, mentioned at 7:160, "and We divided them into twelve tribes," the singular *siḅṭ* meaning a grandchild; that the ranking of the prophets is discussed at 2:285, where the Prophet and the believers are likewise enjoined to make no distinction between the messengers; and that the commentators take this verse to invalidate the selective tendency condemned at 2:85 — "do you then believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?" — while the continuity and wholeness of religion is described at 42:13: "He has prescribed for you as religion that with which He enjoined Nūḥ, and that which We revealed to you, and that with which We enjoined Ibrāhīm, Mūsā and ʿĪsā: that you uphold the religion and become not divided in it."

**āthār.** **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Ibn Kathīr]** report from Abū Hurayrah in al-Bukhārī: the People of the Book used to read the Torah in Hebrew and translate it into Arabic for the Muslims, and the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "Do not affirm the People of the Book and do not reject them, but say: we believe in God and what was sent down to us." Al-Suddī's report from Ibn ʿAbbās adds that the Prophet ﷺ most often recited this verse and "we believe in God, and bear witness that we are submitters" [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Qurṭubī]** records Ibn Sīrīn's practice: when it is said to you, "Are you a believer?" say, "We believe in God and in what was sent down to us and what was sent down to Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl and Isḥāq..." — and he notes that most of the Salaf disliked a man's saying "I am a believer in truth," the discussion of which belongs to Sūrat al-Anfāl. He also gives a subtle case put to one of the earlier scholars: a man is asked, "Do you believe in so-and-so as a prophet?" naming someone he does not know — if he says yes, he may be testifying to prophethood for a non-prophet; if he says no, he may be denying a prophet; what should he do? He should say, "If he is a prophet, then I believe in him." The shape of the verse's own creed is the answer to such cases: belief in what God sent, without dividing the messengers.

**Belief.** **[Saʿdī]** observes that this noble verse contains everything that must be believed, and he uses it to explain the relation of the two terms: *īmān* is the heart's full affirmation of these principles, an affirmation that entails the acts of the heart and the limbs — so that, considered this way, *islām* and all good deeds enter into it as its effects; when *īmān* is used alone, it includes what has been mentioned, and when *islām* is used alone it includes *īmān*; but when the two are joined, *īmān* names what is in the heart of affirmation, and *islām* names the outward deeds — as is also the case when *īmān* is joined to good works. And on "say": the word means to say it with your tongues while your hearts agree with it, for that is the complete saying upon which reward follows — just as speech with the tongue and no belief in the heart is hypocrisy and unbelief, so the saying that is empty of the heart's work has little effect and scant benefit, though a servant is rewarded for it if it is good and accompanied by the root of faith; but there is a difference between the bare statement and one joined to the heart's act. He adds that the imperative to "say" also indicates the public proclamation of the creed and the open declaration of it.

**Reflection.** The verse is the community's answer to every invitation to join one of the older parties, and it is not a compromise but a claim of inheritance: we believe in what was sent down to *us*, and in everything sent down to those before us, without dividing the messengers. The two clauses stand together — the whole of revelation accepted, and no prophet disowned — and **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s ḥadīth gives the practical rule the passage yields: presented with the scriptures of others, neither affirm them wholesale nor reject them wholesale, but answer with this creed. What the verse does, finally, is give the Muslims their own place in the history it has been narrating: not newcomers on the margins of Ibrāhīm's family, but the ones who affirm all of its prophets, and submit to the Lord of them all.


## 2:137

*"So if they believe the like of what you believe, they are rightly guided; and if they turn away, they are only in schism — and God will suffice you against them; and He is the Hearing, the Knowing."*

**Meaning.** The verse states the condition of guidance and then the consequence of refusal [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Jalālayn]. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the sense: if the Jews and Christians affirm God, and what was sent down to you, and what was sent down to Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb and the Tribes, and what Mūsā and ʿĪsā were given, and what all the prophets were given from their Lord — if they affirm and acknowledge all of it as you have affirmed it — then they have been granted success and right guidance and have held to the path of truth; and at that point they are of you and you of them, having entered your community by their acknowledgment. He draws from the verse a principle: God thereby showed that He accepts no deed without faith in the matters He has enumerated, as Ibn ʿAbbās put it — God informed us that faith is the trustworthy handhold, that nothing is accepted without it, and that the Garden is forbidden only to the one who abandons it.

**The comparison.** The phrase "the like of what you believe" needed a defence, and **[Ṭabarī]** gives it: an account was transmitted of Ibn ʿAbbās reading "if they believe in *the One* in whom you believe," saying, "Do not say 'the like of what you believe,' for God has no like" — a scruple against making anything comparable to God. Al-Ṭabarī answers that the canonical reading does not carry that sense: what is compared is the act of belief, not the object believed. The likeness falls between the two affirmations, the faith of these and the faith of those — as when one says, "ʿAmr passed by your brother in the way I passed by him," where the likeness is between the two passings and not between the two men. **[Qurṭubī]** agrees: the comparison is between the two faiths, and he notes that the *bāʾ* may be emphatic — "believe with the like of your belief" — and cites the analogy of "there is nothing like Him" (42:11), where the "like" is superfluous in the same way: the sense is that nothing is as He is. And **[Study Quran]** explains why the point matters: "the like of what you believe" cannot mean that the object of belief is literally similar, since nothing can be "like" God; the sense is that the People of the Book should affirm what the Prophet's followers affirm — and the verse may also refer to belief in an undistorted Torah and Gospel, which would be the like of what the Muslims believe in.

**Schism.** "And if they turn away, they are only in schism" [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Study Quran]. **[Ṭabarī]** explains the consequence: if those who said "be Jews or Christians" turn away and do not believe as you believe, and divide between God and His messengers, affirming some and rejecting others, then they are in disobedience, separation and war against God, His Messenger and you — a reading Qatāda endorsed. **[Saʿdī]** unpacks the word: guidance is knowledge of the truth and action by it; its opposite is straying, whether from knowledge or in action after knowledge — and that is the *shiqāq* they fell into when they turned away, for the person in schism is on one side while God and His Messenger are on the other; and schism necessarily entails open hostility and the kind of enmity that pursues the Messenger with whatever harm its owners can inflict. Hence God's promise to His Prophet that He would suffice him against them. **[Study Quran]** notes that *shiqāq* — which also occurs at 2:176, 22:53, 38:2 and 41:52 — carries the sense of fracture and separation and connotes opposition and hostility. **[Jalālayn]** records how the promise was kept in history: God sufficed him against them by the killing of Qurayẓah, the expulsion of al-Naḍīr and the exaction of the *jizyah* from them. And on "God will suffice you" — *kafā* meaning to be enough, to meet the need, to serve the purpose — **[Study Quran]** observes that the Qurʾān speaks of God's sufficing in many ways: as Reckoner (4:6), Protector (4:45), Knower (4:70), Witness (4:79), Guardian (4:81) and in battle (33:25); that a man's own soul may suffice as a reckoner (17:14); and that Hell itself suffices as a blazing flame (4:55) — with the related *ḥasb* in "God suffices us" (3:173).

**Belief — what this verse defines.** **[Maʿārif]** makes a large claim for the verse: from the beginning of the Sūrah to this point, its verses have been explaining the nature and essence of faith, sometimes succinctly, sometimes in detail; 2:137 defines it in a short phrase that is comprehensive enough to contain all possible details. The earlier verses having established that the only valid religion now is Islam, this verse assures the Muslims that the Jews and Christians can find guidance only "if they believe just as you believe" — and the immediate addressees of "you believe" are the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions. Their faith is thereby set before us as the model, and the verse becomes a divine command laying down the fundamental principle: the only faith acceptable to God is the one adopted by the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, and any doctrine deviating from it in the least is neither valid nor acceptable. One must believe in God and His attributes, the angels, the Books, the messengers and their teachings exactly as they did, without adding or subtracting, without advancing one's own interpretations or distorting the authentic meanings, and without assigning to angels or prophets a station higher or lower than the one assigned by the Prophet's word and deed; and one must be sincere and pure in that faith, for the contrary is hypocrisy. **[Saʿdī]** closes the verse on the two names: God will suffice His Messenger against them because He is the Hearer of all voices, in all languages, whatever the needs they express, and the Knower of what lies before them and behind them, of the unseen and the seen.

**Reflection.** The verse turns the earlier invitation around. The Jews and Christians had said, "Be like us and be guided"; the Qurʾān answers that guidance is believing the like of what the believers believe — and the criterion is the community that received the final revelation, not the older parties. What makes the verse startling in its context is its generosity and its severity at once: nothing in the creed is exclusive to the Muslims except the criterion of following the Prophet ﷺ, and yet that criterion is absolute. **[Maʿārif]**'s reading is the practical one: the Prophet's faith and that of his Companions is not a historical curiosity but the standard, and the verse invites every later generation to measure itself against the community that was taught directly rather than against its own preferences.


## 2:138

*"The dye of God — and who is better than God at dyeing? And Him we worship."*

**Meaning.** The creed the community has just recited is given its name, and the name is taken from a practice of the Christians [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. **[Ṭabarī]** explains: *ṣibghah* is the dye of Islam.
