*"For days numbered. So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days; and upon those who can bear it, a ransom of feeding a poor person. And whoever volunteers good, it is better for him; and that you fast is better for you, if you only knew."*

**Meaning.** The obligation is fixed to a small number, and the exceptions are stated at once [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn] [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Ṭabarī]** takes "days numbered" as the object of an implied verb: *kutiba ʿalaykum al-ṣiyām ... an taṣūmū ayyāman maʿdūdāt* — it was written for you that you fast a few counted days, just as one says *aʿjabanī al-ḍarbu Zaydan*. **[Jalālayn]** reads the phrase as the object of *al-ṣiyām* or of an implied *yaṣūmū*, and explains that God specified a small number as a way of facilitating matters for those under the obligation — the days of Ramaḍān, which will be named below. **[Saʿdī]** draws the same lesson: when God mentioned that He had prescribed the fast, He informed them that it is "a few numbered days," few and at the limit of ease; then He eased it further with the concession for the sick and the traveller, for the hardship that ordinarily attends them, and commanded the make-up in other days when illness has gone and travel ended and rest obtained. **[Ibn Kathīr]** too: God stated that the fast is for a fixed number of days, so that it would not be hard on the hearts and thereby weaken their resolve and their endurance.

**Context: how the fast was imposed.** **[Ṭabarī]** collects the reports on the stages through which the obligation passed, and they are the key to the whole passage. ʿAṭāʾ said: three days of every month were prescribed for them, and the month was not named; that was the fasting of the people before, and then God prescribed Ramaḍān. Ibn ʿAbbās said the same, adding that this was abrogated by what was sent down concerning the fast of Ramaḍān, and that this first fast ran from the night prayer. The fullest report is the ḥadīth of Muʿādh b. Jabal, transmitted by ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī Laylā: that the Messenger of God ﷺ came to Madīnah and fasted ʿĀshūrāʾ and three days of every month; then God sent down the obligation of the month of Ramaḍān, and sent down, "O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you," until "and upon those who can bear it, a ransom of feeding a poor person" — then God laid down a further obligation on the able and healthy resident and eased things for the sick and the traveller, as the next verse says. ʿAlqamah's report, from Ibrāhīm, has the same shape: whoever wished fasted and whoever wished broke his fast and fed half a *ṣāʿ* to a poor man — and then "the month of Ramaḍān ... so whoever among you witnesses the month, let him fast it" abrogated that, and the former verse remained the rule for the old man who cannot fast, who gives half a *ṣāʿ* to a poor man in place of each day. ʿIkrimah and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī report the same sequence. **[Ibn Kathīr]** adds the ḥadīth of ʿĀʾishah: "ʿĀshūrāʾ was a day of fasting; when the obligation of Ramaḍān was revealed, whoever wished fasted and whoever wished did not" — and al-Bukhārī's report from Salamah b. al-Akwaʿ, that when the verse "and upon those who can bear it" came down they had the choice to fast or to feed a poor man for each day, until the following verse abrogated it. **[Study Quran]** notes the same disagreement — some identifying "days numbered" with Ramaḍān itself, others with the pre-Ramaḍān practice — and observes that al-Ṭabarī, among others, holds that those who claim an obligatory fast before Ramaḍān have no firm report for it; three days a month remained and remains a meritorious practice, commonly the thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** works through the verse's five matters. The community is agreed that the sick and the traveller who break the fast must make up the number: "a number of other days" implies the omission *fa-man kāna minkum marīḍan aw musāfiran fa-afṭara fa-l-yaqḍi*, and the *jamhūr* hold that if a town fasted twenty-nine days and a man among them was ill and then recovered, he makes up twenty-nine, not a full month by the calendar — those who said he owes a month's worth of days, like al-Ḥasan b. Ṣāliḥ, are refuted by the wording, which requires the number actually missed. The days need not be consecutive; **[Maʿārif]** spells out that one may make up the tenth day of Ramaḍān before the ninth, and the missed days in any order, since the verse leaves the possibility open. On the question whether in travel it is better to fast or to break the fast, **[Qurṭubī]** reports the schools: Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī held that for one who is strong enough, fasting is better — and the majority position of Mālik and the position of al-Shāfiʿī is that he has the choice — citing Anas, "We travelled with the Prophet ﷺ in Ramaḍān and neither the fasting nor the breaking blamed the other," which Mālik and al-Bukhārī and Muslim all record. ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ and Anas held fasting in travel better for the one able; Abū Ḥanīfah and his companions agreed. Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās held the concession better, and with them Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib, al-Shaʿbī, ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Awzāʿī and Aḥmad, citing "God desires ease for you, and desires not hardship for you" in the next verse. **[Maʿārif]** restricts the ill to one who cannot fast without unbearable hardship or fears the illness will worsen — the following verse's "and He does not want hardship for you" is his warrant — and notes the exactness of the Qurʾānic phrase *ʿalā safarin* rather than *musāfir*: merely leaving home does not create the exemption; the journey must be of a sort that counts, which Abū Ḥanīfah and many jurists fixed by the Prophet's practice and the Companions' usage at what can be covered in three days' walking, later calculated at forty-eight miles; and the state of travelling ends when one resolves to stay fifteen days.

The ransom of the next clause is where the schools divide most sharply. **[Qurṭubī]** reports the classes: those who cannot fast at all — the very old — by consensus break the fast and there is disagreement over whether they owe the ransom; al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad and the people of opinion said they feed a poor person for each day, following Anas, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qays b. al-Sāʾib and Abū Hurayrah and the obvious reading of the verse; Rabīʿah and Mālik said nothing is due of them, though Mālik said that if they fed a poor person for each day he would prefer it. For the pregnant and nursing woman the reports diverge: al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Zuhrī, Rabīʿah, al-Awzāʿī and the people of opinion held that they break the fast and owe no feeding, being like the sick man who breaks and makes up; al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad held they break, feed and make up; Mālik distinguished the pregnant from the nursing woman. **[Jalālayn]** preserves Ibn ʿAbbās's qualification: except for the pregnant woman and the nursing woman who break the fast out of concern for the child — for these two the verse stands and has not been abrogated. The measure: **[Qurṭubī]** gives Mālik's *mudd* by the Prophet's *mudd* for each day broken; Abū Ḥanīfah's a *ṣāʿ* of dates or half a *ṣāʿ* of wheat; the report from Ibn ʿAbbās of half a *ṣāʿ* of wheat; Abū Hurayrah's *mudd* of wheat for the aged who cannot fast; and the practice of Anas b. Mālik, who in his old age, weak from fasting for a year, prepared a dish of food and called thirty poor men and fed them. **[Saʿdī]** resolves the apparent abrogation in the way most commentators do: at the outset of the obligation, because the people were unaccustomed to fasting and the obligation was strict, the Wise Lord graduated them by the easiest road, giving the one who could fast the choice between fasting, which is better, and feeding — as the verse says, "and that you fast is better for you"; afterwards, fasting was made binding on the one who can, while the one who cannot breaks and makes up in other days. But he adds, and calls it the correct position, that "those who can bear it" may also mean those who carry it with a hardship they cannot sustain, such as the very old man: for such a one, feeding a poor person for each day. **[Ibn Kathīr]** adds the reading of the Companions' practice: ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd and others said it means those who find it difficult; and "whoever volunteers good" means whoever fed an extra poor person, following Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss, "another poor man."

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the readings of *yuṭīqūnahu*: the majority with kasrah on the *ṭāʾ* and the *yāʾ* silent, from *yuṭawwiqūnahu*, the vowel moved forward and the *wāw* turned to *yāʾ*; Ḥumayd read it according to the origin; the well-known reading of Ibn ʿAbbās *yuṭawwaqūnahu* with the *ṭāʾ* open and the *wāw* doubled, meaning "they are charged with it"; and from Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿĀʾishah and Ṭāwūs and ʿAmr b. Dīnār *yaṭṭawwaqūnahu*, which is sound Arabic since it comes from *yataṭawwaqūnahu* but is a reading of explanation, not of the Qurʾān. A reading *yaṭīqūnahu* with *yāʾ* after the *ṭāʾ* he calls void and impossible, since the verb derives from *al-ṭawq* and the *wāw* is indispensable — Abū Bakr al-Anbārī supporting the point with Abū Dhuʾayb's verse, "it was said, bear above your collar, for she is loaded." On the amount, the Medinans and Syrians read *fidyatu ṭaʿām* in the construct and *masākīn* in the plural, while Ibn ʿAbbās's reading, which the Kūfans followed and Abū ʿUbayd preferred, is *fidyatun ṭaʿāmu miskīn* in the singular — and Abū ʿUbayd's argument is exact: the singular makes clear the ruling for each day, one poor man per day, whereas the plural leaves the number of the poor unknown; the one can stand for the many, but the many cannot be reduced to one.

**Reflection.** The passage reads as a lesson in how revelation legislated by stages. **[Saʿdī]**'s summary is the whole of it: the Lord, Wise as He is, graduated His servants by the easiest road, then settled the obligation where strength allows; and the abiding rule, agreed upon by the community, is the ransom of the very old and the permanently ill, who cannot hope to recover. What the verse leaves the believer is a choice framed by a promise — "that you fast is better for you, if you only knew" — and a mercy framed by a limit, since the concession is not a licence to abandon the fast but a deferral of it: the days must be paid back, in other days, by the number.


## 2:185

*"The month of Ramadan, in which the Qur'an was sent down — a guidance for mankind, and clear proofs of the guidance and the Criterion. So whoever among you witnesses the month, let him fast it; and whoever is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days. God desires ease for you, and He does not desire hardship for you. So that you may complete the number, and that you may magnify God for having guided you, and haply you may give thanks."*

**Meaning.** The vague "days numbered" of the previous verse is now named, and the reason for the month's honour is stated [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif]. **[Ibn Kathīr]**: God praised the month of Ramaḍān above the other months by choosing it for the sending down of the Glorious Qurʾān, as He did for all the divine books revealed to the prophets; and the revelation is described in three ascending degrees — *hudan li-l-nās*, guidance for the hearts of those who believe and adhere to its commands; *bayyināt min al-hudā*, clear and unambiguous signs and unequivocal proofs for those who understand them, testifying to the truth of the Qurʾān and to the straight path against misguidance; and *al-furqān*, the distinction between truth and falsehood, lawful and prohibited. **[Jalālayn]** adds the three ages of the revelation's descent: the Qurʾān was sent down from the Preserved Tablet to the earthly heaven on the Night of Ordainment, then brought down to the Prophet piece by piece; and it reads *hudan* as a circumstantial qualifier — "guiding away from error." **[Saʿdī]** takes the whole verse as a declaration of favour: the month in which God gave them the Qurʾān, containing guidance for their religious and worldly interests, the clearest exposition of the truth, and the distinction between right and wrong, guidance and misguidance, the people of happiness and the people of ruin — such a month is fit to be a season of worship in which the fast is prescribed. **[Qurṭubī]**: *al-Qurʾān* is a name for God's speech, in the sense of *al-maqrūʾ*, the thing recited, on the pattern of *al-mashrūb* and *al-maktūb*; the ḥadīth's "do not travel with the Qurʾān to the land of the enemy" means the written copy; the word's root is *qaraʾtu al-shayʾ*, I gathered it; and some, like al-Shāfiʿī, held it a proper name underived, as *al-Tawrāt* and *al-Injīl* — though the sound position is that all are derived.

**The naming of the month.** **[Ṭabarī]** takes *shahr* from *shuhrah*, fame or making evident — one says *shahara sayfahu*, he drew his sword; the month is so named because the crescent makes it known, and *ashharnā* when we enter it. *Ramaḍān*: some of those versed in Arabic held it so named for the intensity of the heat that fell in it, until the young camels were scorched by the burning sand — *ramadat al-fiṣāl* — just as the month of the pilgrimage is named Dhū al-Ḥijjah. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same and adds that the fasters' bellies burn with thirst; that *al-ramḍāʾ* is the intensity of heat, as in the ḥadīth about the prayer of the oft-returning "when the young camels are scorched"; that the plural is *ramaḍānāt* and *armiḍāʾ*; and that some said the month is so called because it scorches sins. He mentions, as **[Ṭabarī]** does, that Mujāhid disliked that a man should say "Ramaḍān" alone, saying, "Perhaps it is a name among the names of God; rather we say as God said: *the month of Ramaḍān*." **[Qurṭubī]** also reports from the historians that the first to fast Ramaḍān was Nūḥ, upon him peace, when he came out of the Ark.

**The descent of the Qurʾān.** **[Ṭabarī]** collects the reports of the two descents. Ibn ʿAbbās, in several transmissions: God sent the Qurʾān down to the lowest heaven on the Night of Ordainment, and whenever He wished to reveal something of it He revealed it — which is the meaning of "We sent it down on the Night of Ordainment"; and in another: the whole Qurʾān was sent down at once on the Night of Ordainment in Ramaḍān to the lowest heaven, and it was from its first to its last twenty years; and again: it was sent down from the highest heaven to the heaven of this world at once, then divided in the years afterward — and Ibn ʿAbbās recited, "I swear by the settings of the stars" (56:75). Al-Shaʿbī said, "It has reached us that the Qurʾān came down all at once to the lowest heaven"; and Ibn Jurayj reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Qurʾān was sent down all together upon Jibrīl on the Night of Ordainment, and nothing of it came down except by command — and in each year of the Night of Ordainment everything of the Qurʾān that would come down that year came down. **[Maʿārif]** frames the same with the ḥadīth of Wathīlah b. al-Asqaʿ in Aḥmad's *Musnad*: the pages of Ibrāhīm were revealed on the first night of Ramaḍān, the Torah on the sixth, the Gospel on the thirteenth, and God revealed the Qurʾān on the twenty-fourth of Ramaḍān — and in Jābir's narration, the Psalms on the twelfth and the Gospel on the eighteenth. He draws the contrast: the earlier books came down in their entirety on their dates, but the Qurʾān was sent from the Preserved Tablet to the lowest heaven all at once in Ramaḍān and then revealed to the Prophet gradually over twenty-three years; and he notes that the ḥadīth places the night on the twenty-fourth, which al-Ḥasan identified with the Night of Power. **[Study Quran]** records the same two-stage account, referring to 85:22 and to the discussion at 97:1–2, and quotes the ḥadīth, "When Ramaḍān comes, the gates of the Garden are opened, and the gates of the Fire are locked, and the satans are fettered."

**Rulings.** "So whoever among you witnesses the month, let him fast it." **[Qurṭubī]** takes *shahida* as *ḥaḍara*, present, with an ellipsis: whoever is present in the city during the month, sane, adult, healthy and resident, let him fast it — a general statement made particular by "whoever is ill or on a journey," and note that "the month" is not the direct object but an adverbial of time. Then he sets out a real disagreement among the Companions: ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib, Ibn ʿAbbās, Suwayd b. Ghafalah and ʿĀʾishah — four of the Companions — with Abū Mijlaz and ʿAbīdah al-Salmānī, held that whoever is present at the month's beginning and resident in his town at its start must complete the fast whether he later travels or stays, and that only one whose Ramaḍān began while he was already travelling may break; the majority of the community held that whoever witnesses the month's beginning and end fasts as long as he is resident, and if he travels he may break. The majority position is the sound one, he says, and the established reports support it: al-Bukhārī titled a chapter in explicit rebuttal of the first view, "Chapter: If one fasts some days of Ramaḍān and then travels," and recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet ﷺ set out for Mecca in Ramaḍān and fasted until he reached al-Kadīd, then broke the fast, and the people broke it with him. On the sighting of the crescent: the ḥadīth in Muslim from Kurayb, whom Umm al-Faḍl sent to Muʿāwiyah in Syria, reports that he saw the crescent on Friday night in Syria and arrived in Madīnah at the month's end; Ibn ʿAbbās asked when they had seen the crescent, and when Kurayb said they saw it on Friday night and people fasted, including Muʿāwiyah, Ibn ʿAbbās said, "But we saw it on Saturday night, and we shall not cease fasting until we complete thirty days or see it," and when Kurayb asked whether Ibn ʿAbbās would not be satisfied with Muʿāwiyah's sighting and fast, he said, "No; thus the Messenger of God ﷺ commanded us." Abū ʿUmar reported consensus that distant lands, like al-Andalus and Khurāsān, do not follow one another's sighting, but each land has its own. On the measure of the fast of a town that fasted twenty-nine days while another fasted thirty by sighting, the Ḥanafīs held one day of make-up is owed, resting on "so that you may complete the number," while the Shāfiʿīs, since horizons may differ, did not. **[Jalālayn]** explains why the concession is repeated here even though given in the previous verse: lest anyone think it abrogated by the comprehensive force of "whoever among you witnesses the month."

**Ease, completion, magnification.** **[Qurṭubī]**'s fourteenth matter draws a creed from the verse: "God desires ease for you" proves that God has will — an eternal will subsistent in Him, additional to His essence, as He knows by knowledge and speaks by speech; that is the way of the people of the Sunnah, against those who deny the attributes. He reports Mujāhid and al-Ḍaḥḥāk: the *ease* is the breaking of the fast in travel and the *hardship* is the fasting in travel; but the face of the wording is generality in all affairs of the religion, as in "He has not laid upon you any hardship in religion" (22:78) and the Prophet's "Make things easy and do not make them difficult." **[Saʿdī]** keeps the two sides distinct: the concession belongs precisely to the sick and the traveller, and it was re-stated so that no one should suppose the concession itself was abrogated; then "so that you may complete the number" guards against the thought that the purpose is met by part of the month, and the completion is closed with magnifying God — the *takbīr* from the sighting of Shawwāl's crescent to the end of the ʿĪd sermon — and with thanks for guidance. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads "so that you may magnify God" as the takbīr itself, the meaning being that you should complete the days and say "God is Greatest" for His having guided you to the completion.

**Reflection.** The verse ties the fast to the Book. The month is not holy because of the abstention, but because in it God spoke — beginning a descent that reached the Prophet over twenty-three years and reaches the reciter still. **[Qurṭubī]**'s insistence that the ease of the religion is the general rule, and **[Saʿdī]**'s insistence that the concession belongs only to those it names, together give the balance the passage wants: mercy is a law and not a laxity, and the completion of the number is part of the worship whose ease was decreed.


## 2:186

*"And when My servants ask you concerning Me — I am near. I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me. So let them respond to Me and believe in Me, that haply they may be rightly guided."*

**Meaning.** In the middle of the laws of fasting comes the only verse in the Qurʾān in which God answers a question about Himself without the imperative "say" [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. **[Saʿdī]** opens his comment by naming it a response to a question: some of the Prophet's Companions asked, "O Messenger of God, is our Lord near, that we may whisper to Him, or far, that we should call out to Him?" — and there came down, "And when My servants ask you concerning Me, I am near." God is the Watcher, the Witness, who surveys the secret and what is yet more hidden, who knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal; and He is near to the one who calls on Him with an answer, which is why the verse continues, "I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me." **[Ibn Kathīr]** renders the parenthetical sense: "I am indeed near to them by My knowledge; I respond to the invocations of the supplicant when he calls on Me — without any mediator or intercessor." **[Qurṭubī]** frames the verse's first matter as a correction of a misconception: if they ask you about the Worshipped, tell them He is near, rewarding obedience, answering the one who calls, knowing what the servant does of fasting, prayer and the rest. **[Jalālayn]** says the answer came before they asked — "I am near to them in My knowledge" — and reads "so let them respond to Me" as "let them answer My call to obedience, and let them persevere in faith in Me, that they may be guided aright."

**Stories and occasions.** The reports differ, and each shows a different question [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives four: Muqātil said the verse came down concerning ʿUmar, who had gone in to his wife after the night prayer and regretted it and wept and came to the Prophet ﷺ — this before the concession was revealed, so the verse came down in acceptance of repentance and the abrogation of that rule; another report ties it to those who, when the first rule obliged them to give up food after sleeping, ate and then regretted it. Al-Kalbī, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, has the Jews say, "How does our Lord hear our supplication when you claim that between us and the heaven is five hundred years' distance and the thickness of every heaven the like?" — and the verse came down. And al-Ḥasan gives the question of the people: "Is our Lord near, that we may whisper to Him, or far, that we may call out to Him?" **[Ṭabarī]**'s reports are of the same family: the report of the man who asked, "Is our Lord near so that we may converse with Him in secret, or far so that we should call Him loudly?"; ʿAṭāʾ's report that the people asked, "If only we knew at what hour we should call on Him!"; and another, from Mujāhid, that when "Call on Me, and I will answer you" came down the people said, "Where shall we call on Him?" — and the answer came, "I am near." **[Study Quran]** adds the report of the Bedouin who asked whether the Lord was near enough to whisper to or far enough to shout to, and the report of the Prophet rebuking Companions who raised their voices in prayer on a journey: "You are calling One who is neither deaf nor absent, but are calling One who is Hearing, Near."

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** records the ḥadīth of Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī in Aḥmad, and in the two Ṣaḥīḥs: during a battle the Companions used to raise their voices in takbīr as they climbed and descended, and the Prophet ﷺ came by them and said, "O people, be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling one deaf or absent; you are calling One who is Hearing, Seeing. He whom you call is nearer to one of you than the neck of his mount. O ʿAbdullāh b. Qays, shall I teach you a word that is one of the treasures of the Garden? *Lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Llāh* — there is no might nor strength except in God." And from Anas, in Aḥmad: "God the Exalted says, 'I am as My servant thinks of Me, and I am with him whenever he calls on Me.'" And from Abū Saʿīd: "There is no Muslim who calls on God with a supplication containing no sin and no severing of kinship but that God gives him one of three things: either He hastens his answer for him in this world, or He stores it up for him in the Hereafter, or He turns away from him an evil the like of it." They said, "Then we shall supplicate much" — and he said, "God is more than that." **[Ṭabarī]** adds al-Suddī's gloss: no believing servant calls on God but He answers him — if what he asks for is his provision in this world, God gives it to him; if it is not, He stores it for him to the Day of Resurrection and averts from him a harm by it — and the report that God gave no one supplication and withheld the answer, "for God says, Call on Me, and I will answer you." **[Maʿārif]**, following Ibn Kathīr, notes the placing of the verse in the middle of the fasting verses: it hints that supplication at the breaking of the fast is answered — the Prophet's "The fasting man has a supplication that will be answered at his ifṭār" — and that ʿAbdullāh b. ʿUmar used to gather his family around him at the time of ifṭār and supplicate.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** draws out the doctrine of supplication. The verse's "so let them respond to Me, and believe in Me" carries the condition on the human side — readiness to obey and faith — and it is this that distinguishes the promise: "Call on Me, and I will answer" has no such condition, like "and give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds," while the pledge here is bound with obedience. As for the servant who calls and is not answered, the answer of truth in "I answer" and "I will answer" does not simply entail a response for every caller in every detail or every request: God also says, "Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret; surely He loves not the transgressors" (7:55) — and every one who persists in a major sin knowingly or unknowingly is of the transgressors, whom God has told us He does not love; how then should He answer him? Some of the learned said the answer is given "if He wills," as in "He removes what you call upon, if He wills" (6:41), so that the unrestricted texts are read with the restricted. **[Saʿdī]** classifies what is asked: supplication is of two kinds — the call of worship and the call of need — and nearness is of two kinds: a nearness by knowledge to all creation, and a nearness to His worshippers and those who call on Him by answer, help and success. Whoever calls on his Lord with a present heart and a lawful call, with nothing to prevent the answer such as unlawfully acquired food, has God's promise — especially if he brings the means of answer, which are responding to God's command and believing in Him; and for that reason the verse joins the two: "so let them respond to Me and believe in Me" — that is, that there may come to them right guidance of faith and good deeds, and delusion depart from them. **[Maʿārif]**'s practical ruling is that the verse's "I am near" implies supplication should be made quietly and slowly; raising the voice while calling on God is not desirable, which the occasion of the verse confirms.

**Reflection.** **[Study Quran]** observes that this verse is among the most central and often quoted in the Qurʾān concerning God's nearness and the reciprocity between the servant's call and God's answer, and notes that *duʿāʾ* — prayer, supplication, calling — is spoken of by the Prophet as worship itself. The verse's placement is its own kind of teaching: between the licence for the sick and the completion of the number, God puts nearness, so that the one who must fast and the one excused from it meet in the same open door. And its grammar is a mercy — there is no "say" between the question and the answer, as though the nearness needed no messenger.


## 2:187

*"Made lawful to you, on the night of the fast, is going in to your wives. They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them. God knows that you were betraying yourselves, so He turned toward you and pardoned you. So now lie with them and seek what God has prescribed for you, and eat and drink until the white thread becomes clear to you from the black thread at dawn. Then complete the fast until night. And do not lie with them while you are in retreat in the mosques. These are God's limits, so do not approach them. Thus does God make clear His signs to people, that haply they may be reverent."*

**Meaning.** The last of the fasting laws, and the longest of them, brings a hard rule to an end [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Jalālayn] [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif]. **[Qurṭubī]** begins from the verb itself: the words "made lawful" imply that the thing had been unlawful and was then abrogated; the Companion's report explains what had been unlawful — that a man who, fasting, fell asleep before eating might not eat that night or the following day until evening, and that those who slept, or who had prayed the ʿishāʾ, might not eat, drink or go in to their wives until the next night. **[Jalālayn]** reads the verse as the abrogation of two things at once: the unlawfulness of intercourse in the early phase of Islam and the unlawfulness of eating and drinking after the night prayer. **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes the verb's generosity: *rafath* means sexual intercourse, following Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid and a long list of the early authorities; and "they are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them" — Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Suddī and Muqātil said it means "your wives are a resort for you and you are a resort for them," the garment standing for the mutual covering and need. **[Maʿārif]** confirms that although the literal sense of *rafath* covers everything a husband says or does in seeking his wife's consent, the community agrees that here it means intercourse.

**Stories and occasions.** Three reports are told of this verse, and they explain the phrase "you were betraying yourselves" [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif] [Study Quran]. **[Qurṭubī]** reports al-Barāʾ's narration in al-Bukhārī: when a man among the Companions was fasting and the time of breaking came and he slept before breaking his fast, he would not eat that night or that day until evening; and Qays b. Ṣirmah al-Anṣārī, who worked in the date palms by day while fasting, came at the time of breaking to his wife and asked whether she had food, and she said no, but she would go and seek some — and his day's labour overcame him, and his eyes closed; she returned, and finding him asleep said, "Woe to you!" and when it was midday he fainted, and the matter was mentioned to the Prophet ﷺ, and this verse came down, and they rejoiced greatly. Al-Bukhārī also reports from al-Barāʾ that Qays's next day's fast under such conditions brought the matter to the Prophet. And Abū Dāwūd's report from Ibn Abī Laylā: ʿUmar came to his wife after the fast and she said, "I have slept," and he thought she was making an excuse and went in to her; the verse came down; ʿUmar's own regret and apology are part of the story. **[Qurṭubī]** adds the further report, mentioned earlier in his comment on 2:186, that ʿUmar had gone in to his wife after the ʿishāʾ prayer and regretted it and wept and came to the Prophet ﷺ, and this verse came down before the concession. As for the two threads, **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the famous report of ʿAdī b. Ḥātim: he took two strings, one black and one white, and kept them under his pillow and looked at them through the night, unable to tell them apart, and in the morning told the Prophet ﷺ, who said, "Your pillow is wide indeed, if the white thread and the black thread are beneath it!" — and in another wording, "Your back of the neck is wide if you see the two threads: no, it is the blackness of the night and the whiteness of the day." Al-Bukhārī also reports from Sahl b. Saʿd that when the verse came down some people tied black and white threads to their legs and ate until they could distinguish them, and "of dawn" was revealed, and it became clear to them what was meant.

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** draws the fruits of the verse: the permission of food, drink and intercourse in all the nights of the fast, whether one has slept or not; the proof that intending nearness to God and the purposes of marriage — offspring, the guarding of chastity, the aims of the contract — belongs to "seeking what God has written for you"; the note that among what God wrote for you is the Night of Power, which falls among the nights of Ramaḍān, so that the delight should not make one lose it; and the inference that if one eats and drinks while genuinely unsure whether dawn has come, there is no harm. From the permission's lasting until dawn he derives three things: the recommendation of the pre-dawn meal, *saḥūr*, and of delaying it; the validity of the fast of one whom dawn finds in a state of major impurity from intercourse before washing; and the virtue of completing the fast until night, that is, sunset. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gathers the traditions of *saḥūr*: "Eat the *saḥūr*, for in the *saḥūr* there is blessing"; "The difference between our fast and the fast of the People of the Book is the eating of *saḥūr*"; "The *saḥūr* is a blessed meal, so do not neglect it, even if one of you takes only a draught of water, for God and His angels pray over those who take the *saḥūr*"; and from Zayd b. Thābit, "We took the *saḥūr* with the Messenger of God ﷺ and then rose for prayer" — the interval being what it takes to recite fifty verses. **[Saʿdī]**'s reading of "do not approach them while you are in retreat in the mosques" gives the passage's last institution: *iʿtikāf* is valid only in a mosque; and **[Qurṭubī]**, whose twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth matters take up the question, reports the schools on which mosques: some restricted it to the three mosques built by prophets — the Sacred Mosque, the Prophet's Mosque and that of Jerusalem, reported from Ḥudhayfah and Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib; some to a mosque where the Friday prayer is held, reported from ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd and others and one of Mālik's two positions; and the majority — al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfah and their companions, holding to the generality of "in the mosques" — made it valid in every mosque with an imām and a muʾadhdhin, and with them Ibn ʿUlayyah, Dāwūd b. ʿAlī, al-Ṭabarī and Ibn al-Mundhir. He reports consensus that *iʿtikāf* is not obligatory, being a supererogatory act of nearness performed by the Prophet ﷺ, his Companions and his wives; that whoever binds himself to it by vow must fulfil it; that entering it is disliked for one feared unable to fulfil its rights; and that its minimum is a day and a night in Mālik's and Abū Ḥanīfah's view, while al-Shāfiʿī said the least is a moment with no upper limit and some of the Ḥanafīs allowed an hour — a position that does not make fasting a condition of it. **[Saʿdī]** ends with the verse's own summary: the limits named are the prohibition of food, drink and intercourse in the fast, the prohibition of breaking the fast without excuse, and the prohibition of intercourse for the one in retreat; and "do not approach them" is more emphatic than "do not do them," because drawing near includes both the forbidden act and the paths that lead to it.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** reports the glosses on *rafath*: Ibn ʿAbbās said, "It is intercourse, but God is generous and alludes"; Mujāhid and Qatādah said the same; al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others agreed. Outside this passage, he notes, *rafath* means obscenity in speech, as in the poet's "from idle talk and the *rafath* of..." — the word migrating from speech to the act it alludes to. He records the variant reading attributed to Ibn Masʿūd, *al-rufūth* for *al-rafath*, and Abū ʿUbayd's report that some read the later clause *wa-ttabiʿū mā kataba Allāhu lakum* — "follow what God has written for you" — where ʿAṭāʾ asked Ibn ʿAbbās which reading he used, and he said, "Whichever you wish; but hold to the first." On "seek what God has written for you," **[Ṭabarī]** gives a list: ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, al-Suddī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Rabīʿ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk — offspring, though Mujāhid adds, "if this one does not bear, then that one"; Ibn Zayd — intercourse itself; others through Ibn ʿAbbās — the Night of Power; and Qatādah — the licence God has written for you, "seek the concession I have written for you." **[Ṭabarī]** decides for seeking what God has decreed, which embraces all the reports without excluding any.

**Reflection.** The verse is the passage's fullest picture of the believer's day in Ramaḍān: a night of lawful pleasure and food, a boundary drawn at the first distinct thread of light, a day of complete restraint until night, and for the one who withdraws into the mosque, an even narrower one. Its gentleness is deliberate — "God knows that you were betraying yourselves, so He turned toward you and pardoned you" — the concession given not merely after the fault but, as **[Jalālayn]** puts it, as a relenting before the servants had even turned. And the closing formula, "these are God's limits, so do not approach them," sets the tone of the whole fasting legislation: the command is not only to avoid the forbidden act but to keep a distance from it, which is **[Saʿdī]**'s reason for saying that the believer is commanded to abandon what is forbidden and every road that leads to it.


## 2:188

*"And do not devour your property among yourselves by falsehood, nor proffer it to the judges that you may devour a portion of people's property in sin, while you know."*

**Meaning.** The fasting laws end with the food that is lawful; this verse turns to the wealth that is not [Maʿārif] [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. **[Maʿārif]** sets the connection explicitly: the previous verses forbade lawful things for a fixed time, and this verse forbids unlawful wealth entirely — the purpose of the fast being to train a man to abstain from what is lawful for him, so that abstaining from what is entirely unlawful should be easier; and he adds a second correspondence: one must take care to break the fast with what is lawful, for whoever endures the rigour of the day and then breaks his fast on the unlawful will find his fast unacceptable with God. **[Ṭabarī]** explains the unusual address: "your property among yourselves" means one of you is not to eat the property of another by falsehood; God thus made the devourer of his brother's wealth like the devourer of his own, because He made the believers brothers — the one who fights his brother is as one who fights himself, and the one who reviles him as one who reviles himself, exactly as the Arabs say "my brother and your brother" while meaning "I and you," as in "do not revile yourselves" and "do not kill yourselves." **[Saʿdī]** gives the reason for the possessive: the Muslim should love for his brother what he loves for himself and respect his brother's property as he respects his own — and because devouring another's property emboldens others to devour his when they are able.

**What counts as devouring by falsehood.** **[Saʿdī]** and **[Qurṭubī]** enumerate. **[Saʿdī]**: since the taking of property is of two sorts, by right and by falsehood, and only the falsehood is forbidden, God restricted the prohibition to it; the verse therefore covers usurpation, theft, and the betrayal of a trust or a loan; and also taking property by a forbidden exchange, such as all the contracts of usury and gambling, for these are property taken without a lawful counter-value; and taking it by cheating in sale, purchase, hire and the like; and withholding the wages of hired workers and taking wages for work whose duty was not performed; and taking payment for acts of worship and nearness that are only valid when intended for God's face; and taking from the alms, the charities, the endowments and the bequests when one has no right to them. **[Qurṭubī]**'s second matter: the address covers the whole community of Muḥammad ﷺ, and into it enter gambling, deceit, usurpation, the denial of rights, and everything that the owner's soul does not give freely — or that the Law has forbidden even if the owner's soul gives freely to it, such as the earnings of the prostitute, the gift of the soothsayer, and the price of wine and swine. He adds a limit: a bad bargain (*ghabn*) in trade does not enter, where the seller knew the reality of what he sold, because such a bargain is in effect a gift — a point he says will be treated in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reports the gloss of Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭalḥah, and the same from Mujāhid, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Suddī, Muqātil and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Zayd b. Aslam: the verse concerns the debtor when there is no evidence of the loan, so he denies it and the case goes before the authorities — though he knows the money is not his and that he is a sinner in consuming what is not lawful for him; and their common counsel is, "Do not dispute when you know that you are being unjust."

**The judges' door.** **[Qurṭubī]**'s first matter gives the occasion: the verse came down concerning ʿAbdān b. Ashwaʿ al-Ḥaḍramī, who claimed the property of Imruʾ al-Qays al-Kindī, and the two disputed before the Prophet ﷺ, and Imruʾ al-Qays denied and was about to take an oath, and the verse came down, and he held back from the oath and yielded to ʿAbdān the judgment over his land and did not dispute with him. But the weightier teaching is the one **[Ibn Kathīr]** draws from the closing words "while you know": the ruling of the authorities does not change the reality of truth. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Umm Salamah reports the Prophet ﷺ as saying, "I am only a human being, and the disputants come to me, and one of you may be more eloquent in his argument than another, so that I judge in his favour. Whoever I judge for by taking the right of a Muslim, that is only a piece of fire; let him carry it or leave it." Hence, Ibn Kathīr says, the ruler's judgment does not make lawful what is in fact prohibited or prohibit what is in fact allowed; it applies to the case as it stands. If the judgment accords with the truth there is no harm; otherwise the judge obtains his reward while the cheater obtains the burden of the sin. **[Study Quran]** adds the same reading — a sincere judge's ruling can never render the forbidden lawful, and judges' decisions are to be respected but are not infallible — and refers to the discussion of justice at 4:135.

**Reflection.** The verse joins two crimes that look different and are one: taking by force or stealth, and taking by process. **[Saʿdī]**'s catalogue shows how wide the first is, and **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s ḥadīth shows how useless the second can be, since a favourable judgment awarded against the truth hands the winner nothing but a piece of the Fire. The words "while you know" carry the whole moral weight: the person addressed is not the confused claimant but the one who has no doubt that the property is another's and seeks the bench's help anyway.


## 2:189

*"They ask you about the new moons. Say: They are appointed times for mankind, and for the pilgrimage. And it is not righteousness that you come to houses from their backs; but righteousness is the one who is reverent. So come to houses by their doors, and fear God, that haply you may prosper."*

**Meaning.** Two questions and one old custom are answered together [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the questioners: Muʿādh said, "O Messenger of God, the Jews come to us and ask us many questions about the new moons — why does the crescent appear thin, then grow until it is straight and round, then wane until it returns as it was?" — and God sent down this verse; and it is also said that a group of the Muslims asked the Prophet ﷺ about the crescent, the cause of its darkening and fullness and its differing from the sun's condition, as reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ and others. **[Ṭabarī]**'s reports are of the same shape: Qatādah said they asked the Prophet of God why these crescents were made, and God sent down, "They are appointed times for mankind"; and al-Rabīʿ's report: "Why were the crescents created?" **[Jalālayn]**'s paraphrase puts the question as the natural puzzle — why the moon should be thin, then full, then wane again, unlike the sun — and the answer as the purpose: the appointed times by which people know the seasons of sowing, trade, waiting periods, fasting, breaking the fast and pilgrimage; for if the crescent always looked the same, none of these could be known.

**The appointed times.** **[Ṭabarī]** collects the applications, and their variety is the point. Qatādah: God made them as times for the Muslims' fasting and their breaking of the fast, for their rites and pilgrimage, for the waiting period of their women and the settling of their debts, among other things — "and God knows best what reforms His creation." Al-Rabīʿ: times for their fasting and breaking, their pilgrimage and rites, the waiting period of their women and the falling due of their debts. **[Qurṭubī]** notes the linguistic point: *ahillah* is the plural of *hilāl*, and it is pluralized though it is in reality one, since its states differ from month to month — and the meaning is the months themselves, the crescent being named for the month in which it appears, as the poet says, "two brothers from Najd, on trust, and the month like a clipping of the fingernail." **[Ibn Kathīr]** adds the ḥadīth reported by ʿAbd al-Razzāq from Ibn ʿUmar: "God made the crescents as appointed times for mankind; so fast when you see it and break the fast when you see it, and if it is obscured to you, count thirty days" — a report al-Ḥākim graded sound though the two Shaykhs did not record it. **[Study Quran]** explains the astronomy beneath the image: the *hilāl* is not the astronomically "new" moon, which is invisible, but the first visible crescent; sighting this crescent begins the lunar month, and the Qurʾān's point is religious rather than astronomical — the moon's phases are the calendar by which the acts of worship are timed.

**Houses from their backs.** The second half of the verse abolishes a jāhiliyyah practice. **[Ibn Kathīr]** records al-Barāʾ's report in al-Bukhārī: in the days of ignorance they used to enter the house from its back when they had assumed the state of *iḥrām*, and God sent down, "And it is not righteousness that you come to houses from their backs"; and Abū Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī's report from al-Barāʾ: the Anṣār used to enter their houses from the back when they returned from a journey. **[Study Quran]**'s summary is that the people of Yathrib would return from a festival and enter their houses from the back, considering this a pious act, and the verse returned the emphasis to reverence over a superstition. **[Maʿārif]** describes the practice in its full absurdity: the people in *iḥrām*, if they needed to enter their houses, would come from the back, boring a hole in the wall for the purpose, since they thought entering by the front door forbidden while in *iḥrām* — and they rated this as righteousness. The correction is as brief as it is complete: the verse does not say the practice is unlawful but that it is not *birr*; the *birr* is the one who is reverent; and since entering by the doors is not forbidden, the question of abstaining does not arise. **[Jalālayn]** spells out the same logic. **[Maʿārif]** also observes the placement: with the abolition of this custom and the clarification that lunar months and days govern the religious obligations, the Sūrah passes from fasting to the rites of the pilgrimage, which the next verses take up. **[Study Quran]** notes, on the verse's second clause, a spiritual reading among later commentators — that the three "houses" of the wayfarer's journey have their doors, the Law with its gates of repentance, obedience and reverence, the Path with sincerity, purification and realization of virtue, and the Reality with concentration, contemplation and knowledge — *(digression)*.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** draws the calendar's practical consequences into his twelve matters, and **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s ḥadīth supplies the rule of worship that follows: the month is established by sighting the crescent; if the sky is overcast, thirty days are completed. **[Maʿārif]**'s summary is that the verse settles that lunar months, not solar dates, govern the timing of religious obligations — fasting and pilgrimage alike. And **[Qurṭubī]**, following Qatādah's list, notes that the calendar serves civil life as much as ritual: the buying and selling of people, the waiting periods of women, and the terms of debts are all read off the same crescent, which is why the answer to a religious question about the moon's shape is given in the language of ordinary human times.

**Reflection.** The verse is a small education in how revelation treats inherited custom: it does not attack the practice of entering by the back door as a sin but reclassifies it as irrelevant, and puts reverence in its place. That is the same logic by which the Sūrah has handled qiblah, abrogation and the food laws — the shell matters far less than the fear of God it claims to serve. And the first half of the verse performs the same correction for the heavens: the moon was not created to be marvelled at or debated, but to mark the times of worship, and its changing face is the reason the calendar works at all.


## 2:190

*"And fight in the way of God those who fight you, and do not transgress; truly God loves not the transgressors."*

**Meaning.** With the rites of pilgrimage the Sūrah turns at last to war, and its first word is a restriction [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif]. **[Qurṭubī]**'s first matter states the community's agreement: fighting was forbidden before the emigration, as the Meccan verses made clear — "Repel with that which is better" (41:34), "Pardon them and overlook" (5:13), "Avoid them with a beautiful avoidance" (73:10), "You are not a warder over them" (88:22) — and when the Prophet ﷺ emigrated to Madīnah he was commanded to fight, and this verse came down, as al-Rabīʿ b. Anas and others said. He reports that Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq held the first verse of fighting to be "Permission is given to those who are fought, because they were wronged" (22:39), but the more widely held view is the first. **[Jalālayn]** gives the occasion: after the Prophet ﷺ was prevented from visiting the House in the year of Ḥudaybiyah, a pact was made that he would return the following year with the disbelievers vacating Mecca for three days; having prepared for the ʿumrah, he and the believers were concerned that Quraysh would not keep the agreement and would start fighting, and the Muslims were averse to fighting while in the state of *iḥrām* in the Sacred Precinct and in the sacred months — and so this verse came down. **[Qurṭubī]** fills in the events: the Prophet ﷺ went out with his Companions toward Mecca for the ʿumrah, and when he halted at al-Ḥudaybiyah — named after a well there — the polytheists barred him from the House, and he stayed a month and made a settlement with them to return that year and come back the next. **[Saʿdī]** places the whole passage: these verses contain the command to fight in God's way, which came after the emigration to Madīnah, when the Muslims had grown strong — after they had first been commanded to hold their hands.

**Whom the verse permits and forbids.** **[Maʿārif]** draws the limiting principle from the wording itself: the command is to fight only those disbelievers who come out to fight against you, which means that others are not to be fought — women, children, the very old, priests and monks devoted to quiet religious pursuits, the physically handicapped, and even the casual labourers who work for the disbelievers and do not go out with them; for those named are not fighters. He adds the jurists' qualification: if a woman, an old man or a religious person does take part in the fighting or help the enemy in any way, then killing them becomes permissible, since they fall under "those who fight you." **[Qurṭubī]** works through the classes: women are not killed, though a woman may have a great part in war — supplying wealth, urging on the fighting, tearing her hair and wailing, shaming those who flee — and some scholars held that such activity permits killing them; but when taken captive, enslavement is more useful than killing, since they submit to Islam quickly, change their religion, and cannot flee to their homelands as men can. Children are not killed because the prohibition of killing offspring is established and because they bear no legal obligation. Monks and priests are not killed and not enslaved; what they live on of their property is left to them — and this holds when they keep apart from the disbelievers, following Abū Bakr's instruction to Yazīd b. Abī Sufyān, "You will find people who claim to have shut themselves up for God; leave them and what they claim to have shut themselves up for." **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's list of what transgression includes: mutilating the dead, stealing from the spoils, killing women, children and old people who take no part in the war, killing priests and the residents of houses of worship, and burning down trees or killing animals without real benefit — and Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Muqātil b. Ḥayyān and others said the same. **[Saʿdī]**'s list matches: the prohibition of transgression covers every kind of excess — killing non-combatants, the women, the insane, the children and the monks, mutilating the slain, killing animals and cutting trees without a benefit returning to the Muslims — and it includes making war on those who have accepted the *jizyah*, which is not permitted once they have paid it.

**Was it abrogated?** **[Ṭabarī]** sets out the two positions. One group of interpreters said this is the first verse revealed about the fighting of the people of idolatry: the Muslims were commanded to fight those of the polytheists who fought them and to hold back from those who held back from them — al-Rabīʿ's report: when it came down the Prophet ﷺ fought those who fought him and held back from those who held back, until "Barāʾah" (Sūrah 9) came down; and Ibn Zayd said plainly, "This has been abrogated," reciting "and fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together" (9:36) and "Barāʾah from God and His Messenger ... so when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them" (9:1–5). Another group said the command stands and is not abrogated: what God forbade as transgression is the killing of women and offspring, and the ruling of that prohibition stands today — so nothing of the verse's ruling is abrogated. The report reflects the debate's reach: ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was written to and asked about the verse, as part of a correspondence that runs in Ṭabarī's book.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** records the Buraydah ḥadīth in Muslim: "Go forth in the way of God and fight those who disbelieve in God. Fight, but do not steal from the spoils, do not break faith, do not mutilate, and do not kill a child or the people of the cloisters." And in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Ibn ʿUmar: a woman was found slain in one of the Prophet's battles, and the Prophet ﷺ forbade the killing of women and children. **[Qurṭubī]** reports Abū Bakr's charge to the army's commanders going to Syria and his ten instructions — not to kill a woman, a child or an aged man, not to cut down a fruit-bearing tree, not to destroy a habitation, not to slaughter a sheep or a camel except for food, not to burn or drown palm plantations, not to commit treachery or act unjustly — the earliest charter of the limits of war in Islam.

**Reflection.** The order of the clause is the argument: fight those who fight you, and do not transgress. **[Maʿārif]**'s inference is the one the jurists drew through the centuries — an army's licence is defined by the acts of its enemy, and non-combatants remain non-combatants until they take up the fight. **[Saʿdī]**'s first observation closes the circle from the other side: the phrase "in the way of God" is a demand for sincerity and a prohibition of fighting in the way of a faction or of one's own anger; fighting among Muslims in a time of strife is not what the verse orders. What remains to be said — the lands from which the believers were driven, the holy sites, the sacred months — the next verses take up.


## 2:191

*"And slay them wherever you come upon them, and expel them from where they expelled you; for strife is worse than slaying. But do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you there. So if they fight you, slay them — such is the recompense of the disbelievers."*

**Meaning.** The permission of 2:190 is given its extent, and its limit [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Jalālayn] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** takes *thaqiftumūhum* from the root's sense of skill and perception: *thaqifa* is to be sharp-witted and quick to perceive, and a man is *thaqfun laqfun* when he is sound in handling the matters he takes up — so "wherever you come upon them" means wherever you find their vital points and are able to kill them; he warns against confusing this with *tathqīf*, which means to straighten. And "expel them from where they expelled you": the address is to the Emigrants, driven from their homes and dwellings in Mecca, and God says to them, expel these who fight you and who expelled you from their dwellings as they expelled you from yours. **[Qurṭubī]** notes that the wording is evidence for the killing of the captive, treated in Sūrat al-Anfāl, and agrees with al-Ṭabarī on the addressees: the address is to the Emigrants and the pronoun is for the disbelievers of Quraysh. **[Jalālayn]** reads "expel them from where they expelled you — that is, Mecca — and this was done after the conquest."

**Strife is worse than slaying.** **[Ṭabarī]** identifies *al-fitnah* here as *al-shirk*, association of others with God, and reminds the reader that the word's root is trial and testing; so the sense is that a believer's being tried in his religion until he turns back from it and becomes an idolater after having been a Muslim is worse for him and more harmful than being killed while standing firm in his religion, holding to it, in the right. That is Mujāhid's gloss: "the believer's apostasy to the idol is worse for him than being killed"; and Qatādah's: it is *al-shirk*. **[Qurṭubī]** distinguishes the glosses: *al-fitnah* which they inflicted on you and by which they sought to turn you back to disbelief is worse than being killed — so, on Mujāhid's reading, killing is lighter upon the believer than the trial; and on another, their *shirk* and their disbelief in Him are greater in guilt and more severe than the killing with which they reproached you. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reports the same list — Abū Mālik, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Rabīʿ — and Abu Malik's paraphrase: what you, the disbelievers, commit is far worse than killing. **[Saʿdī]** draws the legal maxim from it, which he calls well known: one commits the lighter of two harms to repel the greater.

**The Sacred Mosque.** **[Qurṭubī]**'s discussion ties the verse to a concrete event: this is evidence that the verse came down concerning the affair of ʿAmr b. al-Ḥaḍramī, killed by Wāqid b. ʿAbdullāh al-Tamīmī on the last day of Rajab, a sacred month, in the expedition of ʿAbdullāh b. Jaḥsh — the killing that the Quraysh took up as proof that the Muslims had violated the sanctity of the sacred month. **[Jalālayn]**'s reading of the exception is that the Muslims were averse to fighting in the Sacred Precinct, which the verse now neither forbids nor permits in the abstract but conditions: do not fight them near the Sacred Mosque until they fight you there; and if they do, then fight — and it notes the variant reading that drops the *alif* of the verbs so that all three are read as "kill" rather than "fight." **[Saʿdī]** explains the mercy beneath the sentence: the fighting at the Sacred Mosque might be supposed an act of corruption in the sacred land, but corruption by *fitnah* — idolatry and blocking the way to God — is greater in God's sight than the corruption of killing; hence no blame attaches to the Muslims in fighting them there, and this continues until they desist from their disbelief and become Muslim. He observes that God's acceptance of their repentance even after what they did — disbelieving in Him, associating partners with Him in the Sacred Mosque, and barring the Messenger and the believers from it — is among His mercy and generosity to His servants.

**Reflection.** The verse is a hard one, and the tradition did not soften it into something else: it permits pursuit, dispossession in kind, and combat in the sanctity of the Precinct itself when the enemy begins it. But every clause is conditional on the enemy's act. "Those who fight you"; "until they fight you"; "if they fight you." **[Saʿdī]**'s summary is that the fighting was *mudāfaʿah* and *muhājamah* — defence and answering attack — and that its whole justification is that the *fitnah* the Muslims were subjected to, being driven from their homes and their faith, is worse than the killing the war entails. The verse thus answers the scruple of the Ḥudaybiyah year: the believers feared to fight in the sacred place and the sacred month, and the answer is that the greater desecration was already done by those who expelled them.
